true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Duplicate `self.downsize` definition silently discards the original method

Two `def self.downsize` methods are now defined (lines 145-147 and 149-151) with different arities: `downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` and `downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})`. In Ruby, the second definition overwrites the first at load time (Ruby emits a 'method redefined' warning), so the original 4-argument signature becomes permanently unreachable. Any existing caller elsewhere in the codebase that calls `OptimizedImage.downsize(from, to, width, height, opts)` with four positional arguments will now raise an ArgumentError (wrong number of arguments) or silently misinterpret `height` as part of the options hash. This is dead/conflicting code that should be removed/merged rather than left as two definitions.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client-side upload size validation no longer respects per-type site settings

`maxSizeKB` in `validateUploadedFile` was changed from `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']` to a hardcoded `10 * 1024`. This removes the distinction between image and attachment size limits and ignores whatever the admin has actually configured (e.g. `max_image_size_kb`, `max_attachment_size_kb`). As a result, client-side validation can now accept files that the server would reject (if the configured limit is lower than 10MB) or reject files the server would accept (if the configured limit is higher), and the error message shown to users will state an incorrect maximum size relative to the server's actual configuration.

true_positives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Percentage dimension string is invalid for gifsicle-based animated downsizing

`OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", allow_animation: SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails)` passes a percentage string as the resize dimension. When `allow_animation` is true and the file is a GIF, this routes to `downsize_instructions_animated` → `resize_instructions_animated`, which runs `gifsicle --resize-fit 80%`. Gifsicle's `--resize-fit`/`--resize` options require an explicit `WxH` pair and do not accept percentage syntax, so the command will fail. Consequence: animated GIFs larger than `max_image_size_kb` will never actually be downsized (the shell command errors out every iteration), the while loop will exhaust all 5 attempts without reducing the file, and the oversized/animated original will still be uploaded, defeating the stated purpose of the feature for this file type.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

false_positives.candidate:
413 error message now shows a hardcoded size instead of the configured max_image_size_kb

In `displayErrorForUpload`, the 413 (entity too large) handler replaced `Discourse.SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb` with a hardcoded `10 * 1024`. If the site's actual configured `max_image_size_kb` (or webserver/proxy upload limit) differs from 10MB, the error message presented to the user will state the wrong maximum allowed size, which is misleading and inconsistent with the rest of the validation logic.

Downsizing an oversized animated GIF can permanently strip its animation

When `SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails` is false (the typical default), the downsizing call falls back to `downsize_instructions`, whose ImageMagick command reads `#{from}[0]` — i.e. only the first frame of the source. Because this logic is now applied directly to the user's original uploaded file (not just to a generated thumbnail), any animated GIF that exceeds `max_image_size_kb` will be silently converted into a static single-frame image before it is ever stored. This is a destructive, user-visible content change with no warning, caused purely by reusing thumbnail-oriented resize instructions on the original upload.

Hardcoded 10MB cap replaces configurable max_image_size_kb for URL-based uploads

The API URL download limit changed from `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` to a hardcoded `10.megabytes`. This removes admin configurability: sites that configure `max_image_size_kb` smaller than 10MB will now allow larger downloads than intended before any downsizing occurs, and sites that configure it larger than 10MB can no longer fetch URLs beyond 10MB even though their own size policy would otherwise permit it. This also applies uniformly regardless of upload `type` (image vs. attachment), losing any type-specific limit that existed before.

In-place resize uses the same path for input and output

`OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, ...)` uses the identical path for both the source and destination of the external `convert`/`gifsicle` command. Tools that open the output file for writing (truncating it) before fully reading/processing the input (gifsicle in particular, via `--output`) risk truncating or corrupting the source file before processing completes, resulting in a zero-byte or corrupted temp file being uploaded. A safer pattern is to write to a distinct temporary path and then replace the original once the conversion succeeds.

No handling for failed downsize attempts or files still over the limit after 5 tries

The loop `while attempt > 0 && tempfile.size > SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` calls `OptimizedImage.downsize` and decrements `attempt`, but never checks the boolean return value of `downsize` (which is false on shell-command failure) nor reports anything if, after 5 attempts, the file is still larger than `max_image_size_kb`. In both cases (repeated failures, or diminishing returns from 80% scaling not reaching the target), the code proceeds to call `Upload.create_for` with a file that may still exceed the configured size limit or may be corrupted, with no user-facing error or log entry indicating the size restriction was not honored.

No tests added for new image auto-downsizing behavior

This PR introduces non-trivial new logic (a bounded retry loop invoking external image-processing commands on the original uploaded file, with different code paths for animated vs. static images) but includes no new or updated specs covering it. Given the identified risks (gifsicle percentage argument failure, animation stripped from GIFs, in-place file corruption potential, and the changed `OptimizedImage.downsize` method signature), the lack of test coverage leaves these regressions and edge cases unverified before merge.

true_positives.golden_comment: The EmbeddableHost model's before_validation callback calls self.host.sub! to strip http://, https://, and path segments, but if self.host is nil, this raises NoMethodError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
before_validation crashes with NoMethodError when host is nil/blank

The `before_validation` callback unconditionally calls `self.host.sub!(...)` twice. If `host` is nil (e.g. the `embeddable_host` param is missing or explicitly blank when creating/updating a host via the admin controller, which assigns `host.host = params[:embeddable_host][:host]` directly), `nil.sub!` raises NoMethodError before the format validation ever runs, turning what should be a normal validation failure into an unhandled 500 error.

true_positives.golden_comment: The update and destroy methods in Admin::EmbeddableHostsController do not validate the existence of the EmbeddableHost record retrieved by ID. If EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first returns nil (i.e., the host does not exist), attempting to call methods on the nil object (e.g., save_host or destroy) will result in a NoMethodError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
update/destroy raise NoMethodError instead of 404 for unknown id

`update` does `host = EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first; save_host(host)` and `destroy` does `host = EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first; host.destroy`. If no record matches `params[:id]` (e.g. stale client state, double-submission, or a race with another admin deleting the host), `host` is nil and the subsequent `host.host = ...` or `host.destroy` call raises NoMethodError, resulting in an unhandled 500 error instead of a clean 404/error response.

true_positives.golden_comment: record_for_host compares lower(host) = ? but does not normalize the parameter’s case, so mixed‑case referer hosts may fail to match even though comparison intends to be case‑insensitive.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Host lookup is only half case-insensitive, can fail to match

`record_for_host` does `where("lower(host) = ?", host).first`, lower-casing only the database column but not the `host` variable used for comparison (`host = uri.host`, which preserves whatever case the referer/embed URL used, e.g. 'MySite.com'). If the stored host or the inbound host differs only in case, the match fails even though the intent is clearly to be case-insensitive. This can cause legitimate embeds to be rejected with 'invalid referer host'. Existing tests only use all-lowercase hosts, so this gap is not covered.

true_positives.golden_comment: The contents of `category_fabricator.rb` and `embeddable_host_fabricator.rb` have been swapped, resulting in the loss of original category fabricators and potentially causing errors in fabricator usage.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Fabricator file contents were swapped with embeddable_host_fabricator.rb

`category_fabricator.rb` now defines only the `:embeddable_host` fabricator, while the category fabricators (`:category`, `:diff_category`, `:happy_category`, `:private_category`) that used to live here were moved into the newly added `spec/fabricators/embeddable_host_fabricator.rb`. The file names no longer match their contents (the Fabrication gem loads all files regardless of name, so tests still pass, but this is clearly an accidental swap that will confuse anyone looking for category or embeddable_host fabricators by filename) and should be corrected before merge.

true_positives.golden_comment: The SQL query in the `app/controllers/admin/embeddable_hosts_controller.rb` file uses string interpolation (`'#{h}'`) to insert values, which is vulnerable to SQL injection. It should use parameter binding or proper quoting to prevent this security vulnerability.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Migration builds INSERT via unescaped string interpolation

`execute "INSERT INTO embeddable_hosts (host, category_id, created_at, updated_at) VALUES ('#{h}', #{category_id}, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP)"` interpolates the previous `embeddable_hosts` setting value directly into raw SQL without quoting/escaping. If any historical value contains a single quote or other SQL-significant character, the migration will fail with a syntax error (or, in the worst case, execute unintended SQL). `connection.quote(h)` (or a parameterized execute) should be used instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: The migration accesses execute(...)[0]['id'] without checking if the query returned any rows, which causes a crash when no embed_category setting exists. This can lead to a broken feature when attempting to edit category/host relationships.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Migration crashes when embed_category/uncategorized_category_id were never explicitly saved to site_settings

The migration does `category_id = execute("SELECT c.id FROM categories AS c INNER JOIN site_settings AS s ON s.value = c.name WHERE s.name = 'embed_category'")[0]['id'].to_i`. SiteSetting rows are only persisted to the `site_settings` table when an admin explicitly changes a value away from its default; on virtually every installation that never customized `embed_category` (default '') there is no matching row, so the query returns zero rows and `result[0]` is nil. Calling `nil['id']` raises NoMethodError, aborting the migration. The same problem exists for the fallback query at lines 14-16 for `uncategorized_category_id` (default -1, also usually unset). Since both guards are missing (unlike the properly-guarded `embeddable_hosts` query a few lines below), this migration will fail to run on most real databases, blocking deploy of this feature entirely.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Because this migration inserts embeddable_hosts rows with raw SQL, any existing embeddable_hosts values that include http:// or /https:// or path segments won’t go through the EmbeddableHost model’s normalization, so the new host lookup (which compares only the bare host) may fail for migrated data. Consider ensuring that migrated hosts are normalized to the same format as newly created EmbeddableHost records so existing embedding configurations keep working.

false_positives.candidate:
Host format validation rejects many legitimate modern TLDs

`validates_format_of :host, :with => /\A[a-z0-9]+([\-\.]{1}[a-z0-9]+)*\.[a-z]{2,5}(:[0-9]{1,5})?(\/.*)?\Z/i` restricts the TLD portion to 2-5 letters. Many valid gTLDs in use since well before 2015 are longer than 5 characters (e.g. `.company`, `.technology`, `.community`), so hosts using them will be rejected as invalid even though they are perfectly legitimate domains, limiting the usability of this new admin feature.

No uniqueness validation on host allows duplicate records

`EmbeddableHost` has no `validates_uniqueness_of :host` (case-insensitive). The admin UI and controller allow creating multiple `EmbeddableHost` rows with the same host value pointing at different categories; `record_for_host`/`host_allowed?` will silently pick whichever one happens to be returned first by the DB, giving inconsistent/undefined category routing for topic embeds without any error or warning to the admin.

embeddable_hosts resource routes lack matching controller actions

`resources :embeddable_hosts, constraints: AdminConstraint.new` generates the full set of RESTful routes (index, new, show, edit, in addition to create/update/destroy), but `Admin::EmbeddableHostsController` only implements `create`, `update`, and `destroy`. Requests to the unimplemented routes (index/show/new/edit) will raise `AbstractController::ActionNotFound` rather than a clean 404, which is unnecessary attack surface/noise for routes that are never used by the UI; `resources :embeddable_hosts, only: [:create, :update, :destroy]` would be more correct.

find embedded test does not actually exercise the requested id

The 'find embedded' test was changed from `store.find('fruit', 1)` to `store.find('fruit', 2)`, asserting that the result's `colors` are ids `[1, 2]`. However, the `/fruits/:id` pretender route in create-pretender.js.es6 is unchanged and always returns `fruits[0]` (the apple record with color_ids `[1,2]`) regardless of the requested id. Fruit id 2 (banana) actually only has `color_ids: [3]` in the fixture data. The test therefore passes only because the mock server ignores the id parameter, not because the embedded-ids hydration logic was verified against the record it claims to fetch; a real regression in id-based lookups would go undetected by this test.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unsubscribe action crashes when no TopicUser row exists

`tu = TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])` can return nil, e.g. if the logged-in user navigates directly to `/t/:slug/:id/unsubscribe` for a topic they have never visited/been notified about (no TopicUser record has been created for that pair yet). The very next line, `tu.notification_level`, then raises `NoMethodError: undefined method 'notification_level' for nil:NilClass`, producing an unhandled 500 error instead of creating/updating the preference (e.g. via the existing `TopicUser.change` helper, which already handles record creation).

true_positives.golden_comment: Typo in property name: 'stopNotificiationsText' should be 'stopNotificationsText' (missing 'n' in 'Notifications')
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Typo in computed property name stopNotificiationsText

The computed property is misspelled `stopNotificiationsText` (should be `stopNotificationsText`). It still works because the template at app/assets/javascripts/discourse/templates/topic/unsubscribe.hbs references the same misspelled name, but the typo makes the binding hard to discover via search and is a latent trap: fixing the spelling in only one of the two files later will silently break the unsubscribe page's message.

false_positives.candidate:
No automated test coverage for the new unsubscribe feature

The PR introduces a security-sensitive controller action (`TopicsController#unsubscribe`), a new model method (`Topic#unsubscribe_url`), and a breaking change to the `unsubscribe_link` translation contract, but adds no controller or model specs covering: a successful unsubscribe for a `regular`-level user, the downgrade behaviour for `watching`/`tracking` users, the slug-mismatch redirect, or the case where no TopicUser row yet exists. The only spec touched here just adds `unsubscribe_url` to an existing MessageBuilder test's options without asserting that the value is actually rendered into the body/html output, or exercising the case where `add_unsubscribe_link` is true but `unsubscribe_url` is missing.

PR description gives no information about the feature

The PR description is just "Test 2", with no explanation of the new unsubscribe feature's behavior (including the watching/tracking-to-regular downgrade semantics), rationale, or what was tested, despite the change spanning 18 files including routes, mailer templates, and a new user-facing flow. This makes it hard for reviewers and future maintainers to understand intent or verify completeness.

Unsubscribe copy overstates the effect for watching/tracking users

When the user's current notification_level is above `regular` (e.g. `watching` or `tracking`), the action only downgrades them to `regular` rather than muting (lines 107-111), but the user-facing text shown immediately after (`topic.unsubscribe.stop_notifications` in config/locales/client.en.yml: "You will stop receiving notifications for <title>") and the equivalent copy in the email (`unsubscribe_link` in config/locales/server.en.yml) both unconditionally claim all notifications for the topic will stop. A user who was `watching`/`tracking` and is merely downgraded to `regular` can still receive notifications for direct replies/mentions, contradicting what they were told.

Unsubscribe mutates notification state via a GET request with no CSRF protection The `unsubscribe` action calls `tu.save!` to change the user's topic notification level, but it is only reachable via GET (`skip_before_filter :check_xhr, only: [:show, :unsubscribe, :feed]` and `get "t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe"` in config/routes.rb). Rails' CSRF protection does not cover GET requests, so any authenticated user whose browser loads this URL as a side effect (e.g. an `` embedded on another page, a link preview/prefetch by an email client, or a security scanner following links) will have their topic subscription silently changed without consent. State-mutating actions should not be exposed as unprotected GET endpoints.

unsubscribe_link translation now requires unsubscribe_url, risking MissingInterpolationArgument for other callers

The shared `unsubscribe_link` i18n string was changed to require a new `%{unsubscribe_url}` interpolation value. `Email::MessageBuilder#body` and `#html_part` (lib/email/message_builder.rb) call `I18n.t('unsubscribe_link', template_args)` whenever `opts[:add_unsubscribe_link]` is truthy, regardless of whether `unsubscribe_url` was supplied. Only `UserNotifications#send_notification_email` was updated in this PR to pass `unsubscribe_url`; any other existing or future caller of `build_email`/`MessageBuilder` with `add_unsubscribe_link: true` but without `unsubscribe_url` will now raise `I18n::MissingInterpolationArgument` and fail to send, where previously the same call worked fine.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
should_block? mutates and persists match stats as a side effect of validation, causing double counting

`BlockedEmail.should_block?` increments `match_count`, sets `last_match_at`, and saves the record every time it is called. It is invoked from `EmailValidator#validate_each` (lib/validators/email_validator.rb:13), which runs as part of `User` validations. `UsersController#create` (app/controllers/users_controller.rb:168) explicitly calls `user.valid?` before calling `user.save` (line 172), and `save` internally re-runs validations. Because `email_changed?` is true for a brand-new unsaved user both times, validations (and therefore the BlockedEmail side effect) run twice for every single sign-up attempt against a blocked address, so `match_count` is incremented twice (and `last_match_at` recomputed twice) per attempt, corrupting the very statistics this feature is meant to track. The side effect is also persisted outside of the `User` save/transaction (validations run before the AR save transaction begins), so the counters are updated even if the `User` save subsequently fails, or if `valid?` is called anywhere else (forms, specs, console) without ever creating a user.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked email lookup and uniqueness are case-sensitive, allowing the block to be bypassed by case variation

`BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` and the `validates :email, presence: true, uniqueness: true` on line 5 do no case normalization. Elsewhere in the app, email comparisons are explicitly case-normalized (e.g. `UsersController#change_email` uses `Email.downcase`), but `BlockedEmail` does not. As a result, an admin who blocks "Spammer@EXAMPLE.com" will fail to block a sign-up using "spammer@example.com" (or any other casing variant), defeating the purpose of the feature. It also permits multiple rows for the same logical address differing only in case, since the uniqueness check is case-sensitive by default.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

false_positives.candidate:
Domain whitelist/blacklist validation behavior has no test coverage after being moved into EmailValidator

The domain-restriction logic (`email_in_restriction_setting?` plus the whitelist/blacklist branches) was moved out of `User` (previously `email_validator`/`email_in_restriction_setting?`, deleted from app/models/user.rb in this PR) into `lib/validators/email_validator.rb`. The new spec file only covers the new "blocked email" branch via `BlockedEmail.should_block?` and adds no example for `SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist`/`email_domains_blacklist` behavior, so this pre-existing, non-trivial logic is left untested after the refactor. Additionally, any prior spec that exercised the now-removed `User#email_validator`/`User#email_in_restriction_setting?` methods directly would fail since those methods no longer exist on `User`.

Non-atomic match_count increment risks lost updates under concurrent requests

`record.match_count += 1; record.last_match_at = Time.zone.now; record.save` reads the counter into memory and writes it back without any locking or atomic SQL update. If two sign-up attempts for the same blocked email happen concurrently (a realistic scenario for exactly the kind of repeated spam/bot signups this feature targets), both requests can read the same starting value and each save overwrites the other's increment, silently losing hits/undercounting match_count. This should use an atomic update such as `update_counters`, `increment!`, or a raw SQL `match_count = match_count + 1`.

action_type column has no DB default or range validation, relying only on an app-level callback

The `action_type` column is declared `null: false` with no database default, and the only place a default is applied is the `before_validation :set_defaults` callback in app/models/blocked_email.rb (lines 21-23), which only runs through ActiveRecord's validation path. There is also no validation constraining `action_type` to the two defined enum values (`actions[:block]`/`actions[:do_nothing]`). The spec file's own comment ("If we manually load the table with some emails...") suggests bulk/manual loading is an expected use case; such inserts bypassing ActiveRecord callbacks would violate the NOT NULL constraint unless `action_type` is explicitly supplied, and any out-of-range value stored would silently be treated as "do nothing" by `should_block?`'s equality check rather than raising an error.

rejectedEmails default array literal is shared across controller instances and never reset

`rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` assigns a single array object as the default value directly on the controller definition instead of creating a fresh array per instance (e.g. via `init`). In Ember, object/array literals used as defaults this way are shared by reference across every instance created from the same class/mixin definition rather than instantiated per object — a well known Ember pitfall. Because the array is also never cleared anywhere (no reset on modal open/close or `init`), once an email is pushed into `rejectedEmails` it stays rejected for the lifetime of that shared array object. If the "Create Account" controller is ever recreated (e.g. the modal reopened, or in a shared/kiosk browser session), a previously rejected email — even from an unrelated earlier attempt, or one that the server would no longer reject (e.g. an admin unblocked it) — will continue to be permanently flagged invalid client-side with no way to retry short of a full page reload.

true_positives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
postMessage origin check uses substring match instead of exact comparison

`discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1` rejects a message only if `e.origin` cannot be found anywhere inside `discourseUrl`. Because `indexOf` performs a substring search rather than an origin equality check, an attacker-controlled origin that is merely a prefix/substring of the real discourseUrl (e.g. `http://example.co` when discourseUrl is `http://example.com/`) will pass this check and be allowed to send `discourse-resize` messages that control the iframe's height, defeating the intended origin restriction.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Access control relies solely on the client-supplied Referer header

`ensure_embeddable` authorizes embedding purely by comparing `request.referer`'s host to `SiteSetting.embeddable_host`. The Referer header is fully attacker-controlled on non-browser requests (curl, scripts, server-to-server calls), so this check can be trivially bypassed to call `/embed/best`, triggering TopicEmbed/TopicRetriever logic (including outbound HTTP fetches) for arbitrary allowed hosts without ever being embedded on the real site. It also doesn't verify scheme, so http and https referers are treated identically.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
poll_feed assumes every feed item has a non-nil content field

`content = CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` calls `.scrub` directly on `i.content` without checking for nil. Many RSS 2.0 feeds only populate `description` and not a `content`/`content:encoded` element, so SimpleRSS would return nil for `i.content`, causing a NoMethodError that aborts processing of the entire feed for that run (sidekiq_options retry: false means the job silently fails with no retry).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

false_positives.candidate:
Full feed poll executed synchronously and redundantly on every embed cache miss

`perform_retrieve` calls `Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` directly and synchronously (bypassing Jobs.enqueue) whenever feed polling is enabled and the requested embed isn't found. This means every single unmatched embed request re-fetches and re-processes the *entire* configured RSS/Atom feed inline within the RetrieveTopic job, duplicating the work already done by the hourly scheduled PollFeed job. Under load (many simultaneous first-time embed requests), this can cause repeated, expensive network fetches of the whole feed and increases the window for the race condition described in TopicEmbed.import.

No test coverage for referer-host mismatch rejection

The spec covers 'missing embeddable_host' and 'missing referer' failure cases, but never exercises the actual host-mismatch branch of `ensure_embeddable` (`URI(request.referer).host != SiteSetting.embeddable_host`), which is the core security check of the controller. A regression in that comparison (e.g. the substring/case-sensitivity issues noted elsewhere) would not be caught by this test suite.

Outbound fetch of user-controlled embed_url has no scheme/SSRF restriction

`import_remote` calls `open(url).read` (Kernel#open from open-uri) on a URL that ultimately originates from the public, unauthenticated `embed_url` query parameter in EmbedController#best. The only restriction applied upstream (TopicRetriever#invalid_host?) checks that the URI's host matches SiteSetting.embeddable_host, but the scheme, port, and full path are attacker-controlled. This allows triggering server-side requests to arbitrary ports/paths on the configured host (SSRF), and relies on the Kernel#open/open-uri pattern which is also known to execute shell commands if the string begins with a pipe character — a defense-in-depth concern given this value flows from request params through two layers before reaching open().

Pre-existing migration modified to add force: true

This migration (dated 2013-12-23) already existed prior to this PR and is being edited to add `force: true` to `create_table`. Editing an already-committed migration changes its behavior depending on whether an environment has already run it: environments that ran the old version have a table without the force-drop semantics, while fresh environments running the edited version will drop-and-recreate on every migrate (or fail unexpectedly on table already existing in edge cases). The correct approach is a new migration if the table needs to be recreated, to keep migration history reproducible across all environments.

TopicEmbed.import mutates the caller-supplied contents argument

`contents << "\n<hr>..."` mutates the string object passed in by the caller via the `<<` operator rather than creating a new string. This is a surprising side effect for callers that reuse the string afterward, and will raise a FrozenStringError if the caller passes a frozen string literal (e.g. under `# frozen_string_literal: true`), which is increasingly common in Ruby codebases.

Transient 'loading' placeholder response is cached for 1 minute like the final content

`discourse_expires_in 1.minute` is applied unconditionally regardless of whether the controller rendered the real topic view or the transient 'loading' placeholder (which itself auto-reloads client-side after 30 seconds, per app/views/embed/loading.html.erb). If this response is cached by any intermediary (browser cache, CDN), the client-side reload after 30s can be served the same stale cached 'loading' page for up to 60 seconds, delaying display of the actual content well past when it became available.

Unhandled race condition on unique embed_url constraint

`TopicEmbed.import` checks `embed = TopicEmbed.where(embed_url: url).first` and only creates a new TopicEmbed via `create!` if none exists. There's a unique index on embed_url (see db/migrate/20131217174004_create_topic_embeds.rb), but the check-then-create is not atomic. Two concurrent imports for the same URL (e.g. the hourly PollFeed job and a user-triggered RetrieveTopic job, which can itself invoke PollFeed synchronously — see lib/topic_retriever.rb) can both see `embed.blank?` as true and both attempt `TopicEmbed.create!`, causing one to raise an unhandled ActiveRecord error (RecordNotUnique/RecordInvalid) and crash the job instead of gracefully falling back to the update path.

Unsanitized raw HTML from imported content rendered directly in embed view

Posts imported via TopicEmbed.import use cook_method raw_html (see app/models/post.rb Post#cook), which causes Post#cook to simply `return raw` and skip PrettyText's sanitization pipeline entirely. That raw content (scraped via Readability from arbitrary remote URLs, or pulled from an RSS/Atom feed) is then rendered unescaped here with `raw post.cooked`. Any script tags or event handlers present in the source page/feed will execute inside the embed iframe (and via postMessage/window.parent access can potentially reach the embedding site). Since the content source is an external, non-Discourse-controlled URL/feed, this is a stored XSS vector that bypasses the normal content-safety pipeline used for all other posts.

X-Frame-Options value 'ALLOWALL' is not a standard directive

The X-Frame-Options header only defines DENY, SAMEORIGIN and ALLOW-FROM <uri> as valid values. 'ALLOWALL' is not part of the spec; some browsers may ignore the unrecognized value (making the header a no-op) while others could treat it conservatively and block framing, which would silently break the embed feature for some users/browsers. Omitting the header (the real intent here) would be the correct way to allow framing by any origin.

disqus.thor loses category assignment and original thread timestamp without replacement

The `--category`/`-c` method_option and the category-resolution logic were removed entirely, and the topic-creation call was switched from `PostCreator.new(user, title:, raw:, created_at: Date.parse(t[:created_at]), category: category_id)` to `TopicEmbed.import_remote(user, t[:link], title: t[:title])`, which does not accept a category or created_at. This silently drops two previously supported behaviors (assigning an imported thread to a category, and preserving the original Disqus thread's creation date for the topic's first post) with no replacement, which will surprise existing users of this import task.

feed_key method is defined but never used

`feed_key` builds a Redis key intended to track feed modification state (e.g. for conditional GET / Last-Modified caching), but it is never referenced anywhere in poll_feed.rb or elsewhere in the diff. This looks like an incomplete feature: the feed is always fully fetched and fully re-processed on every hourly run with no change-detection short-circuit, which is wasteful for large feeds and puts unnecessary load on the external feed source.

poll_feed's core RSS-processing logic is untested

All tests in this file only verify the guard conditions in `execute` (feed_polling_enabled?, feed_polling_url, embed_by_username) and stub out `poll_feed` itself. The actual `poll_feed` method — RSS/Atom parsing via SimpleRSS, URL fallback logic, and the `CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` call that can raise on nil content — has no test coverage at all, so bugs such as the nil-content crash noted elsewhere would not be caught.

false_positives.candidate:
Fallback behavior is now enabled unconditionally in every environment

Previously `config.i18n.fallbacks = true` was only set in production, profile, and cloud66 production configs; development/test presumably ran without fallbacks. This new initializer enables `I18n::Backend::Fallbacks` and the custom `FallbackLocaleList` for all environments, including test and development. This silently changes behavior so that missing translations in those environments now resolve to the default locale or English instead of raising, which can mask genuine missing-translation bugs during development and in the test suite.

Fallback chain now depends on a DB/cache-backed SiteSetting instead of a static config value

The previous `config.i18n.fallbacks = true` approach relied only on `I18n.default_locale`, a static value available at boot. The new `FallbackLocaleList#[]` calls `SiteSetting.default_locale` on every fallback resolution, which requires the `site_settings` table/cache to be available. If any translation lookup occurs before migrations have run (fresh install, `rake db:migrate`, `assets:precompile` on a new deployment, etc.), this will raise a DB error where translation previously worked fine with the static fallback.

Fallback-locale loading only wired into the controller request cycle

`I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` is only invoked from `ApplicationController#set_locale`. Any code path that sets `I18n.locale` outside of a web request (Sidekiq jobs, mailers rendering in a user's locale, rake tasks, console usage) never calls this method. Because `lib/freedom_patches/translate_accelerator.rb` requires translation files to be explicitly loaded with `I18n.ensure_loaded!`/`load_locale` before lookups work, the fallback locales (site default locale, `:en`) will not be loaded in those contexts, so fallback translations will silently fail to resolve (returning nil/raising `I18n::MissingTranslationData`) even though the feature appears to work for normal page requests.

LRU translation cache is not invalidated when SiteSetting.default_locale changes

The cache key `"#{key}#{config.locale}#{config.backend.object_id}"` only accounts for the requested locale, not the locale a fallback translation actually came from. Since the fallback chain now depends on the mutable `SiteSetting.default_locale` (added in config/initializers/i18n.rb), changing that setting at runtime does not bust already-cached fallback results. Users/admins can keep seeing translations resolved under the old default locale until the 300-entry LRU naturally evicts those keys or the process restarts, producing stale/incorrect localized content.

No tests added for the new fallback behavior

This PR introduces a new `FallbackLocaleList` class, a new `I18n.ensure_loaded!`/`I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` loading path, and changes `ApplicationController#set_locale`, but no spec files were added or updated to verify fallback ordering, lazy-loading of fallback locale files, or interaction with the LRU translation cache. This is user-facing localization behavior and should have test coverage before merging.

It gates the call to `webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context)` both in `authenticate()` (line 115) and in the overridden `challenge(context, error, field)` (line 137); `fillContextForm` populates the WebAuthn challenge/rpId/conditional-UI attributes that enable the browser's passkey autofill UI on the combined username/password form. Before this change, that call ran precisely when `context.getUser() == null` (the normal/first-time login path, with no pre-selected user) — this is the primary use case for discoverable-credential/passkey autofill login, and was explicitly commented as 'setup webauthn data when the user is not already selected'. After the change, the call only fires when a user is already set (the new re-authentication scenario this PR targets), so for every normal fresh login attempt (no pre-selected user) the WebAuthn attributes are never populated and passkeys conditional UI will not be offered — this removes functionality rather than adding the new re-authentication support, and conflicts with existing/updated tests that still expect the webauthn form/autofill to appear for fresh, non-reauthenticated logins (e.g. PasskeysUsernamePasswordFormTest#webauthnLoginWithDiscoverableKey, PasskeysOrganizationAuthenticationTest's non-discoverable-key flow). The fix for re-authentication should be additive to, not a replacement for, the existing null-user case.

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative-offset "advanced" pagination path will raise a Django exception, not work as advertised

In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `enable_advanced_features` is set and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative `start_offset`. Django's `QuerySet.__getitem__` explicitly disallows negative slice bounds and raises `ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported.")` for any negative start/stop. This means the entire "negative offset / bidirectional pagination" feature that this PR is centered on will always throw an unhandled exception (500 error) the moment it is actually exercised, rather than providing the claimed performance benefit. Since a client can control `cursor.offset` via the opaque cursor string (parsed by `Cursor.from_string` without validation), any user granted `enable_advanced_features` (superuser or org member with global access) can trivially trigger this crash.

true_positives.golden_comment: When requests are authenticated with API keys or org auth tokens (which have user_id=None), organization_context.member is None. Line 71 attempts to access organization_context.member.has_global_access without checking if member is None, causing an AttributeError crash when optimized_pagination=true is used, even though the request passed all permission checks with valid org:write scope.

If a non-superuser request reaches this endpoint with `organization_context.member` unset (e.g., certain staff/service-account flows that don't carry an org membership), this line will raise an `AttributeError` and turn into an unhandled 500 error instead of a graceful permission denial.

false_positives.candidate:
Comment added without any corresponding behavior change or validation

A comment claiming "Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios" was added above `self.offset = int(offset)`, but no actual validation or logic changed here — `Cursor` already stored whatever integer offset was given, positive or negative, with no guard. The comment implies this is where negative-offset support was introduced/enabled, which is misleading since no enforcement exists here either before or after this change, and could confuse future maintainers trying to find where negative-offset handling is implemented.

Misleading comment claims Django ORM "properly handles negative slicing automatically"

The comment above the negative-offset branch states that "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" and that the operation "is safe". This is factually incorrect — Django's QuerySet slicing explicitly rejects negative indices with a ValueError. The comment will mislead future maintainers into believing this code path is safe/functional when it is not (see the related bug finding), making debugging harder.

New query parameter bypasses the endpoint's existing validation serializer

`use_optimized = request.GET.get("optimized_pagination") == "true"` reads a raw GET parameter directly instead of going through `AuditLogQueryParamSerializer`, which is used for all other query parameters (`event`, `actor`). This is inconsistent with the endpoint's established validation pattern, is undocumented (the endpoint is marked EXPERIMENTAL but this parameter isn't reflected anywhere), and silently no-ops for any value other than the exact string "true" with no error feedback to the caller.

No tests added for OptimizedCursorPaginator or the new audit-log pagination branch

This PR introduces a new paginator class (`OptimizedCursorPaginator`) with a non-trivial, non-standard code path (negative-offset handling) and wires it into `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint` behind a permission+query-param gate, but no unit or integration tests were added for either the paginator's negative-offset behavior or the endpoint's new `optimized_pagination`/advanced-access branch. Given the bug where negative offsets raise an exception (see related finding), basic tests exercising this path would have caught the problem before merge.

Shared BasePaginator.get_result modified for an audit-log-only feature, with a comment that contradicts the actual behavior

`BasePaginator.get_result` (used by `Paginator`, `DateTimePaginator`, and every other consumer across the codebase, not just the audit log endpoint) was changed to clamp offsets with `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`. The accompanying comment claims this change is meant to "allow negative offsets to enable efficient bidirectional pagination," but the code actually does the opposite — it clamps negative offsets to zero when not `cursor.is_prev`, silently discarding/changing behavior that previously would have surfaced as an error for a negative offset. Modifying this widely-shared base class for the sake of one experimental audit-log feature risks unintended regressions in dozens of unrelated paginated endpoints, and no new tests were added to validate the change against existing paginator behavior.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset branch will raise an exception, not optimize anything

When `enable_advanced_features` is true and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative `start_offset` (and potentially negative `stop`). Django QuerySets explicitly disallow negative slice indices and raise an exception (`AssertionError`/`ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported`) in `QuerySet.__getitem__`. This means the newly-added "advanced" negative-offset pagination path is non-functional and will crash any request that reaches it (e.g. a superuser manually crafting a cursor string with a negative offset), rather than providing the described performance optimization.

true_positives.golden_comment: In BasePaginator.get_result(), when cursor.is_prev is True, it sets start_offset = offset without clamping, allowing negative offset values to be passed to queryset slicing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Shared BasePaginator.get_result silently changed offset-clamping behavior for all paginated endpoints

`start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` modifies `BasePaginator.get_result`, which is the base class used by `Paginator`, `DateTimePaginator`, and other widely-used paginators across the whole codebase, not just the spans-buffer feature this PR is about. Previously, a negative cursor offset (e.g. from a tampered/corrupted cursor string) would fail loudly via Django's queryset slicing restriction; now it is silently clamped to 0 for forward cursors, changing pagination semantics without any accompanying tests or documentation of the new contract, and leaving the `is_prev` branch still able to pass a negative offset straight into queryset slicing (same crash risk as before, just for a different code path).

true_positives.golden_comment: Accessing .has_global_access on organization_context.member can raise an AttributeError when organization_context is None, particularly for non-superuser non-member users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unconditional access to organization_context.member attribute can crash the endpoint

`enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` is evaluated on every GET request to this endpoint, regardless of the `optimized_pagination` query parameter. If the requesting user is not a superuser, `organization_context.member` is accessed; for callers where `member` is `None` (e.g. a non-member caller permitted through some other path) this raises an `AttributeError`. Additionally, `has_global_access` does not appear to be an existing attribute on the organization member RPC model used elsewhere in the codebase, which would make this crash on every non-superuser request to the audit log endpoint, not just when the new optimized-pagination feature is requested. This turns what should be an opt-in feature into a potential 500 error for normal customer use of the audit log API.

false_negatives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key uses floor/ceil on a datetime key (order_by='-datetime'), causing TypeError.

false_positives.candidate:
Misleading comment claims negative-offset support with no corresponding behavior change

The added comment states "Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios... This enables efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions" directly above `self.offset = int(offset)`, which is unchanged code. No validation or new behavior was actually added here; the comment implies a capability that doesn't exist in this file and is misleading to future readers trying to understand where negative-offset support is implemented or guarded.

No test exercises the new insert-time span eviction behavior

The PR's stated purpose is to add eviction during insert for the spans buffer (capping segments at 1000 spans via `zpopmin` in add-buffer.lua), but the only changes to this test file are adding the new required `end_timestamp_precise` field to existing `Span(...)` constructions. No test inserts more than 1000 spans into a single segment to verify that old spans are correctly evicted, that the segment is capped at the expected size, or that the root span survives eviction. The core new behavior introduced by this PR is therefore untested.

No tests added for new OptimizedCursorPaginator class

`OptimizedCursorPaginator` is a substantial new class (~90 lines) with a non-trivial negative-offset code path, but no test file changes accompany it in this PR. Given that the negative-offset branch appears to be broken (see related finding on queryset negative slicing), the absence of any unit test means this bug would not be caught before merging or in CI.

Redirect-depth loop limit reduced 10x with explanatory comment removed

The loop bound for walking the redirect chain was reduced from `0, 10000` to `0, 1000`, and the comment explaining the known correctness limitation ("theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly") was deleted entirely rather than updated. This makes it 10x more likely in practice for deeply-nested span trees to hit the redirect-depth cutoff and be incorrectly merged/split, and removes the only documentation warning maintainers about this risk, with no explanation given for why the limit was lowered.

Removed oversized-segment safety check and metric with no replacement observability

The previous check in `_load_segment_data` that dropped and logged (via `metrics.incr("spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded")` and `logger.error`) segments whose span count exceeded `max_segment_spans` was removed without any replacement. The new insertion-time eviction in `add-buffer.lua` silently trims excess spans via `zpopmin` and does not report whether/how many spans were evicted (the script's return tuple `{redirect_depth, span_key, set_key, has_root_span}` carries no eviction count), so there is no metric or log anywhere indicating that spans are being dropped from an oversized segment. This is a loss of operational visibility into data loss that previously existed.

Unrelated, untested, privilege-gated pagination feature bundled into audit log endpoint

This endpoint now branches into a brand-new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` code path based on a client-supplied `optimized_pagination` query parameter, gated only by `is_superuser`/`has_global_access`. This change is unrelated to the PR's stated purpose (spans buffer eviction), has no new tests covering the branch, and (per the related finding in paginator.py) the underlying negative-offset logic it enables is broken and will raise an exception at runtime. Shipping an untested, privilege-gated alternate code path with vague comments like "this is safe" inside an unrelated PR is risky and should be reviewed/tested on its own, or removed if unintentional.

max_segment_spans parameter is now dead/disconnected from the actual eviction threshold

`SpansBuffer.__init__` still accepts and stores `max_segment_spans: int = 1001`, but nothing in the class uses this value anymore (the only prior usage, in `_load_segment_data`, was removed). The actual span-count cap enforced during insertion is now hardcoded as `1000` inside `add-buffer.lua` and is not derived from or passed through this configuration value. This leaves a misleading, non-functional configuration knob: changing `max_segment_spans` has no effect on behavior, and the real cap (1000) is off-by-one from the stated default (1001) and only discoverable by reading the Lua script.

zpopmin eviction can remove the segment's root span, corrupting flushed output

When a segment's span count exceeds 1000, `redis.call("zpopmin", set_key, span_count - 1000)` evicts the lowest-scored (oldest `end_timestamp_precise`) entries with no protection for the span that is the segment's root (`is_segment_span`). If the root span's end timestamp happens to be lower than one or more of its children's (e.g. due to clock skew or async child spans finishing later), the root span's payload can be evicted from the sorted set while the separate `has_root_span` boolean flag remains true. Later, `flush_segments` in buffer.py determines `is_segment` by comparing `segment_span_id == val["span_id"]` only over the spans actually present in the set; if the root span was evicted, no span in the flushed output will have `is_segment: true`, even though the segment was flushed via the root-span timeout path. This silently produces segments lacking a root span marker, which downstream consumers expecting exactly one root span per segment may not handle correctly.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache key built from hash() of project id tuple risks collisions

The cache key `f"error_upsampling_eligible:{organization.id}:{hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))}"` relies on Python's built-in `hash()` of an integer tuple to disambiguate different project-id sets within the same organization. Hash collisions between distinct tuples are possible (hash() truncates to a fixed-width integer), which could cause one set of projects to incorrectly reuse another set's cached eligibility result for up to 60 seconds, silently enabling or disabling upsampling for the wrong query. A deterministic string key built from the sorted ids directly (e.g. joined by commas) would avoid this risk entirely and is no more expensive.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling eligibility check uses the wrong dataset variable

Inside `_get_event_stats`, the function parameter is named `scoped_dataset` (the dataset actually being queried for this specific call), but the eligibility check calls `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)` using the outer closed-over `dataset` variable from `get()` instead of the local `scoped_dataset` parameter. In the simple path these happen to be equal, but `get_event_stats_factory`'s `fn` calls `_get_event_stats` with different dataset values (e.g. `discover` for the errors-only/transactions-only split queries, or `split_dataset`) when handling dashboard-widget discover splitting. In those calls, the upsampling decision is computed against the wrong dataset, so the `count()`→`upsampled_count()` transform can be incorrectly applied or skipped for the dataset that is actually executed, producing inconsistent/incorrect counts for dashboard widgets using the discover-split code path.

false_positives.candidate:
Misleading/contradictory docstring about cache freshness

The docstring of `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` states the function 'reads the allowlist configuration fresh each time... This is intentional to ensure we always have the latest configuration state.' In reality, its caller `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` wraps this function's result in a 60-second cache, so the configuration is not read fresh on every call — only on cache misses. This contradicts the stated intent and could mislead future maintainers into believing allowlist changes take effect immediately, when in fact they can be delayed up to 60 seconds.

New upsampled_count() function is public, bypassing allowlist gating

The new `upsampled_count` SnQLFunction is registered without `private=True`, unlike other internal-only aggregate functions in the same converter. This means any user can directly type `upsampled_count()` in a Discover/Events query, bypassing the allowlist check in `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects`/`_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` entirely. Depending on how `sample_weight` is populated for non-allowlisted projects (NULL vs default value), this could either return misleading data or raise a SQL error (e.g. converting NULL to a non-nullable Int64), since the function assumes sample_weight is always present 'per our data model requirements' — an assumption the public API doesn't enforce.

No tests for the public cached entry point or cache invalidation

The test file only exercises the private helpers `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, `_is_error_focused_query`, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`, and `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling`. The PR's headline feature — the 60-second caching behavior in `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` (cache hit/miss paths, correct bool-vs-None handling) — and `invalidate_upsampling_cache` are never directly unit tested. Given the PR title explicitly calls out 'performance optimizations' via caching, the caching logic itself (the riskiest new behavior) has no dedicated test coverage.

Stray gitlink/submodule artifact added to the repository

A new top-level entry `sentry-repo` is added that is a gitlink pointing to commit `a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a` (the PR's own base commit), with no corresponding `.gitmodules` entry shown in the diff. This looks like an accidental artifact from a bad rebase/squash or local tooling leftover rather than an intentional change. Committing a dangling gitlink with no submodule registration can confuse `git status`/`git submodule` tooling and CI checkout steps, and should be removed before merge.

Test helper overloads generic 'sample_rate' field and silently swallows all errors

`_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` writes into the generic top-level `normalized_data["sample_rate"]` key whenever `contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate` is present, for any event type processed by `store_event` (not just errors). This repurposes a field name that is also used elsewhere in Sentry for transaction/dynamic sampling semantics, risking ambiguity if both mechanisms ever intersect on the same event. Additionally, both exception-handling blocks use bare `except Exception: pass`, silently discarding malformed `client_sample_rate` values or unexpected `contexts` shapes, which can mask bugs in tests relying on this helper instead of surfacing a clear failure.

Transform only matches exact 'count()' string, silently ignoring aliased forms

`transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` only rewrites a column when its lowercased/stripped value equals exactly `"count()"`. Any other valid representation of the same aggregate — e.g. `"count() as total"`, or `count()` embedded in an equation — is left untouched with no warning or fallback, so the request silently uses the raw (non-upsampled) count. There is no test covering this partial-match limitation, and callers have no way to know the transform was skipped for their specific column form.

invalidate_upsampling_cache is never called anywhere

`invalidate_upsampling_cache` is introduced with a docstring stating it 'should be called when the allowlist configuration changes to ensure cache consistency', but nothing in this PR (or apparently the rest of the codebase) calls it. As written, it is dead code, and the 60-second eligibility cache set in `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` has no actual invalidation path wired to allowlist option changes. This either means the function is unused dead code that should be removed, or an integration point (e.g. an options-changed signal handler) is missing, leaving stale upsampling decisions for up to 60 seconds with no way to force a refresh.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes the get_multi result preserves the input order; dict value order is not guaranteed to match error_ids, so event data can be paired with the wrong ID (missing nodes also shift alignment).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
fetch_error_details misaligns error ids with event data when ids repeat or are missing

`fetch_error_details` builds `node_ids` from `error_ids` (which may contain duplicates, e.g. if the same error occurred multiple times in a replay) and fetches them via `nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)`, then zips `error_ids` with `events.values()`. Because dict keys must be unique, duplicate node ids collapse into a single entry in the `events` dict, making `events.values()` shorter than `error_ids`. `zip()` silently truncates to the shorter sequence, so after the first duplicate (or any backend behavior that omits missing keys rather than returning them with `None`), every subsequent `(event_id, data)` pair is shifted and misattributed to the wrong `error_id`, producing incorrect titles/timestamps/messages in the generated AI summary log. A safer implementation would look up each entry explicitly via `events.get(node_id)` keyed by the corresponding node id rather than relying on positional correspondence between two independently constructed sequences.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup code input has no normalization, but generated codes are lowercase hex only

`crypto.randomBytes(5).toString("hex")` (setup.ts) always produces lowercase hex characters, but the `TextField` used to collect the backup code here has no `autoCapitalize="off"`/lowercasing/trim applied, and the server-side comparison (`backupCodes.indexOf(credentials.backupCode.replaceAll("-", ""))` in next-auth-options.ts and disable.ts) is an exact, case-sensitive string match. true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup code validation/consumption has a check-then-update race (TOCTOU)

The backup-code login path reads `user.backupCodes`, decrypts it, checks `indexOf` for a match, then later re-encrypts and writes back the array with the used code nulled out (lines 139-156). There is no transaction, row lock, or optimistic version check between the read and the write. minimumTokenResponseSchema uses computed property keys `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` intending (per the comment) to allow any numeric property to pass as the expiry and allow other properties through. However, calling `.toString()` on a Zod schema instance does not produce a wildcard matcher — it produces a fixed, identical string literal for both expressions (Zod schemas don't override toString()), so both computed keys collapse onto the same literal key, and the second (optional/unknown) overwrites the first. The resulting schema is effectively just `{ access_token: string }`. Because Zod objects strip unrecognized keys from the parsed result by default, every other field returned by a self-hosted credential-sync endpoint (expiry, refresh_token, etc.) is silently discarded whenever APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set. This defeats the entire purpose of the sync feature: expiry/refresh data never survives the parse.

If more than one credential row matches, `findFirst` picks an arbitrary one and the subsequent `update` will overwrite that record's `key`, potentially corrupting an unrelated, working connection for a different account than the one the self-hoster intended to sync. true_positives.matched_candidate:
Non-atomic retryCount increment can race across concurrent cron invocations

Both the success-path failure branch (line ~184) and the catch block (line ~195) update retryCount by computing `reminder.retryCount + 1` in application code from a value fetched earlier in the same request, rather than using Prisma's atomic `{ increment: 1 }`. If the cron endpoint is invoked more than once concurrently (e.g. duplicate cron triggers, retried HTTP calls, multiple instances), two processes can read the same stale retryCount and write the same incremented value, losing an update. This means a reminder could fail many more than twice yet never reach retryCount > 1, defeating the intended cleanup logic and leaving broken reminders stuck in the scheduling loop indefinitely.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
retryCount deletion branch is not scoped to SMS method

The new OR clause `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` in the deleteMany call has no `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` filter, unlike the sibling condition. The function is documented/intended to operate only on SMS reminders, but as written it will delete ANY WorkflowReminder row (EMAIL, WHATSAPP, SMS) whose retryCount happens to exceed 1, regardless of method. Since `retryCount` is a shared column on the WorkflowReminder model (not SMS-specific), any future code path that increments retryCount for non-SMS reminders (or any data migration/bug that sets retryCount>1) will cause this cron job to silently delete unrelated email/whatsapp reminders. This should be `{ method: WorkflowMethods.SMS, retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` to keep the deletion scoped correctly.

false_positives.candidate:
No tests added for new retry/deletion behavior

This PR introduces a behavioral change (failed SMS reminders are now deleted after two failures) that affects data integrity (permanent deletion of WorkflowReminder rows). No unit/integration tests were added to verify that retryCount increments correctly on failure, that reminders are deleted only after exceeding the retry threshold, or that successful sends are unaffected. Given the destructive nature of the deleteMany query, this logic should have test coverage to prevent regressions (e.g., accidental deletion of valid reminders or failure to ever clean up broken ones).

Stale comment does not describe the new retryCount-based deletion

The comment above the deleteMany call still reads "delete all scheduled sms reminders where scheduled date is past current date", but the query now also deletes any reminder (regardless of method, see related finding) whose retryCount exceeds 1. The comment was not updated to describe this second deletion condition, which will mislead future maintainers reading only the comment about what rows are removed.

Transient errors are treated the same as permanent failures, causing premature deletion of valid reminders

Any error thrown while scheduling the SMS (network blip, Twilio rate limiting/outage, temporary API failure, etc.) increments retryCount exactly the same way as a permanent failure like an invalid phone number. Because the cron runs repeatedly and only allows 2 failures before the reminder is deleted (deleteMany with retryCount > 1), a short period of transient Twilio/network issues across two consecutive cron runs will cause legitimate, otherwise-valid workflow reminders to be permanently deleted before the scheduled date, even though the underlying booking/reminder was fine. There is no distinction between retryable and non-retryable errors, so the fix can silently drop reminders that should have eventually succeeded.

false_positives.candidate:
Caching behavior test coverage removed without replacement

The previous `describe("Caching", ...)` block, which verified that `getAuthorizationConditions()` and `getFilterConditions()` return cached results on repeated calls, has been deleted entirely in this PR and not replaced with an equivalent test using the new `Prisma.Sql` return types. The service still implements `cachedAuthConditions`/`cachedFilterConditions` caching (lines 49-50, 84-95), but after this change there is no test asserting that caching still works correctly (e.g. that a second call doesn't re-run repository/database lookups) with the new SQL-fragment return type.

Constructor's options type no longer enforces required teamId for team scope

The constructor parameter type was changed from the strict discriminated union `InsightsBookingServiceOptions` (where `teamId: number` is required when `scope === "team"`) to the new, looser `InsightsBookingServicePublicOptions`, where `teamId?: number` is optional regardless of scope. Previously, omitting `teamId` for a team-scoped call was a compile-time TypeScript error. Now it compiles fine, and an incorrect call is only caught by the internal Zod validation at runtime, silently falling back to `NOTHING_CONDITION` (i.e., the query returns zero rows) rather than surfacing an explicit error. This can mask integration bugs as 'no data' instead of a clear failure.

PR explicitly admits the rewritten integration tests were never actually run

The PR description states: "I encountered test runner configuration issues, so please verify the tests actually pass" and "The test runner had configuration issues during development, so manual verification of test execution is critical." This means the substantially rewritten authorization/filter-condition test suite for a security-sensitive code path (org/team/user scoping of booking data) was never confirmed to pass before submission. Given the high-risk nature of this change (authorization logic), merging without actually executing `TZ=UTC yarn test packages/lib/server/service/__tests__/insightsBooking.integration-test.ts` risks landing tests that don't actually validate the intended behavior (false confidence) or that fail outright.

PR's own diagram misrepresents insightsBooking.ts as unchanged context

The PR's mermaid diagram classifies `packages/lib/server/service/insightsBooking.ts` as "context" (no-edit, white) while the changed-files table and the actual diff show 73 insertions / 82 deletions to this file, including removal of the `findMany` method and changing the return types of `getAuthorizationConditions`/`getFilterConditions`/`buildAuthorizationConditions` from Prisma object where-clauses to raw `Prisma.Sql` fragments. This mislabeling, combined with the description framing this as purely a test update, could cause reviewers to under-scrutinize a substantial production authorization-logic change.

Public `findMany()` method removed with no visible update to callers

The diff removes the previously-existing `async findMany(findManyArgs: Prisma.BookingTimeStatusDenormalizedFindManyArgs)` method (visible as deleted lines in the diff) and replaces it with `getBaseConditions()`, which only returns the combined SQL `WHERE` fragment instead of performing a query. This PR only touches this service file and its test file; no other files are shown being updated to account for the removal/renaming of this method. If any production code (trpc routers, insights handlers, etc.) still calls `.findMany()` on `InsightsBookingService`, it will fail to compile or throw at runtime after this merges. This is a breaking API change that the PR description frames merely as a 'test update'.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Plain Error thrown instead of TRPCError with proper code

When the credential isn't found or doesn't belong to the user, the handler throws a plain `Error("Credential not found or access denied")` instead of a `TRPCError` with a code like `NOT_FOUND` or `FORBIDDEN`. tRPC will surface this as an `INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR` (HTTP 500), which is misleading for monitoring/alerting and prevents the client from distinguishing an authorization failure from an actual server error, unlike the convention typically used in sibling handlers.
