false_positives.candidate:
Cache deletion does not invalidate connectedCalendars query, leaving stale cache status in UI

The `deleteCacheMutation` only calls `onSuccess?.()` on success, unlike `disconnectMutation` which explicitly invalidates `utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` and `utils.viewer.apps.integrations` in its `onSettled`. If the parent component's `onChanged`/`onSuccess` prop doesn't itself trigger a refetch of the connectedCalendars query (it is optional and may be undefined), the dropdown will continue to show the old `cacheUpdatedAt` timestamp and cache-status UI after the cache has actually been deleted, giving the user incorrect information about cache state.

Directly instantiates CalendarCacheRepository, bypassing the CalendarCache factory/mock abstraction

Elsewhere in the codebase (e.g. GoogleCalendarService) calendar cache access goes through `CalendarCache.init(...)`, which is the abstraction responsible for choosing between the real `CalendarCacheRepository` and the `CalendarCacheRepositoryMock` (presumably gated by license/feature flag, given the mock exists specifically to disable calendar-cache behavior). Here, `new CalendarCacheRepository()` is instantiated directly, bypassing that selection logic. This means cache-status lookups run unconditionally regardless of whether the calendar-cache feature is actually enabled/licensed for the deployment, which is inconsistent with how the rest of the codebase gates this functionality.

No automated tests for the new deleteCache mutation, cache-status repository method, or UI dropdown

This PR introduces a new tRPC mutation (`deleteCache`), a new repository method (`getCacheStatusByCredentialIds`), and a new UI component (`CredentialActionsDropdown`) that handles destructive actions (cache deletion, app disconnection) behind confirmation dialogs, but no unit, integration, or e2e tests were added for any of this logic. The PR's own review checklist acknowledges testing was manual-only and limited due to lack of a connected Google Calendar integration, leaving the deletion authorization logic, cache-status mapping, and dropdown rendering conditions unverified by CI.

Ownership check excludes team/organization-owned credentials

The authorization check `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { id: credentialId, userId: user.id } })` only matches credentials with a direct `userId`. Team- or organization-managed Google Calendar credentials (where `userId` may be null and access is granted via team membership) will fail this check and the user will be unable to delete cache for those credentials even if they are legitimately authorized to manage them, despite the feature targeting calendar integrations broadly.

dev:cron now relies on npx tsx without adding tsx as a dependency

The `dev:cron` script was changed from `ts-node cron-tester.ts` (using the already-declared `ts-node` devDependency) to `npx tsx cron-tester.ts`, but `tsx` is not added to `devDependencies`. Using `npx` will attempt to fetch the package from the npm registry at invocation time (or use a globally cached version), which can produce version drift across environments and fails in network-restricted/offline CI or dev setups, unlike the project's convention of relying on locked workspace dependencies via yarn.

getCacheStatusByCredentialIds ignores cache expiry, showing stale timestamps as if cache is active

`getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` groups by `credentialId` and returns `_max(updatedAt)` without filtering on `expiresAt >= now()`. As a result, a credential whose cache rows have long expired will still report a 'last updated' timestamp, and the UI (CredentialActionsDropdown) will present it as current cache status. This misleads users into believing cached data is still being served when in fact the next read will be a cache miss and hit the live API.

updateManyByCredentialId incorrectly bumps updatedAt for all selected calendars of the credential, not just the ones actually refreshed

`fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache` operates on the `selectedCalendars` parameter it is given (which can be a subset of all selected calendars for a credential, e.g. the `remainingCalendars` passed in from `unwatchCalendar`). After updating the cache only for that subset, it calls `SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})`, which updates the `updatedAt` field for *every* SelectedCalendar row tied to that credential, including ones that were not part of the `selectedCalendars` argument and were not actually refreshed in this call. This causes `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt` to misrepresent when a specific calendar's data was last cached, which is a data integrity issue even though the field isn't yet surfaced in the frontend (the PR author's own notes flag uncertainty about whether this update is needed at all).

true_positives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Immediate cancellation path never deletes or updates the WorkflowReminder DB row

In `deleteScheduledEmailReminder`, when `immediateDelete` is true, the function calls SendGrid to cancel the scheduled send and then simply `return`s — it never deletes the WorkflowReminder row nor sets `cancelled: true`. This leaves a stale row in the database that still looks 'scheduled' (scheduled=true, cancelled=null/false) even though the underlying email was cancelled. The row only gets cleaned up later by the unrelated generic cleanup in scheduleEmailReminders.ts (`deleteMany` where `scheduledDate <= now`), once its original scheduledDate passes, potentially leaving inconsistent/stale state in the table for a long time and making this data unreliable for any other logic or UI that inspects WorkflowReminder rows in the meantime.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.

The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

false_positives.candidate:
A single failed SendGrid cancellation aborts cancellation of all other reminders in the same cron run

The new cancellation loop wraps the entire `for (const reminder of remindersToCancel)` loop (including the SendGrid `client.request` call for every reminder and the final `Promise.all`) in one try/catch. If the SendGrid cancel request throws for one reminder (e.g. transient network error, stale/invalid batch id), the loop stops immediately and none of the remaining reminders in that batch get their cancellation request sent during this cron invocation, nor are their WorkflowReminder rows deleted. Because the cron only runs every 15 minutes and only reminders due within the next hour are considered, a persistently-failing single entry can repeatedly block processing of the rest of the batch on every subsequent run (since the same failing item is encountered again before reaching later items), risking that otherwise-cancellable reminders are still sent by SendGrid because the cancel call never reaches them in time. Cancellation and deletion should be handled per-item with its own try/catch so one failure doesn't block the others.

Defense-in-depth ownership check dropped from WorkflowReminder cancel/delete mutations

Previously (e.g. in workflows.tsx update mutation) the WorkflowReminder deletion query included an ownership guard directly in the Prisma `where` clause (`booking: { userId: ctx.user.id }`), so even if an upstream bug allowed another user's reminder id to reach this code, the mutation itself would affect 0 rows. The new shared helpers `deleteScheduledEmailReminder`/`deleteScheduledSMSReminder` (used from multiple callers including trpc routers) perform `update`/`delete` solely by `id`, with no ownership check baked into the query. This removes a layer of protection against reminder ids leaking across callers/users and now relies entirely on each caller's upstream query having correctly scoped the reminder list.

Generic past-due cleanup can delete a cancelled reminder before its SendGrid cancellation request is ever sent

The handler first runs an unconditional cleanup: `prisma.workflowReminder.deleteMany({ where: { method: EMAIL, scheduledDate: { lte: now } } })`, deleting any EMAIL reminder whose scheduledDate has passed, regardless of its `cancelled` flag. This runs before the new cancellation block that queries `cancelled: true` reminders due within the next hour. Because the cron runs every 15 minutes, if a reminder is marked `cancelled: true` less than one cron interval before its `scheduledDate`, the next cron execution may find `scheduledDate <= now` already true by the time it runs and delete the row in the first cleanup step — without ever having issued the SendGrid 'cancel' request for it. If SendGrid had not yet actually sent the email at that instant, it will still go out as originally scheduled, since it was never told to cancel. This narrow but real race window undermines the PR's goal for reminders cancelled close to their send time.

No automated tests for the new cancellation logic despite history of a broken prior fix

The PR description states that the previous fix (PR #6991) for this exact issue 'was wrong and didn't work as expected.' This PR introduces new, non-trivial logic (the `cancelled` flag lifecycle across emailReminderManager.ts, smsReminderManager.ts, and the new cron cancellation block in scheduleEmailReminders.ts) that is central to actually fixing the reported bug, yet no unit/integration tests are added to verify that cancelled/rescheduled bookings' scheduled reminders are correctly prevented from sending. Given the history of this exact feature being silently broken in production, the lack of test coverage is a significant risk for a repeat regression.

Old booking's workflow reminders are cancelled before confirming the reschedule actually succeeded

The cancellation of `originalRescheduledBooking.workflowReminders` happens unconditionally right before calling `eventManager.reschedule(...)`, regardless of whether that reschedule call later succeeds. Further down, the code explicitly checks `if (results.length > 0 && results.some((res) => !res.success))` and merely logs an error without rolling back — the booking's calendar/video integrations may fail, but the original booking's reminders have already been cancelled irreversibly (for EMAIL, moved to immediate-SendGrid-cancel / for SMS, outright deleted from Twilio and the DB). This can leave a booking that effectively did not get successfully rescheduled with no reminders scheduled at all.

Reschedule flow cancels old EMAIL reminders immediately via SendGrid, reintroducing the exact limit bug this PR fixes

When rescheduling a booking, the old booking's EMAIL workflow reminders are cancelled with `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId, true)` — the `immediateDelete=true` flag causes an immediate SendGrid 'cancel' API call. According to the PR description, calling this SendGrid endpoint immediately is exactly what caused the original bug: SendGrid only allows up to 100 pending cancellations, and once that limit is hit, new cancellations fail silently and reminder emails keep being sent. The fix elsewhere (handleCancelBooking.ts, bookings.tsx `requestReschedule`) correctly avoids this by calling `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId)` without the immediate flag, deferring the actual SendGrid cancellation to the new CRON job that only cancels within the last hour before send. This reschedule code path is the one explicitly named in the PR title ('...and rescheduled bookings...') yet still uses the broken immediate-cancel strategy, so under moderate reschedule volume the same SendGrid pending-cancellation limit can be hit again and reminder emails for rescheduled bookings can still be sent.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.

Same issue as in vital/lib/reschedule.ts: `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => {...})` now awaits the newly-async `getCalendar(...)` inside the callback, but forEach does not wait for the returned promises. false_positives.candidate:
Dynamic imports are evaluated eagerly, defeating the purpose of lazy loading

All entries of the appStore object are built with `import("./appname")` calls placed directly inside an object literal. Because this literal is evaluated once, synchronously, as soon as the module is first loaded, every one of the ~26 dynamic import() calls fires immediately and in parallel, exactly like the previous static imports. None of them is deferred until the specific app is actually needed. As a result, every consumer (getCalendar, videoClient, handleCancelBooking, etc.) still triggers loading of all app packages up front, but now each access additionally requires an `await`, adding complexity and promise-resolution overhead without achieving true on-demand/lazy loading. To actually defer loading, each entry would need to be a function returning the import (e.g. `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")`), invoked only when that specific app is required.

Example comment references a non-existent module path

The comment `// example: import("./example"),` doesn't match the actual folder name. The previous code's commented-out import referenced `"./_example"` (with a leading underscore), which is the real folder used to keep the example app excluded from the registry. If a developer later copies this comment to register a new app, it will point at a module that doesn't exist.

Nested forEach(async) race widened by newly-async getCalendar, risking dropped deletions from final Promise.all

In the recurring-event branch, `bookingToDelete.user.credentials.filter(...).forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); ... apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent); })` is not awaited by the surrounding code. `apiDeletes` is only consolidated and awaited much later via `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` (line ~652), relying on other intervening awaits in the function to give these detached async callbacks enough time to push their results. Converting the previously-synchronous `getCalendar` call to `await getCalendar(credential)` adds an extra asynchronous hop before each callback even starts its inner loop, widening the race window during which `apiDeletes` may not yet contain the recurring-booking's calendar deletion promises when the final Promise.all executes, risking recurring-booking calendar events that are never actually deleted on cancellation.

No tests cover the new async appStore / getCalendar / getVideoAdapters behavior

This PR converts appStore's values to Promises and makes getCalendar, getVideoAdapters, and getCalendarCredentials asynchronous, touching booking cancellation, rescheduling, calendar/video event creation, and payment flows across many files. Several of these changes introduce race conditions around unresolved promises inside `Array.prototype.forEach` callbacks (see findings on vital/wipemycalother reschedule.ts, bookings.tsx, and handleCancelBooking.ts). No unit or integration tests were added or updated to verify that calendar/video events are still correctly created, updated, and deleted during these flows after the conversion, so these regressions would not be caught by CI.

forEach with async callback no longer reliably initiates calendar deletion before later steps run

Same issue as in vital/lib/reschedule.ts: `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => {...})` now awaits the newly-async `getCalendar(...)` inside the callback, but forEach does not wait for the returned promises. The loop no longer guarantees the calendar/video deletion requests are even started before the function continues to send the reschedule email and returns. The surrounding try/catch also cannot catch rejections raised inside these detached async callbacks.

getVideoAdapters resolves credentials sequentially instead of in parallel

The rewritten `getVideoAdapters` uses a `for...of` loop with `await appStore[appName as keyof typeof appStore]` inside, resolving each credential's app module one at a time rather than concurrently (e.g. via `Promise.all`). For bookings with multiple video credentials this unnecessarily serializes independent promise resolutions on every call to createMeeting/updateMeeting/deleteMeeting/getBusyVideoTimes, adding avoidable latency compared to a parallelized implementation.

requestReschedule forEach no longer waits for (or even reliably starts) calendar/video deletion before sending the reschedule email and webhooks

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => {...})` was previously a synchronous callback that called `getCalendar` synchronously, so the deletion request was always issued inside the loop before the mutation continued. Now `getCalendar` is awaited inside the async callback, and since forEach ignores the promises returned by async callbacks, the deletion requests may not even be initiated before the code proceeds to `await sendRequestRescheduleEmail(...)` and subsequently dispatches BOOKING_CANCELLED webhooks. This changes the ordering guarantees of the reschedule flow and can leave stale calendar/video events behind while users are already notified of the reschedule.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working-hours boundary check never evaluates the slot's end time

In the new working-hours check added to `checkIfIsAvailable`, both `start` and `end` are computed from `slotStartTime` (`const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();`). `end` should be derived from `slotEndTime` (i.e. slot start + event length) to verify the whole booking fits before the organizer's/fixed host's working hours end. Because `end` duplicates `start`, the check `end > workingHour.endTime` is equivalent to `start > workingHour.endTime`, so a slot whose start is inside the window but whose end (after adding eventLength) extends past the working-hours end time is not flagged as unavailable. This directly undermines the PR's stated goal of correctly respecting a fixed host's hours for round-robin events, allowing bookings that run past a fixed host's actual availability window.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dead code: dayjs instances compared with strict equality always evaluate false

`if (dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes"))` compares two freshly created dayjs objects with `===`, which is always false regardless of their represented time, since they are different object references. This branch, apparently intended to detect a zero-duration date override (e.g. representing a fully blocked day), can never trigger. As written this is unreachable/dead logic, and any scenario relying on detecting start === end for an override silently falls through to the later branches instead of being handled as intended.

false_positives.candidate:
Date-override day matching depends on implicit server-local timezone

The date-override day match (`dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes").format("YYYY MM DD") === slotStartTime.format("YYYY MM DD")`) builds `dayjs(date.start)` without `.utc()`, so its displayed date/format depends on the Node process's local timezone. `slotStartTime`, however, is explicitly `.utc()`. If the server (or a developer's machine, or CI) is not running with TZ=UTC, this comparison can disagree with the rest of the file, which consistently uses explicit `.utc()`/`.tz()` conversions elsewhere, causing date overrides to be matched to the wrong day or missed entirely depending on deployment environment.

No test covers the primary fix: fixed-host date overrides blocking round-robin slots

The PR description states its main purpose is to make date overrides of fixed hosts taken into account for round-robin events so slots aren't offered when a fixed host is unavailable. The only test changes add a second timezone assertion to the existing single-user 'Check for Date overrides' test (no scheduling type / no hosts). There is no new test combining a ROUND_ROBIN event with a fixed host that has a date override and a non-fixed round-robin host that is available, to verify that the slot is excluded. Given the newly added/changed availability logic in `checkIfIsAvailable` (working hours and date-override checks per fixed host) contains at least one concrete bug (see other findings), this is exactly the scenario that should have automated coverage but does not.

Override offset adjustment can cross midnight but only the time-of-day is kept

The new override start/end computation shifts `override.start`/`override.end` by `offset` minutes (the difference between invitee and organizer UTC offsets) and then extracts only `.hour() * 60 + .minute()`. When the offset difference between organizer and invitee pushes the adjusted time across a day boundary (common for large timezone differences, e.g. near the International Date Line), the date portion is discarded and only the wrapped time-of-day is kept, which can make the override appear to apply on the wrong day or produce an incorrect time window instead of being excluded/moved to the adjacent day.

Override timezone offset computed from a field that is typed optional without a fallback

`const organizerUtcOffset = dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone).utcOffset();` passes `override.timeZone` directly to `.tz()`. `TimeRange.timeZone` (packages/types/schedule.d.ts) is declared optional (`timeZone?: string`), so nothing in the type system guarantees it is set. If any caller of `getSlots`/`getTimeSlots` supplies `dateOverrides` without a `timeZone` (the field was only newly introduced and is only populated by the one call site touched in this PR), `.tz(undefined)` will silently fall back to some default/local timezone behavior rather than failing, producing incorrect offsets and therefore incorrect override slot times instead of a clear error.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
KeyError risk when comparing authenticated user against missing 'sender' metadata

In `GitHubInstallation.dispatch()`, the new check `pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user") != integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` accesses `integration.metadata["sender"]` with direct dict indexing instead of `.get()`. _ensure_processes_alive() now wraps the restart kill with `if isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process): process.kill()` (lines 253-257). false_positives.candidate:
Offset commits are issued from a dedicated background thread instead of the main strategy thread

_commit_loop runs on its own daemon thread started in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.__init__ and calls self.commit_function(committable), which ultimately invokes the arroyo `commit` callback passed into create_with_partitions. Arroyo processing strategies are designed to be driven single-threadedly by the StreamProcessor's main loop (submit/poll/join); none of the other modes in this same file (serial, parallel, batched-parallel) invoke the commit callback from a separate thread. Calling `commit` concurrently with the main thread's own poll()/submit() activity deviates from that contract and risks races in whatever internal bookkeeping the Commit implementation performs, since it is not documented/guaranteed to be safe for concurrent use from worker threads.

Offsets are marked complete (and committed) even when processing raises an exception

In OrderedQueueWorker.run(), the finally block always calls self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(...) regardless of whether result_processor succeeded or raised an exception caught by the preceding 'except Exception' clause. This contradicts the guarantee stated in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy's docstring ('Only commits offsets after successful processing'): a message whose processing failed is treated identically to a successfully processed one, so its offset becomes eligible for commit and will never be retried or reprocessed — a processing failure silently advances the committed offset past the failed message.

Per-queue queue.Queue() has no maxsize, so the claimed backpressure doesn't exist

Each internal queue created in FixedQueuePool.__init__ (queue.Queue()) is unbounded, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() never raises arroyo's MessageRejected to signal backpressure regardless of queue depth. Despite the docstrings on FixedQueuePool and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy explicitly claiming 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', no bound is enforced anywhere, so a slow or stuck group (or an overall slow downstream) can grow its queue without limit while the consumer keeps reading from Kafka, risking unbounded memory growth instead of the intended backpressure.

Uses Python 3.13-only queue.Queue.shutdown()/queue.ShutDown API

FixedQueuePool.shutdown() calls q.shutdown(immediate=False), and OrderedQueueWorker.run() catches queue.ShutDown. Both queue.Queue.shutdown() and the queue.ShutDown exception were introduced in Python 3.13. On earlier Python runtimes, q.shutdown() raises AttributeError; since that call is wrapped in a bare 'except Exception', the failure is silently logged rather than propagated, meaning the queue is never actually put into a shutdown state. Worker threads blocked in work_queue.get() are consequently never woken and will hang indefinitely instead of shutting down, defeating the entire purpose of FixedQueuePool.shutdown()/close().

close() shuts down the queue pool without draining it first

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() immediately calls self.queue_pool.shutdown() without first calling the already-implemented FixedQueuePool.wait_until_empty() helper. FixedQueuePool.shutdown() only gives each worker a 5 second join() timeout; if there is still a backlog when close() runs, items may not finish processing within that window (a timed-out join() does not stop the thread, it just stops waiting), so close() can return while unprocessed/uncommitted work is still in flight, risking those messages being left in an inconsistent processed/committed state depending on what happens after close() returns.

close()/terminate() permanently destroy the shared queue pool, breaking processing after any rebalance

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() (and terminate()) calls self.queue_pool.shutdown(), which stops all OrderedQueueWorker threads and shuts down every internal queue.Queue permanently. The FixedQueuePool instance, however, is created once in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__ and reused across every subsequent call to create_with_partitions (e.g. after Kafka partition rebalances) — exactly like parallel_executor/multiprocessing_pool in result_consumer.py, which are intentionally only torn down in ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown() at final process exit, never per-strategy-close. Because arroyo calls close()/terminate() on the current strategy whenever it is being replaced (which happens on every rebalance, not just final shutdown), the first rebalance kills the workers and shuts down the queues. Any create_with_partitions call afterwards reuses the now-dead queue_pool: submit() pushes items into shut-down queues (raising queue.ShutDown, silently caught and the offset marked 'complete' without any real processing), so messages after the first rebalance are effectively dropped while the consumer appears healthy.

get_committable_offsets iterates the offsets dict without a lock protecting its structure

get_committable_offsets() takes list(self.all_offsets.keys()) and then separately locks per-partition to read self.all_offsets[partition]. The all_offsets defaultdict's key set can be mutated from another thread calling add_offset for a partition never seen before (defaultdict.__missing__ inserting a new key) without any lock protecting the dict's structure itself — only the per-partition lock (created lazily, after the key may already need to be inserted) guards the inner set contents. Enumerating dict.keys() into a list while another thread inserts a new key concurrently can race, and in CPython can even raise RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration, which would crash the background commit loop thread.

test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts behavior inconsistent with the implementation

This test mocks the result processor to raise on the first call and succeed on the second, then asserts `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`, implying a processing failure should block the offset commit. But per OrderedQueueWorker.run()'s finally block, offsets are always marked complete regardless of exceptions, so the commit loop should still compute and commit an offset for test_partition once both items complete (which happens almost immediately since the mocked calls return synchronously). This makes the assertion likely to fail or flake against the real implementation, or indicates the test does not actually validate any failure-handling guarantee.

false_positives.candidate:
Per-resource cache miss now forces a full permissions DB requery on every mismatched Check call

Previously `getUserPermissions`/`getAnonymousPermissions` returned the cached permission map unconditionally whenever any entry existed for the user+action, regardless of whether it covered the requested resource, so a single cache entry served all Check calls for that action for the whole 30s TTL. Now, `Check` calls `getCachedIdentityPermissions` and, if the cached map doesn't contain the specific requested scope, always falls through to `getIdentityPermissions` which performs a full DB permissions query (deduplicated via singleflight only for truly concurrent calls). For workloads that call Check sequentially for many distinct resource names under the same action (e.g. authorizing each item of a list one at a time), every resource not already present in the cached scope map now triggers its own DB round trip, and is only protected from repeat DB hits via the new per-resource permDenialCache (keyed by name+parent) on subsequent identical calls. This can multiply DB load roughly proportional to the number of distinct resources checked, compared to the previous single-query-per-TTL-window behavior, and is not bounded/debounced beyond the exact (name, parent) tuple.

Permission-denial cache key collides across identity types sharing the same UID

`userPermDenialCacheKey(checkReq.Namespace.Value, checkReq.UserUID, checkReq.Action, checkReq.Name, checkReq.ParentFolder)` (defined in pkg/services/authz/rbac/cache.go) builds the cache key purely from the parsed subject UID, action, name and parent folder, without including the identity type. Anonymous subjects ("anonymous:0") and the render-service subject ("render:0") both resolve to UserUID=="0" (see the test file's own usage of these literal subjects), so a denial recorded for one identity type (e.g. render service denied on some action) will be returned for the other identity type (e.g. an anonymous user) on the next Check call for the same namespace/action/name/folder, even though their actual permission semantics (getRendererPermissions vs getAnonymousPermissions) are completely different and unrelated. Unlike the existing permCache which deliberately uses separate key schemes per identity type (userPermCacheKey vs anonymousPermCacheKey, and no caching at all for render), this new denial cache does not preserve that separation. The result is an incorrect deny being served to a different identity than the one it was computed for, causing availability/correctness regressions (legitimate requests incorrectly denied) that only clear once the 30s denial TTL expires.

permissionCacheUsage metric mislabels a used-but-denying cache lookup as a cache miss

When `getCachedIdentityPermissions` returns a cached permission map (err == nil) but `checkPermission` evaluates it as not allowed, the code falls through to the line `s.metrics.permissionCacheUsage.WithLabelValues("false", checkReq.Action).Inc()`, recording this as a cache miss even though the cache was actually read and used to make a (negative) decision before falling back to the DB. This mislabels cache effectiveness, making dashboards built on this metric appear to show a lower cache hit rate than what is actually happening, which could mislead capacity planning/alerting based on this metric.

Queries get interpolated twice when shard splitting delegates to time splitting

`runShardSplitQuery()` (lines 49-52) now interpolates every target once via `datasource.applyTemplateVariables(query, request.scopedVars, request.filters)` before grouping by shard. For each shard group, `splitQueriesByStreamShard()` then builds a `subRequest` from these already-interpolated targets (with the shard selector injected) and passes it to `runSplitQuery()` (line 163). CreateOrUpdateDevice first runs CountDevices to check if the limit has been reached, and only if `count >= s.deviceLimit` falls back to update-only mode; otherwise it proceeds to INSERT a new device row. This check-then-act sequence is not wrapped in a transaction or any locking mechanism. Under concurrent anonymous requests (which is exactly the scenario the device limit is meant to guard against, e.g. traffic spikes or multiple server instances in HA), multiple goroutines/requests can all read a count below the limit simultaneously and then all insert new devices, allowing the actual number of active devices to exceed `deviceLimit`. A new configuration key `device_limit` under `[auth.anonymous]` (mapped to `Cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit`) is introduced here, but no accompanying documentation was added: there is no update to the sample/defaults ini files or to the configuration reference docs describing the setting, its default (0 = unlimited), or its effect. The PR's entire motivation is a MySQL-specific deadlock between annotation cleanup and concurrent inserts (grafana/grafana#64979), caused by a single DELETE-with-subquery statement. Since `objInfo.UpdatedObject` is invoked independently by each store (each using its own view of the "old" object), Legacy and Storage can end up computing and persisting different final objects, especially for patch-style updates. This undermines the stated goal of Mode 3 ("write to unified storage and then asynchronously write to legacy as a safety measure") because the legacy copy may not actually mirror what was stored in unified storage.

Duplicate checksum entry added for grafana/pkg/apimachinery go.mod

The line `github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery v0.0.0-20240701135906-559738ce6ae1/go.mod h1:DkxMin+qOh1Fgkxfbt+CUfBqqsCQJMG9op8Os/irBPA=` already existed in the file and is added again by this diff, producing a duplicate entry. In Create (and similarly in Delete line 110, Update line 135, DeleteCollection line 163) the async goroutine does `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, 10*time.Second, ...)` using the `ctx` that was passed into the method, which is ultimately the HTTP request context. Go's net/http cancels the request context as soon as the handler (i.e. this Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection call and the rest of the request pipeline) returns and the response has been written. Since the goroutine is launched right before the function returns, in practice the derived context is cancelled almost immediately, well before the intended 10s timeout elapses, so the asynchronous write to legacy storage is very likely to be aborted mid-flight. This defeats the entire purpose of Mode 3's "write to legacy as a safety net" behavior: legacy will frequently fall out of sync without any visible error to the caller (errors are only logged/metriced inside the goroutine). The context used for the detached write should not inherit cancellation from the request (e.g. use `context.Background()` or `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` plus the desired timeout).

Consequently these tests would pass even if the goroutine were never launched, called the legacy store with wrong arguments, or if any of the metric-mislabeling bugs introduced in this PR regressed further — the new asynchronous behavior added by this PR is effectively untested.

The goroutines spawned in Create, Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection (lines 50, 108, 134, 161) call into `d.Legacy.*` with no `recover()`. An unrecovered panic in any of these detached goroutines (e.g. triggered by a bug or unexpected state in a legacy store implementation) will crash the entire Grafana process, since Go terminates the program on an unhandled panic in any goroutine, not just the one serving the HTTP request. When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` instead of `d.recordStorageDuration`. Legacy was never invoked on this path (the function returns before the async legacy call), so this mislabels a Storage failure as a Legacy failure, corrupting the dual-writer metrics used for monitoring/alerting.

In `Update`, when `d.Storage.Update` fails, `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` is called instead of `d.recordStorageDuration`. As with Create, Legacy.Update is never reached on this path, so the error is incorrectly attributed to the legacy backend instead of storage, making the dual-writer metrics misleading.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions contains dead/misleading logic that always returns false

The new helper always returns false regardless of the feature flag value: `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)`; `if enabled { return false }`; `return false`. Both branches return the same literal, so the computed `enabled` value (and the feature-flag lookup itself) is completely unused/irrelevant, and the variable name `enabled` is also inverted relative to what it actually measures (it is true when the flag is NOT enabled). This makes the code highly misleading: a future maintainer could easily believe toggling `FlagSqlExpressions` re-enables SQL expressions, when in fact it never will with this implementation, and there's no comment explaining that this is an intentional, hard-coded kill-switch for a security fix (CVE-2024-9264). This should be simplified to an explicit `return false` with a clear comment, to avoid confusion and accidental 'fixes' that re-enable the vulnerable code path.

true_positives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Misleading public error message when SQL expressions are effectively disabled

NewSQLCommand calls sql.TablesList(rawSQL), which now always fails because pkg/expr/sql/db.go's DB.RunCommands is a stub that unconditionally returns errors.New("not implemented"). When this happens, NewSQLCommand returns errutil.BadRequest("sql-invalid-sql", errutil.WithPublicMessage("error reading SQL command")), which tells the user their SQL is invalid, when the real reason is that the feature has been completely disabled/stubbed out. Any code path that reaches NewSQLCommand without going through ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery's explicit "sqlExpressions is not implemented" check (e.g. UnmarshalSQLCommand, used for raw-node parsing) will surface this confusing message instead of a clear explanation, making it harder for users/admins to diagnose why previously working SQL expressions now fail.

false_positives.candidate:
Leftover DuckDB-specific code/naming contradicts stated PR goal of removing DuckDB references

The PR description states the intent is to "Remove reference to DuckDB", but TablesList still names its local variable `duckDB` (`duckDB := NewInMemoryDB()`) and still constructs a DuckDB-specific SQL command (`SELECT json_serialize_sql('%s')`) to pass to RunCommands, even though the underlying DB is now a stub that always returns "not implemented" and has nothing to do with DuckDB. This leftover naming/logic is confusing: it implies the code still talks to a DuckDB engine with a real SQL dialect, when in fact it is now dead code whose output is always discarded due to the stub's unconditional error. This should be cleaned up or at minimum commented to reflect that the underlying engine has been removed.

No test coverage added for disabling SQL expressions

This PR's core behavior change is that QueryTypeSQL now always errors out with "sqlExpressions is not implemented" via enableSqlExpressions(), which is the security-relevant fix. No test changes are included in the diff to verify this behavior (e.g., a test that ReadQuery returns an error for QueryTypeSQL regardless of feature flag state), nor are there tests for the new pkg/expr/sql/db.go stub (DB.TablesList/RunCommands/QueryFramesInto) to confirm they always fail safely. Given the severity of the vulnerability being fixed, a regression test preventing silent re-enablement of SQL expression execution is important and currently missing.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs() reads the index cache map without holding cacheMu, racing with concurrent writes

bleveBackend.TotalDocs() iterates over b.cache without acquiring cacheMu (neither RLock nor Lock), while BuildIndex() now writes to the same map under a lock that only protects the final cache assignment (b.cache[key] = idx). This PR adds a new call site for TotalDocs() in resource/search.go's searchSupport.init(), invoked immediately after the background watch-event goroutine is started (which can trigger new BuildIndex calls via getOrCreateIndex). This creates a genuine unsynchronized concurrent map read/write, which in Go can panic at runtime ("fatal error: concurrent map read and map write") or produce corrupted/garbage results. TotalDocs should take cacheMu.RLock()/RUnlock() like GetIndex does.

false_negatives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.

false_positives.candidate:
Init() is now a no-op if called again after construction, which may silently break other callers relying on it

Init() still uses sync.Once and is now invoked internally during NewResourceServer. Any other code path in the codebase that calls ResourceServer.Init(ctx) later (e.g. as part of a module/service lifecycle contract, with a different context carrying its own cancellation/tracing) will be a silent no-op because the Once has already fired during construction with an internally-created background context. The PR description itself raises this exact concern ("Does anything else depend on initializing US lazily? What could this break?") but the diff does not show any audit or update of such callers. If any lifecycle manager expects Init(ctx) to perform the actual initialization work tied to its own context, that expectation is now silently violated.

NewResourceServer now blocks indefinitely on search index build with no timeout or cancellation path

NewResourceServer calls s.Init(ctx) synchronously before returning, and Init in turn calls searchSupport.init which builds the full search index for every namespace returned by GetResourceStats. The context used is derived from context.Background() with no deadline, so there is no bound on how long server construction can take for large installations with many/large namespaces. Previously this cost was paid lazily on the first gRPC call (which had its own problems per the PR description), but now any process that constructs a ResourceServer (app startup, tests, other callers) will block for however long index building takes, with no way to time out, report partial progress, or fail fast. This can turn into very long or hanging startups in production without any visible health/readiness signal during that window.

Postgres integration test skipped rather than fixed, potentially masking a startup regression from the new synchronous Init

This test exercises ResourceServer/module startup (waiting only 500ms for the HTTP server to become available) and is now skipped for postgres with the comment "test not working with postgres in Drone. Works locally." Given this PR moves ResourceServer initialization (including search index building) to be synchronous at construction time, it is plausible that the added latency is exactly what causes this test to fail intermittently under Drone's resource constraints for postgres. Skipping the test instead of investigating removes coverage for the very scenario (server startup timing) that this PR changes, and may hide a real regression rather than fixing it.

Shared `err` and `totalBatchesIndexed` variables are written concurrently by multiple goroutines in searchSupport.init

In searchSupport.init(), the errgroup with SetLimit(s.initWorkers) launches one goroutine per namespace that does `totalBatchesIndexed++` and `_, _, err = s.build(...)` followed by `return err`, where both `err` and `totalBatchesIndexed` are variables shared across all goroutines without any synchronization (mutex/atomic). Previously this race was largely masked because bleve.BuildIndex held a single mutex across its entire body, effectively serializing the actual work done inside s.build() for different namespaces. This PR's locking change in bleve.go (lock now only guards the final cache write) removes that serialization, so multiple goroutines can now genuinely run s.build() concurrently, widening the race window. The consequence is real: one goroutine's error can be overwritten by another's success (or vice versa) before its own `return err` executes, so group.Wait() may incorrectly report success even though a particular namespace failed to build its index (or report a failure for a namespace that actually succeeded), and totalBatchesIndexed can lose increments. Given this path now runs synchronously at every server startup and failures are supposed to block startup, silently losing an error here is a data-integrity risk (a namespace could end up with a stale/missing index with no error surfaced).

Trace-context propagation fix is incomplete — several spans still discard the updated context

The PR fixes span-context propagation in resource/search.go and in sql/backend.go's GetResourceStats (ctx, span := ...), but other methods in the same file still discard the span-carrying context with `_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, ...)` and then pass the original (un-updated) ctx to nested calls, e.g. WriteEvent (line 158, passing ctx to b.create/b.update/b.delete), ReadResource (line 353), and ListIterator (line 388, passing ctx to listAtRevision/listLatest). As a result, spans created inside create/update/delete, dbutil.QueryRow calls in ReadResource, and listAtRevision/listLatest will not be properly parented under the WriteEvent/Read/List spans, leaving the exact trace-propagation bug the PR claims to fix still present in several high-traffic code paths.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Test cleanup removes a non-existent IDP alias instead of the one actually created

In the new `testCacheIDPForLogin` test, after creating identity providers with aliases like "idp-alias-" + i (and later "idp-alias-20"), cleanup is registered as `getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove)` (also repeated at the idp-alias-20 creation point). The literal string "alias" is passed instead of the actual alias that was created, so the cleanup action targets a non-existent identity provider named "alias" rather than the ones actually created by the test. As a result, none of the up-to-21 identity providers created by this test are properly removed during cleanup, leaking realm state across test runs/test methods and risking alias-conflict failures or inflated counts in subsequent tests that rely on a clean realm/IDP set.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

false_positives.candidate:
Login cache sub-key is unnecessarily split by organizationId for FetchMode.REALM_ONLY

`getForLogin` computes `searchKey = organizationId != null ? organizationId : ""` and stores results in the per-mode `IdentityProviderListQuery` under that sub-key, regardless of fetch mode. However, for `FetchMode.REALM_ONLY` the default `getForLogin` implementation completely ignores `organizationId` (it forces `ORGANIZATION_ID=null` in the search options), so the result is identical for any organizationId value. If `getForLogin(REALM_ONLY, orgA)` and `getForLogin(REALM_ONLY, orgB)` are both invoked, they will be cached as two separate sub-entries with identical content, causing redundant delegate queries and unnecessary cache growth instead of reusing a single REALM_ONLY entry.

remove() now always performs an extra backend lookup for the IDP by alias, even when not needed

Previously, `idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias)` was only invoked inside the `if (isInvalid(cacheKey))` branch when a backend lookup was actually required. The refactor moved this call out to the top of remove(), so `idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias)` is now executed unconditionally on every removal, even when the cache entry is still valid and already available via `realmCache.getCache().get(cacheKey, ...)`. This adds an unnecessary delegate/DB round trip to every identity-provider removal purely to support the new login-cache invalidation check, instead of reusing the already-available cached model when present.

update() uses the org-aware wrapped model for login-cache invalidation decisions, which can mask real eligibility changes

In update(), `idpById` is obtained via `getById(model.getInternalId())`, which is the cache-aware method of this same class and therefore wraps the result with `createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel(...)`. That wrapper overrides `isEnabled()` to also factor in the live state of the linked organization (`org.isEnabled()`), while the underlying `getForLogin()` query that actually populates the cached ID list filters strictly on the IDP's raw, persisted `enabled` column (via `LoginFilter`), independent of the organization's current status. `registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate(idpById, model)` then calls `getLoginPredicate().test(idpById)`, which invokes the wrapped (live) `isEnabled()`. If the linked organization happens to be disabled at the moment of the update, `idpById.isEnabled()` returns false even though the IDP's raw `enabled` flag (and therefore its actual membership in the cached login ID list) is true. Comparing this masked value against the predicate result for the raw `model` passed to update() can make the method wrongly conclude that login-eligibility 'didn't change' (both evaluate false) when in fact the IDP's raw eligibility did change (e.g. toggling hideOnLogin), causing the login caches to be left stale instead of invalidated. Note that remove() correctly avoids this by using `idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias)` (the raw, unwrapped delegate) rather than the cache/organization-aware getById(); update() should do the same for consistency and correctness.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider() does not return a BouncyCastle provider, violating the documented contract

CryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider() is documented as returning 'BouncyCastle security provider. Can be either non-FIPS or FIPS based provider'. This implementation instead returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, which is whatever JCA provider backs the JVM's default keystore type (typically the JDK's built-in SUN provider), completely unrelated to BouncyCastle. Other providers that don't rely on BouncyCastle (e.g. WildFlyElytronProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider()) simply return null, which is the established convention for 'no BC provider'. Returning an arbitrary unrelated Provider instance here is inconsistent with that convention and can mislead any code that relies on this method's contract (e.g. diagnostics, provider registration logic) if this CryptoProvider instance is ever the active one.

true_positives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dead code: throwaway ASN1Encoder instances created and discarded

In concatenatedRSToASN1DER(), two ASN1Encoder instances are created and `write()` is called on them, but the results are never used or assigned (lines 114-115); the actual return value is built via separate, freshly-created ASN1Encoder instances a few lines later. This is leftover/dead code from development that performs unnecessary object allocation and encoding work on every signature conversion call, and should be removed before merging.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract method order() breaks existing CryptoProvider implementors

CryptoProvider.order() is added as a plain abstract method (no default implementation). CryptoProvider is a public, SPI-loaded extension point (discovered via META-INF/services and ServiceLoader in CryptoIntegration). Any existing third-party or downstream implementation of this interface that is not updated to implement order() will fail to compile/load. Since this interface is explicitly designed for pluggable crypto backends (FIPS vs non-FIPS, custom providers), this is a breaking API change that should either provide a default method (e.g. `default int order() { return 100; }`) or be clearly called out as a breaking change in release notes.

false_negatives.golden_comment: When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

false_positives.candidate:
ES384/ES512 tests reuse a single default-curve EC key, never exercising real signature lengths for those algorithms

The single EC KeyPair used across all three tests (testES256/testES384/testES512) is generated with `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()` without specifying a curve, which defaults to a 256-bit curve (e.g. secp256r1/P-256) regardless of the algorithm under test. For ES384 and ES512 the real R/S components should be ~48 and ~66 bytes respectively, but because the same P-256 key is reused, the actual signature always has ~32-byte components that get zero-padded to the expected length in asn1derToConcatenatedRS/concatenatedRSToASN1DER. As a result, the tests never exercise the encoder/decoder with genuinely large R/S values (e.g. values requiring a leading 0x00 byte near the boundary of a 48- or 66-byte field), reducing their ability to catch boundary bugs specific to the larger curves these algorithms are meant to represent.

Removed fail-fast check for multiple CryptoProviders now silently resolves ties non-deterministically

Previously, detecting more than one CryptoProvider on the classpath threw an IllegalStateException, which protected against misconfiguration (e.g. accidentally shipping both a FIPS and non-FIPS crypto module together). Now, detectProvider() just sorts by order() and silently keeps the first. All of DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider return the same order() value of 200, so if two of them ever end up on the same classpath/classloader, the choice between them depends on the arbitrary ServiceLoader iteration order (not guaranteed to be stable across JVMs/OS), rather than failing loudly. In a FIPS-mandated deployment this could silently select the non-FIPS provider instead of raising an error, which is a meaningful loss of a safety net with potential compliance/security consequences.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Possible NullPointerException when the all-clients fallback resource does not exist

In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), when no resource exists for the specific client the code falls back to AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and immediately calls authz.getStoreFactory().getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource) without checking whether the returned resource is null. getResourceTypeResource() returns null whenever the 'Clients' all-resource-type Resource cannot be found (e.g. for realms where it was never created, or where supportsAuthorizationSchema() returns false at call time). Passing a null Resource into findByResource() is likely to throw a NullPointerException instead of simply denying the permission, turning an authorization check failure into an unhandled server error.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.

In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.

In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

false_positives.candidate:
No end-to-end test coverage for the ClientScopeModel-level V2 permission methods

ClientPermissionsV2 overrides canManageClientScopes(), canViewClientScopes(), canListClientScopes(), canManage(ClientScopeModel) and canView(ClientScopeModel), which gate the global Client Scopes admin REST API (/admin/realms/{realm}/client-scopes). None of the tests added in this PR exercise that REST API with a caller that only has Clients-resource-type FGAP permissions (e.g. creating/listing/deleting a client scope via the admin client). The existing tests only cover per-client default/optional client-scope assignment on a specific ClientModel, which goes through canManage(ClientModel)/canConfigure(ClientModel), not the ClientScopeModel-specific methods, leaving a meaningful chunk of new behavior untested.

No test coverage for the MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE scope / canMapClientScopeRoles()

AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS now includes the MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE scope and ClientPermissionsV2.canMapClientScopeRoles() checks it, but none of the new tests in this file (or elsewhere in the PR) exercise this scope. testMapRolesAndCompositesOnlyOneClient only grants/tests MAP_ROLES and MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE (plus CONFIGURE). Without a dedicated test, a regression in canMapClientScopeRoles() or the MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE evaluation path would go unnoticed.

Unconditional UnsupportedOperationException now reachable for every client via MgmtPermissionsV2.clients()

MgmtPermissionsV2.clients() now always returns ClientPermissionsV2 instead of falling back to the V1 ClientPermissions implementation as it did before this PR (clients() was not previously overridden). ClientPermissionsV2 overrides isPermissionsEnabled(), setPermissionsEnabled(), getPermissions(), resource(), managePermission(), configurePermission(), viewPermission(), mapRolesPermission(), mapRolesClientScopePermission(), mapRolesCompositePermission(), canExchangeTo() and exchangeToPermission() to unconditionally throw new UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported in V2") for ANY client, not only ones related to the new 'Clients' resource-type functionality. Any existing admin REST call that still relies on these methods when ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled -- e.g. GET/PUT .../clients/{id}/management/permissions to toggle fine-grained permissions on a client, or a Standard Token Exchange authorization check via canExchangeTo() -- will now throw an unchecked exception where it previously worked by falling back to V1 behavior. There is no guard at the call sites to avoid reaching these methods, so this is a functional regression likely to surface as unhandled exceptions/500 errors for unrelated, pre-existing admin operations.

canManageClientScopes() Javadoc is a copy-paste of canManage() and doesn't describe client-scope semantics

The Javadoc added for canManageClientScopes() (lines 52-57) is identical, word for word, to the Javadoc of canManage() directly above it (lines 40-45): both state 'Returns true if the caller has MANAGE_CLIENTS role... For V2 only: Also if it has permission to MANAGE'. The comment never mentions client scopes at all, so it fails to document what, if anything, differentiates this method from canManage(), which is misleading for future readers/maintainers trying to understand what permission this method actually checks.

getResourceName() has no branch for the new CLIENTS resource type

getResourceName() special-cases USERS_RESOURCE_TYPE to return a friendly label ('All users' for the all-resource Resource, or the username for individual user resources), but after this PR adds CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE to the schema there is no equivalent 'if (CLIENTS.getType().equals(resourceType))' branch. For Client-type permissions the method falls through to 'return resource.getDisplayName()'. Resources for clients are created via getOrCreateResource() (and the all-resource 'Clients' Resource in init()) without ever setting a displayName, so this will return null/blank instead of a friendly client name (e.g. the client's clientId, or 'All clients'), unlike the equivalent Users case. This leaves permission resource names unresolved/blank wherever this API is surfaced (e.g. admin console display of resources tied to a Clients-type scope permission).

init() is a no-op for already-initialized realms, so the new Clients scopes/resource are never backfilled

AdminPermissionsSchema.init() returns immediately (lines 226-228) if realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() != null, i.e. if the Admin Permissions client/resource-server was already created (which happens the first time Admin Fine-Grained Authorization V2 is enabled for a realm). This PR adds three new scopes (CONFIGURE, MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE, MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE) and a new 'Clients' all-resource-type Resource to the schema, but there is no migration/backfill logic to add them to resource servers that were initialized before this change. For any realm that already had FGAP V2 enabled prior to upgrading, attempting to create a Client-resource-type permission will fail: getOrCreateResource() looks up each required scope via scopeStore.findByName(resourceServer, scopeName) and explicitly throws new ModelException("No scopes found.") if any of CONFIGURE/MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE/MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE is missing, and the 'Clients' all-resource-type Resource itself (used for all-clients permissions) will not exist either. This effectively breaks the new Clients permission feature for all pre-existing FGAP V2 deployments unless an administrator manually recreates the Admin Permissions client.

true_positives.golden_comment: Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance
true_positives.matched_candidate:
RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE value changed from 4 to 3, repurposing exit code 4

RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE was previously 4 and is now changed to 3, with the freed-up value 4 reassigned to the new FEATURE_DISABLED constant. The update-compatibility check/metadata commands already existed before this PR (only +4/+7 line diffs were needed to add the feature-flag gating), meaning this exit code contract was already shipped and could be relied upon by external automation/scripts that branch on exit code 4 meaning 'recreate update required'. After this change, the same scripts will now interpret exit code 4 as 'feature disabled' and exit code 3 as 'recreate required', silently breaking any existing integration built against the previous exit code semantics. This renumbering is not mentioned in the PR description and should be called out as a breaking change (or avoided by picking an unused code for FEATURE_DISABLED).

false_negatives.golden_comment: Incorrect method call for exit codes. The picocli.exit() method calls System.exit() directly, which is problematic:

false_positives.candidate:
CAUTION about rolling-updates feature requirement is overly broad relative to actual default behavior

The new CAUTION block states unconditionally that 'the feature rolling-updates must be enabled. Otherwise, the {project_name} Operator will fail', placed directly under the 'Managing Keycloak Operator Updates' heading before any mention of the optional update.strategy field. This reads as if the feature flag is required any time this section's functionality (including the default/unconfigured behavior) is used. But per the accompanying UpgradeTest.java changes, when updateStrategy is left unset (no 'update' stanza in the CR), the Operator falls back to legacy (pre-rolling-updates) behavior without requiring the feature flag at all. The caution should clarify that the feature is only required when explicitly setting the `update.strategy` field, not for all uses of the Operator's update handling, to avoid confusing users into thinking the flag is always mandatory.

No test for operator failing when update.strategy is set without the rolling-updates feature enabled

The updated docs (docs/guides/operator/advanced-configuration.adoc) explicitly state: 'While on preview stage, the feature rolling-updates must be enabled. Otherwise, the Operator will fail.' However, createInitialDeployment() in this test only ever enables the ROLLING_UPDATES feature together with a non-null UpdateStrategy, and only exercises the default (updateStrategy == null, feature not enabled) and explicit-strategy-with-feature-enabled combinations. There is no test exercising the documented failure path where an explicit update.strategy is configured in the Keycloak CR while the rolling-updates feature is left disabled, so the documented 'Operator will fail' behavior is never verified by this test suite.

testFeatureNotEnabled does not assert the new FEATURE_DISABLED exit code

testFeatureNotEnabled only checks the printed error message ('Unable to use this command. The preview feature ...') but never asserts that the process exits with CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED (4), which is the new behavior introduced by this PR. Since this PR also changes RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE from 4 to 3 and introduces FEATURE_DISABLED as 4, the actual exit code values are an important, easily-regressed part of the contract and should be explicitly verified by this test (and by the recreate-path tests) rather than relying solely on message text.

true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
canManage() treats VIEW-only group permission as sufficient to manage groups

In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() (no-arg, realm-wide check), the method returns true via `hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)` — i.e. it accepts either VIEW or MANAGE scope. This is identical to canView()'s body except for the admin-role check, and it means an admin who was granted only a read-only 'view' permission on the Groups resource type is treated as if they also have 'manage' permission. Since GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup() calls `auth.groups().requireManage()` to authorize creating new top-level groups, a user with only VIEW scope on Groups would be able to create (and, via other requireManage() call sites, modify) groups, which is a privilege escalation. Compare with canManage(GroupModel) and canManageMembership(GroupModel) in the same class, and with UserPermissions.canManage(), none of which accept VIEW as sufficient for MANAGE — confirming this is inconsistent/incorrect. The call should check only AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() returns authz resource IDs instead of group IDs, and per-group resources are not discoverable

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() calls `resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE, groupResource -> ...)` to enumerate group-scoped authorization resources, then calls `hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), ...)` and adds `groupResource.getId()` to the result set. However: (1) individual per-group resources are created via AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource(), which never calls resource.setType(...) (unlike the legacy V1 GroupPermissions.initialize(), which explicitly sets `groupResource.setType("Group")`), so findByType(server, "Groups", ...) will not find per-group resources at all — it will only match the single 'all-groups' placeholder resource created during schema init (which does have its type set). (2) Even for that placeholder, `groupResource.getId()` is the authorization resource's own internal ID, not a GroupModel id; hasPermission(String groupId, ...) expects a real GroupModel id (it looks the resource up via `resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId)`, and resources are named by the group's id per resolveGroup()). As a result this method either returns an empty set (making the group-based DB pre-filter in UsersResource/BruteForceUsersResource a no-op, relying solely on slower per-user canView checks) or, when an 'all-groups' VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permission exists, returns a bogus id that does not correspond to any real group, which would be used as a UserModel.GROUPS search filter and could incorrectly exclude all users even though the admin should see them via blanket group-membership permission. This should use `groupResource.getName()` (not getId()) and the underlying resources need a type set so findByType can actually locate them.

The change moves the feature check outside, so the listener is only registered if the feature is enabled at the moment registerListener() is invoked (typically once, at provider/session-factory initialization). If the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ feature is toggled on after this registration happens (e.g. in test harnesses or deployments that enable the feature dynamically after providers have already been initialized), RoleRemovedEvent/ClientRemovedEvent/GroupRemovedEvent cleanup of permissions will silently stop firing, whereas previously it would have resumed working as soon as the flag became true. This is a behavior change that is not obviously covered by tests.

testManageAllGroups() only verifies that granting MANAGE scope on the all-groups resource allows group creation/update; there is no test asserting that an admin granted only VIEW (or VIEW_MEMBERS) scope on Groups is still forbidden from creating/updating/deleting groups. Such a test would have caught the canManage() bug in GroupPermissionsV2 where VIEW scope is incorrectly treated as sufficient for manage operations. Additionally, there is no test exercising an 'all-groups' level VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permission and verifying that user search via group membership actually returns the expected users, which would have revealed the getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() id-mapping bug.

The public static method `ModelToRepresentation.searchGroupModelsByAttributes(session, realm, attributes, first, max)` was removed outright (callers were updated to call `session.groups().searchGroupsByAttributes(...)` directly in GroupsResource). Although this class lives in server-spi-private, it is a public API surface; removing a public method without a deprecation cycle can break any other internal or external module that still references it directly, since there is no compiler-visible deprecation warning period.

Removed short-circuit for global group-view permission when listing subgroups

getSubGroups() previously computed `canViewGlobal = auth.groups().canView()` once and used `.filter(g -> canViewGlobal || auth.groups().canView(g))`, short-circuiting per-subgroup evaluation when the caller already has global view rights. The change replaces this with `.filter(auth.groups()::canView)`, which invokes canView(GroupModel) for every subgroup even when the admin already has global view permission. For FGAP V2, canView(GroupModel) performs a resource lookup and policy evaluation per call, so for groups with many subgroups this reintroduces an evaluation (and potential DB query) per subgroup instead of a single check, which is a performance regression compared to the previous behavior.

Removed short-circuit for global group-view permission when listing top-level groups

getGroups() previously cached `canViewGlobal = groupsEvaluator.canView()` and used `.filter(g -> canViewGlobal || groupsEvaluator.canView(g))` to avoid a per-group permission evaluation when the caller already has blanket view rights. This was changed to `.filter(groupsEvaluator::canView)`, so canView(GroupModel) — which for FGAP V2 can trigger a resource lookup and policy evaluation — now runs once per group returned by the query instead of being short-circuited by a single global check, which can be a notable performance regression for realms with many groups.

getResourceName() does not resolve a friendly display name for Group resources

getResourceName() special-cases USERS_RESOURCE_TYPE to translate the resource's internal name (the user's UUID) into the user's username (or 'All users' for the catch-all resource), but no equivalent branch was added for the newly introduced GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE even though group resources are created the same way (named by the group's UUID via resolveGroup()). As a consequence, any UI or API that calls getResourceName() for a group-scoped scope-permission will fall through to `resource.getDisplayName()` and show the raw group UUID (or whatever default display name is stored) instead of the group's actual name, unlike the symmetric behavior implemented for Users.

```
if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;
return isUUID().matches(items[1]);
```
Two problems: (1) the grant-type shortcut occupies characters 4-5 (0-indexed) of the 6-char context prefix (2 chars session type + 2 chars token type + 2 chars grant type), so `substring(3, 5)` is off by one and will essentially never equal the intended shortcut; (2) even if the indices were correct, the condition is inverted — it returns `false` (no match) when the shortcut *does* match, instead of when it does *not* match. Negative-offset "advanced" pagination path will raise a Django exception, not work as advertised

In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `enable_advanced_features` is set and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative `start_offset`.
