Misleading comment claims Django ORM "properly handles negative slicing automatically"

The comment above the negative-offset branch states that "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" and that the operation "is safe". This is factually incorrect — Django's QuerySet slicing explicitly rejects negative indices with a ValueError. The comment will mislead future maintainers into believing this code path is safe/functional when it is not (see the related bug finding), making debugging harder.

Shared BasePaginator.get_result modified for an audit-log-only feature, with a comment that contradicts the actual behavior

`BasePaginator.get_result` (used by `Paginator`, `DateTimePaginator`, and every other consumer across the codebase, not just the audit log endpoint) was changed to clamp offsets with `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`. The accompanying comment claims this change is meant to "allow negative offsets to enable efficient bidirectional pagination," but the code actually does the opposite — it clamps negative offsets to zero when not `cursor.is_prev`, silently discarding/changing behavior that previously would have surfaced as an error for a negative offset. Modifying this widely-shared base class for the sake of one experimental audit-log feature risks unintended regressions in dozens of unrelated paginated endpoints, and no new tests were added to validate the change against existing paginator behavior.

New query parameter bypasses the endpoint's existing validation serializer

`use_optimized = request.GET.get("optimized_pagination") == "true"` reads a raw GET parameter directly instead of going through `AuditLogQueryParamSerializer`, which is used for all other query parameters (`event`, `actor`). This is inconsistent with the endpoint's established validation pattern, is undocumented (the endpoint is marked EXPERIMENTAL but this parameter isn't reflected anywhere), and silently no-ops for any value other than the exact string "true" with no error feedback to the caller.

bleveBackend.TotalDocs() iterates over b.cache without acquiring cacheMu (neither RLock nor Lock), while BuildIndex() now writes to the same map under a lock that only protects the final cache assignment (b.cache[key] = idx). This PR adds a new call site for TotalDocs() in resource/search.go's searchSupport.init(), invoked immediately after the background watch-event goroutine is started (which can trigger new BuildIndex calls via getOrCreateIndex). false_positives.candidate:
Shared `err` and `totalBatchesIndexed` variables are written concurrently by multiple goroutines in searchSupport.init

In searchSupport.init(), the errgroup with SetLimit(s.initWorkers) launches one goroutine per namespace that does `totalBatchesIndexed++` and `_, _, err = s.build(...)` followed by `return err`, where both `err` and `totalBatchesIndexed` are variables shared across all goroutines without any synchronization (mutex/atomic). Previously this race was largely masked because bleve.BuildIndex held a single mutex across its entire body, effectively serializing the actual work done inside s.build() for different namespaces. This PR's locking change in bleve.go (lock now only guards the final cache write) removes that serialization, so multiple goroutines can now genuinely run s.build() concurrently, widening the race window. The consequence is real: one goroutine's error can be overwritten by another's success (or vice versa) before its own `return err` executes, so group.Wait() may incorrectly report success even though a particular namespace failed to build its index (or report a failure for a namespace that actually succeeded), and totalBatchesIndexed can lose increments. Given this path now runs synchronously at every server startup and failures are supposed to block startup, silently losing an error here is a data-integrity risk (a namespace could end up with a stale/missing index with no error surfaced).

NewResourceServer now blocks indefinitely on search index build with no timeout or cancellation path

NewResourceServer calls s.Init(ctx) synchronously before returning, and Init in turn calls searchSupport.init which builds the full search index for every namespace returned by GetResourceStats. The context used is derived from context.Background() with no deadline, so there is no bound on how long server construction can take for large installations with many/large namespaces. Previously this cost was paid lazily on the first gRPC call (which had its own problems per the PR description), but now any process that constructs a ResourceServer (app startup, tests, other callers) will block for however long index building takes, with no way to time out, report partial progress, or fail fast. This can turn into very long or hanging startups in production without any visible health/readiness signal during that window.

Init() is now a no-op if called again after construction, which may silently break other callers relying on it

Init() still uses sync.Once and is now invoked internally during NewResourceServer. Any other code path in the codebase that calls ResourceServer.Init(ctx) later (e.g. as part of a module/service lifecycle contract, with a different context carrying its own cancellation/tracing) will be a silent no-op because the Once has already fired during construction with an internally-created background context. The PR description itself raises this exact concern ("Does anything else depend on initializing US lazily? What could this break?") but the diff does not show any audit or update of such callers. If any lifecycle manager expects Init(ctx) to perform the actual initialization work tied to its own context, that expectation is now silently violated.

Trace-context propagation fix is incomplete — several spans still discard the updated context

The PR fixes span-context propagation in resource/search.go and in sql/backend.go's GetResourceStats (ctx, span := ...), but other methods in the same file still discard the span-carrying context with `_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, ...)` and then pass the original (un-updated) ctx to nested calls, e.g. WriteEvent (line 158, passing ctx to b.create/b.update/b.delete), ReadResource (line 353), and ListIterator (line 388, passing ctx to listAtRevision/listLatest). As a result, spans created inside create/update/delete, dbutil.QueryRow calls in ReadResource, and listAtRevision/listLatest will not be properly parented under the WriteEvent/Read/List spans, leaving the exact trace-propagation bug the PR claims to fix still present in several high-traffic code paths.

Postgres integration test skipped rather than fixed, potentially masking a startup regression from the new synchronous Init

This test exercises ResourceServer/module startup (waiting only 500ms for the HTTP server to become available) and is now skipped for postgres with the comment "test not working with postgres in Drone. Works locally." Given this PR moves ResourceServer initialization (including search index building) to be synchronous at construction time, it is plausible that the added latency is exactly what causes this test to fail intermittently under Drone's resource constraints for postgres. Skipping the test instead of investigating removes coverage for the very scenario (server startup timing) that this PR changes, and may hide a real regression rather than fixing it.

false_positives.candidate:
close()/terminate() permanently destroy the shared queue pool, breaking processing after any rebalance

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() (and terminate()) calls self.queue_pool.shutdown(), which stops all OrderedQueueWorker threads and shuts down every internal queue.Queue permanently. The FixedQueuePool instance, however, is created once in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__ and reused across every subsequent call to create_with_partitions (e.g. after Kafka partition rebalances) — exactly like parallel_executor/multiprocessing_pool in result_consumer.py, which are intentionally only torn down in ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown() at final process exit, never per-strategy-close. Because arroyo calls close()/terminate() on the current strategy whenever it is being replaced (which happens on every rebalance, not just final shutdown), the first rebalance kills the workers and shuts down the queues. Any create_with_partitions call afterwards reuses the now-dead queue_pool: submit() pushes items into shut-down queues (raising queue.ShutDown, silently caught and the offset marked 'complete' without any real processing), so messages after the first rebalance are effectively dropped while the consumer appears healthy.

Uses Python 3.13-only queue.Queue.shutdown()/queue.ShutDown API

FixedQueuePool.shutdown() calls q.shutdown(immediate=False), and OrderedQueueWorker.run() catches queue.ShutDown. Both queue.Queue.shutdown() and the queue.ShutDown exception were introduced in Python 3.13. On earlier Python runtimes, q.shutdown() raises AttributeError; since that call is wrapped in a bare 'except Exception', the failure is silently logged rather than propagated, meaning the queue is never actually put into a shutdown state. Worker threads blocked in work_queue.get() are consequently never woken and will hang indefinitely instead of shutting down, defeating the entire purpose of FixedQueuePool.shutdown()/close().

Offsets are marked complete (and committed) even when processing raises an exception

In OrderedQueueWorker.run(), the finally block always calls self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(...) regardless of whether result_processor succeeded or raised an exception caught by the preceding 'except Exception' clause. This contradicts the guarantee stated in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy's docstring ('Only commits offsets after successful processing'): a message whose processing failed is treated identically to a successfully processed one, so its offset becomes eligible for commit and will never be retried or reprocessed — a processing failure silently advances the committed offset past the failed message.

test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts behavior inconsistent with the implementation

This test mocks the result processor to raise on the first call and succeed on the second, then asserts `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`, implying a processing failure should block the offset commit. But per OrderedQueueWorker.run()'s finally block, offsets are always marked complete regardless of exceptions, so the commit loop should still compute and commit an offset for test_partition once both items complete (which happens almost immediately since the mocked calls return synchronously). This makes the assertion likely to fail or flake against the real implementation, or indicates the test does not actually validate any failure-handling guarantee.

Per-queue queue.Queue() has no maxsize, so the claimed backpressure doesn't exist

Each internal queue created in FixedQueuePool.__init__ (queue.Queue()) is unbounded, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() never raises arroyo's MessageRejected to signal backpressure regardless of queue depth. Despite the docstrings on FixedQueuePool and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy explicitly claiming 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', no bound is enforced anywhere, so a slow or stuck group (or an overall slow downstream) can grow its queue without limit while the consumer keeps reading from Kafka, risking unbounded memory growth instead of the intended backpressure.

get_committable_offsets iterates the offsets dict without a lock protecting its structure

get_committable_offsets() takes list(self.all_offsets.keys()) and then separately locks per-partition to read self.all_offsets[partition]. The all_offsets defaultdict's key set can be mutated from another thread calling add_offset for a partition never seen before (defaultdict.__missing__ inserting a new key) without any lock protecting the dict's structure itself — only the per-partition lock (created lazily, after the key may already need to be inserted) guards the inner set contents. Enumerating dict.keys() into a list while another thread inserts a new key concurrently can race, and in CPython can even raise RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration, which would crash the background commit loop thread.

Offset commits are issued from a dedicated background thread instead of the main strategy thread

_commit_loop runs on its own daemon thread started in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.__init__ and calls self.commit_function(committable), which ultimately invokes the arroyo `commit` callback passed into create_with_partitions. Arroyo processing strategies are designed to be driven single-threadedly by the StreamProcessor's main loop (submit/poll/join); none of the other modes in this same file (serial, parallel, batched-parallel) invoke the commit callback from a separate thread. Calling `commit` concurrently with the main thread's own poll()/submit() activity deviates from that contract and risks races in whatever internal bookkeeping the Commit implementation performs, since it is not documented/guaranteed to be safe for concurrent use from worker threads.

close() shuts down the queue pool without draining it first

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() immediately calls self.queue_pool.shutdown() without first calling the already-implemented FixedQueuePool.wait_until_empty() helper. FixedQueuePool.shutdown() only gives each worker a 5 second join() timeout; if there is still a backlog when close() runs, items may not finish processing within that window (a timed-out join() does not stop the thread, it just stops waiting), so close() can return while unprocessed/uncommitted work is still in flight, risking those messages being left in an inconsistent processed/committed state depending on what happens after close() returns.

Users/admins can keep seeing translations resolved under the old default locale until the 300-entry LRU naturally evicts those keys or the process restarts, producing stale/incorrect localized content.

Because the inner async call isn't returned, the outer promise resolves as soon as the delete/add request finishes, not after the member list reload (`findMembers`) completes. Any caller that chains off `removeMember()`/`addMembers()` to know when the UI data is fresh (current callers don't, but this is a latent bug) will get a false 'done' signal before `members`/`user_count` have actually been updated.

Unconditional group.save() after membership mutation can report an error after the change already persisted

`add_members` and `remove_member` call `group.add(user)` / `group.users.delete(user_id)` (which persist the membership change immediately via the join table), and then separately call `group.save` to decide the HTTP response. If `group.save` fails for any reason unrelated to membership (e.g. a validation on `name`/`alias_level` that happens to be in a bad state), the controller will return a 422 error even though the membership change already took effect in the database. The old `update_patch` code for incremental membership changes never checked `save` at all for this reason. This inconsistency between the reported result and actual persisted state can confuse the admin UI (which only calls `findMembers()` to refresh on success).

Breaking response-format change to /groups/:name/members.json has no accompanying test update

The `members` action's response shape changed from a plain serialized array to `{ members: [...], meta: { total, limit, offset } }`. This is a breaking change for any consumer of this JSON endpoint. No spec file for `GroupsController` is included in this PR's diff, so there is no verification that the new shape is correct, and any pre-existing spec asserting the old array format would now fail. The PR should add/update tests covering the new pagination metadata and format for this public endpoint.

Username input is not cleared after successfully adding members

The `addMembers` action contains `// TODO: should clear the input` and indeed never resets `this.get('usernames')` after a successful add. After adding members, the user-selector field retains the previously entered usernames, which can mislead the admin into re-submitting the same usernames or being confused about the current state of the input.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The remove_member test uses xhr :put to call the remove_member action, but the route defines delete 'members' => 'groups#remove_member' requiring DELETE method.
Expected to return a value at the end of function - code paths without explicit returns will return undefined

The route provides the group's ID in params[:id], but the code attempts to read it from params[:group_id], causing the action to fail. This results in a broken feature when trying to access group memberships.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
should_block? mutates and persists match stats as a side effect of validation, causing double counting

`BlockedEmail.should_block?` increments `match_count`, sets `last_match_at`, and saves the record every time it is called. It is invoked from `EmailValidator#validate_each` (lib/validators/email_validator.rb:13), which runs as part of `User` validations. `UsersController#create` (app/controllers/users_controller.rb:168) explicitly calls `user.valid?` before calling `user.save` (line 172), and `save` internally re-runs validations. Because `email_changed?` is true for a brand-new unsaved user both times, validations (and therefore the BlockedEmail side effect) run twice for every single sign-up attempt against a blocked address, so `match_count` is incremented twice (and `last_match_at` recomputed twice) per attempt, corrupting the very statistics this feature is meant to track. The side effect is also persisted outside of the `User` save/transaction (validations run before the AR save transaction begins), so the counters are updated even if the `User` save subsequently fails, or if `valid?` is called anywhere else (forms, specs, console) without ever creating a user.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the same design flaw: the predicate method (`should_block?` / `should_block_email?`) causes side effects by updating and saving match statistics during a read/check operation, leading to inaccurate statistics when just checking validity.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked email lookup and uniqueness are case-sensitive, allowing the block to be bypassed by case variation

`BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` and the `validates :email, presence: true, uniqueness: true` on line 5 do no case normalization. Elsewhere in the app, email comparisons are explicitly case-normalized (e.g. `UsersController#change_email` uses `Email.downcase`), but `BlockedEmail` does not. As a result, an admin who blocks "Spammer@EXAMPLE.com" will fail to block a sign-up using "spammer@example.com" (or any other casing variant), defeating the purpose of the feature. It also permits multiple rows for the same logical address differing only in case, since the uniqueness check is case-sensitive by default.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the same vulnerability: the email lookup in `BlockedEmail` is case-sensitive, which allows users to bypass the block by altering the casing of their email address.

false_positives.candidate:
Non-atomic match_count increment risks lost updates under concurrent requests

`record.match_count += 1; record.last_match_at = Time.zone.now; record.save` reads the counter into memory and writes it back without any locking or atomic SQL update. If two sign-up attempts for the same blocked email happen concurrently (a realistic scenario for exactly the kind of repeated spam/bot signups this feature targets), both requests can read the same starting value and each save overwrites the other's increment, silently losing hits/undercounting match_count. This should use an atomic update such as `update_counters`, `increment!`, or a raw SQL `match_count = match_count + 1`.

rejectedEmails default array literal is shared across controller instances and never reset

`rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` assigns a single array object as the default value directly on the controller definition instead of creating a fresh array per instance (e.g. via `init`). In Ember, object/array literals used as defaults this way are shared by reference across every instance created from the same class/mixin definition rather than instantiated per object — a well known Ember pitfall. Because the array is also never cleared anywhere (no reset on modal open/close or `init`), once an email is pushed into `rejectedEmails` it stays rejected for the lifetime of that shared array object. If the "Create Account" controller is ever recreated (e.g. the modal reopened, or in a shared/kiosk browser session), a previously rejected email — even from an unrelated earlier attempt, or one that the server would no longer reject (e.g. an admin unblocked it) — will continue to be permanently flagged invalid client-side with no way to retry short of a full page reload.

The domain-restriction logic (`email_in_restriction_setting?` plus the whitelist/blacklist branches) was moved out of `User` (previously `email_validator`/`email_in_restriction_setting?`, deleted from app/models/user.rb in this PR) into `lib/validators/email_validator.rb`. The new spec file only covers the new "blocked email" branch via `BlockedEmail.should_block?` and adds no example for `SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist`/`email_domains_blacklist` behavior, so this pre-existing, non-trivial logic is left untested after the refactor. Additionally, any prior spec that exercised the now-removed `User#email_validator`/`User#email_in_restriction_setting?` methods directly would fail since those methods no longer exist on `User`.

action_type column has no DB default or range validation, relying only on an app-level callback

The `action_type` column is declared `null: false` with no database default, and the only place a default is applied is the `before_validation :set_defaults` callback in app/models/blocked_email.rb (lines 21-23), which only runs through ActiveRecord's validation path. There is also no validation constraining `action_type` to the two defined enum values (`actions[:block]`/`actions[:do_nothing]`). The spec file's own comment ("If we manually load the table with some emails...") suggests bulk/manual loading is an expected use case; such inserts bypassing ActiveRecord callbacks would violate the NOT NULL constraint unless `action_type` is explicitly supplied, and any out-of-range value stored would silently be treated as "do nothing" by `should_block?`'s equality check rather than raising an error.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

true_positives.golden_comment: Mixing float: left with flexbox causes layout issues. Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.

Right-alignment of .panel now depends on unverified DOM nesting under the new flex container

`.panel` previously used `float: right;` to self-position within `.d-header`. It was changed to `margin-left: auto;` plus `@include order(3);`, which only right-aligns the element if `.panel` is a direct flex-item child of `.contents` (the element that now has `display: flex`). Likewise `.title { float: left; }` was removed entirely. If the actual template markup does not make `.title` and `.panel` direct children of `.contents` (e.g. if there is an intermediate wrapper), both the left title and the right-aligned panel will lose their positioning entirely, since no float fallback remains. The PR does not demonstrate (via markup reference, screenshot, or test) that this structural assumption holds.

true_positives.golden_comment: -ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.

Non-existent vendor-prefixed property in align-items mixin

This is not a property that Internet Explorer or any browser ever implemented (the correct and already-present IE10 flexbox alignment prefix is `-ms-flex-align`, on the preceding line). The `-ms-align-items` declaration is dead/invalid CSS that will be silently ignored by all browsers, adding no value and indicating the mixin wasn't verified against actual vendor-prefix requirements.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the exact same problem as the golden comment: that `-ms-align-items` is not a valid CSS property in any version of IE/Edge and that `-ms-flex-align` is the correct property.

Float-based child layout breaks after parent becomes a flex container

Per the CSS Flexbox spec, float has no effect on flex items (it is computed as none), so these declarations become dead code. In particular the action/dismiss button, which previously relied on float: right to sit at the far right of the row, now has no mechanism (no margin-left:auto, order, or justify-content) to stay right-aligned and will simply follow normal flex document order next to the description text. Since 1.5% is relative to the container width, the gap between the avatar icon and the description text will shrink or grow depending on viewport/container width instead of staying proportional to the fixed-size icon, and the removed vertical offsets likely alter text alignment versus the icon. No corresponding flex-basis/width was added to .topic-avatar to make this proportional spacing correct.

false_negatives.golden_comment: -webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.

`include_website_name` missing the `?` suffix breaks conditional inclusion

Every other manually-defined inclusion guard in this file follows the `include_#{attr}?` naming convention (e.g. `include_email?`, `include_card_image_badge_id?`, `include_card_image_badge?`, `include_suspend_reason?`), and the `untrusted_attributes`/`private_attributes` macros generate methods named with the trailing `?` as well. The newly added method is defined as `def include_website_name` (no `?`), so the serializer framework never calls it to decide whether to include the `website_name` attribute. As a result, `website_name` is unconditionally serialized for every user (even when `website` is blank, producing a `website_name: null` entry), instead of being gated by `website.present?` as intended.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the main point of the golden comment, which is that the `include_website_name` method is missing the required `?` suffix needed by the serializer for conditional attribute inclusion. Although the golden comment also mentions a secondary issue regarding string mutation (`'.' << website_host`), the core functional bug matches completely.

false_positives.candidate:
`website_name` is not covered by the `website` untrusted-attribute restriction, leaking site info to low-trust/anonymous viewers

`:website` is listed in `untrusted_attributes`, which hides it from anonymous viewers of TL0 users via `scope.restrict_user_fields?`. The new derived field `website_name` (added at line 43/137) is computed from the same `website` data but is not included in that `untrusted_attributes` list, and its own gate (`include_website_name`, see separate finding) never checks `scope.restrict_user_fields?`. Consequently, even when the raw `website` value is correctly hidden for a restricted viewer, the derived `website_name` (hostname or hostname+path) is still exposed in the API response, leaking information the attribute list was designed to protect.

Untrusted-attribute test does not cover the new `website_name` field

The `untrusted_attributes` array used by the "with a TL0 user seen as anonymous" spec (`%i{bio_raw bio_cooked bio_excerpt location website profile_background card_background}`) was not updated to include `:website_name`. Since `website_name` is derived from the restricted `website` field but is not actually hidden for untrusted/anonymous viewers (see related bug in `user_serializer.rb`), this test gives false confidence that sensitive website data is properly hidden; it does not fail despite the leak.

true_positives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
postMessage origin check uses substring match instead of exact comparison

`discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1` rejects a message only if `e.origin` cannot be found anywhere inside `discourseUrl`. Because `indexOf` performs a substring search rather than an origin equality check, an attacker-controlled origin that is merely a prefix/substring of the real discourseUrl (e.g. `http://example.co` when discourseUrl is `http://example.com/`) will pass this check and be allowed to send `discourse-resize` messages that control the iframe's height, defeating the intended origin restriction.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the same vulnerability: the origin validation uses `indexOf` (substring matching) instead of an exact origin check, allowing an attacker with a partial/matching domain name to bypass the check.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Access control relies solely on the client-supplied Referer header

`ensure_embeddable` authorizes embedding purely by comparing `request.referer`'s host to `SiteSetting.embeddable_host`. The Referer header is fully attacker-controlled on non-browser requests (curl, scripts, server-to-server calls), so this check can be trivially bypassed to call `/embed/best`, triggering TopicEmbed/TopicRetriever logic (including outbound HTTP fetches) for arbitrary allowed hosts without ever being embedded on the real site. It also doesn't verify scheme, so http and https referers are treated identically.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue point out the same security vulnerability in the embedding authorization mechanism: relying on the `Referer` header for validation/access control is insecure because referer headers are easily spoofed/attacker-controlled and can be trivially bypassed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
poll_feed assumes every feed item has a non-nil content field

`content = CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` calls `.scrub` directly on `i.content` without checking for nil. Many RSS 2.0 feeds only populate `description` and not a `content`/`content:encoded` element, so SimpleRSS would return nil for `i.content`, causing a NoMethodError that aborts processing of the entire feed for that run (sidekiq_options retry: false means the job silently fails with no retry).
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same bug: calling `.scrub` on `i.content` without checking for `nil`, as many RSS feeds only populate `description` and leave `content` nil, leading to a crash.

false_positives.candidate:
Unsanitized raw HTML from imported content rendered directly in embed view

Posts imported via TopicEmbed.import use cook_method raw_html (see app/models/post.rb Post#cook), which causes Post#cook to simply `return raw` and skip PrettyText's sanitization pipeline entirely. That raw content (scraped via Readability from arbitrary remote URLs, or pulled from an RSS/Atom feed) is then rendered unescaped here with `raw post.cooked`. Any script tags or event handlers present in the source page/feed will execute inside the embed iframe (and via postMessage/window.parent access can potentially reach the embedding site). Since the content source is an external, non-Discourse-controlled URL/feed, this is a stored XSS vector that bypasses the normal content-safety pipeline used for all other posts.

X-Frame-Options value 'ALLOWALL' is not a standard directive

The X-Frame-Options header only defines DENY, SAMEORIGIN and ALLOW-FROM <uri> as valid values. 'ALLOWALL' is not part of the spec; some browsers may ignore the unrecognized value (making the header a no-op) while others could treat it conservatively and block framing, which would silently break the embed feature for some users/browsers. Omitting the header (the real intent here) would be the correct way to allow framing by any origin.

Outbound fetch of user-controlled embed_url has no scheme/SSRF restriction

`import_remote` calls `open(url).read` (Kernel#open from open-uri) on a URL that ultimately originates from the public, unauthenticated `embed_url` query parameter in EmbedController#best. The only restriction applied upstream (TopicRetriever#invalid_host?) checks that the URI's host matches SiteSetting.embeddable_host, but the scheme, port, and full path are attacker-controlled. This allows triggering server-side requests to arbitrary ports/paths on the configured host (SSRF), and relies on the Kernel#open/open-uri pattern which is also known to execute shell commands if the string begins with a pipe character — a defense-in-depth concern given this value flows from request params through two layers before reaching open().

Unhandled race condition on unique embed_url constraint

`TopicEmbed.import` checks `embed = TopicEmbed.where(embed_url: url).first` and only creates a new TopicEmbed via `create!` if none exists. There's a unique index on embed_url (see db/migrate/20131217174004_create_topic_embeds.rb), but the check-then-create is not atomic. Two concurrent imports for the same URL (e.g. the hourly PollFeed job and a user-triggered RetrieveTopic job, which can itself invoke PollFeed synchronously — see lib/topic_retriever.rb) can both see `embed.blank?` as true and both attempt `TopicEmbed.create!`, causing one to raise an unhandled ActiveRecord error (RecordNotUnique/RecordInvalid) and crash the job instead of gracefully falling back to the update path.

TopicEmbed.import mutates the caller-supplied contents argument

`contents << "\n<hr>..."` mutates the string object passed in by the caller via the `<<` operator rather than creating a new string. This is a surprising side effect for callers that reuse the string afterward, and will raise a FrozenStringError if the caller passes a frozen string literal (e.g. under `# frozen_string_literal: true`), which is increasingly common in Ruby codebases.

Full feed poll executed synchronously and redundantly on every embed cache miss

`perform_retrieve` calls `Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` directly and synchronously (bypassing Jobs.enqueue) whenever feed polling is enabled and the requested embed isn't found. This means every single unmatched embed request re-fetches and re-processes the *entire* configured RSS/Atom feed inline within the RetrieveTopic job, duplicating the work already done by the hourly scheduled PollFeed job. Under load (many simultaneous first-time embed requests), this can cause repeated, expensive network fetches of the whole feed and increases the window for the race condition described in TopicEmbed.import.

feed_key method is defined but never used

`feed_key` builds a Redis key intended to track feed modification state (e.g. for conditional GET / Last-Modified caching), but it is never referenced anywhere in poll_feed.rb or elsewhere in the diff. This looks like an incomplete feature: the feed is always fully fetched and fully re-processed on every hourly run with no change-detection short-circuit, which is wasteful for large feeds and puts unnecessary load on the external feed source.

Pre-existing migration modified to add force: true

This migration (dated 2013-12-23) already existed prior to this PR and is being edited to add `force: true` to `create_table`. Editing an already-committed migration changes its behavior depending on whether an environment has already run it: environments that ran the old version have a table without the force-drop semantics, while fresh environments running the edited version will drop-and-recreate on every migrate (or fail unexpectedly on table already existing in edge cases). The correct approach is a new migration if the table needs to be recreated, to keep migration history reproducible across all environments.

disqus.thor loses category assignment and original thread timestamp without replacement

The `--category`/`-c` method_option and the category-resolution logic were removed entirely, and the topic-creation call was switched from `PostCreator.new(user, title:, raw:, created_at: Date.parse(t[:created_at]), category: category_id)` to `TopicEmbed.import_remote(user, t[:link], title: t[:title])`, which does not accept a category or created_at. This silently drops two previously supported behaviors (assigning an imported thread to a category, and preserving the original Disqus thread's creation date for the topic's first post) with no replacement, which will surprise existing users of this import task.

The spec covers 'missing embeddable_host' and 'missing referer' failure cases, but never exercises the actual host-mismatch branch of `ensure_embeddable` (`URI(request.referer).host != SiteSetting.embeddable_host`), which is the core security check of the controller. A regression in that comparison (e.g. the substring/case-sensitivity issues noted elsewhere) would not be caught by this test suite.

All tests in this file only verify the guard conditions in `execute` (feed_polling_enabled?, feed_polling_url, embed_by_username) and stub out `poll_feed` itself. The actual `poll_feed` method — RSS/Atom parsing via SimpleRSS, URL fallback logic, and the `CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` call that can raise on nil content — has no test coverage at all, so bugs such as the nil-content crash noted elsewhere would not be caught.

`discourse_expires_in 1.minute` is applied unconditionally regardless of whether the controller rendered the real topic view or the transient 'loading' placeholder (which itself auto-reloads client-side after 30 seconds, per app/views/embed/loading.html.erb). If this response is cached by any intermediary (browser cache, CDN), the client-side reload after 30s can be served the same stale cached 'loading' page for up to 60 seconds, delaying display of the actual content well past when it became available.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

true_positives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Percentage dimension string is invalid for gifsicle-based animated downsizing

`OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", allow_animation: SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails)` passes a percentage string as the resize dimension. When `allow_animation` is true and the file is a GIF, this routes to `downsize_instructions_animated` → `resize_instructions_animated`, which runs `gifsicle --resize-fit 80%`. Gifsicle's `--resize-fit`/`--resize` options require an explicit `WxH` pair and do not accept percentage syntax, so the command will fail. Consequence: animated GIFs larger than `max_image_size_kb` will never actually be downsized (the shell command errors out every iteration), the while loop will exhaust all 5 attempts without reducing the file, and the oversized/animated original will still be uploaded, defeating the stated purpose of the feature for this file type.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the exact same bug as the golden comment: passing '80%' as dimensions to OptimizedImage.downsize fails for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true because gifsicle --resize-fit requires WxH geometry rather than a percentage.

false_positives.candidate:
Downsizing an oversized animated GIF can permanently strip its animation

When `SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails` is false (the typical default), the downsizing call falls back to `downsize_instructions`, whose ImageMagick command reads `#{from}[0]` — i.e. only the first frame of the source. Because this logic is now applied directly to the user's original uploaded file (not just to a generated thumbnail), any animated GIF that exceeds `max_image_size_kb` will be silently converted into a static single-frame image before it is ever stored. This is a destructive, user-visible content change with no warning, caused purely by reusing thumbnail-oriented resize instructions on the original upload.

In-place resize uses the same path for input and output

`OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, ...)` uses the identical path for both the source and destination of the external `convert`/`gifsicle` command. Tools that open the output file for writing (truncating it) before fully reading/processing the input (gifsicle in particular, via `--output`) risk truncating or corrupting the source file before processing completes, resulting in a zero-byte or corrupted temp file being uploaded. A safer pattern is to write to a distinct temporary path and then replace the original once the conversion succeeds.

No handling for failed downsize attempts or files still over the limit after 5 tries

The loop `while attempt > 0 && tempfile.size > SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` calls `OptimizedImage.downsize` and decrements `attempt`, but never checks the boolean return value of `downsize` (which is false on shell-command failure) nor reports anything if, after 5 attempts, the file is still larger than `max_image_size_kb`. In both cases (repeated failures, or diminishing returns from 80% scaling not reaching the target), the code proceeds to call `Upload.create_for` with a file that may still exceed the configured size limit or may be corrupted, with no user-facing error or log entry indicating the size restriction was not honored.

Hardcoded 10MB cap replaces configurable max_image_size_kb for URL-based uploads

The API URL download limit changed from `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` to a hardcoded `10.megabytes`. This removes admin configurability: sites that configure `max_image_size_kb` smaller than 10MB will now allow larger downloads than intended before any downsizing occurs, and sites that configure it larger than 10MB can no longer fetch URLs beyond 10MB even though their own size policy would otherwise permit it. This also applies uniformly regardless of upload `type` (image vs. attachment), losing any type-specific limit that existed before.

413 error message now shows a hardcoded size instead of the configured max_image_size_kb

In `displayErrorForUpload`, the 413 (entity too large) handler replaced `Discourse.SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb` with a hardcoded `10 * 1024`. If the site's actual configured `max_image_size_kb` (or webserver/proxy upload limit) differs from 10MB, the error message presented to the user will state the wrong maximum allowed size, which is misleading and inconsistent with the rest of the validation logic.

No tests added for new image auto-downsizing behavior

This PR introduces non-trivial new logic (a bounded retry loop invoking external image-processing commands on the original uploaded file, with different code paths for animated vs. static images) but includes no new or updated specs covering it. Given the identified risks (gifsicle percentage argument failure, animation stripped from GIFs, in-place file corruption potential, and the changed `OptimizedImage.downsize` method signature), the lack of test coverage leaves these regressions and edge cases unverified before merge.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working-hours boundary check never evaluates the slot's end time

In the new working-hours check added to `checkIfIsAvailable`, both `start` and `end` are computed from `slotStartTime` (`const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();`). `end` should be derived from `slotEndTime` (i.e. slot start + event length) to verify the whole booking fits before the organizer's/fixed host's working hours end. Because `end` duplicates `start`, the check `end > workingHour.endTime` is equivalent to `start > workingHour.endTime`, so a slot whose start is inside the window but whose end (after adding eventLength) extends past the working-hours end time is not flagged as unavailable. This directly undermines the PR's stated goal of correctly respecting a fixed host's hours for round-robin events, allowing bookings that run past a fixed host's actual availability window.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue directly identifies the exact same bug as the golden comment: `end` time is being calculated using `slotStartTime` instead of `slotEndTime`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))

`if (dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes"))` compares two freshly created dayjs objects with `===`, which is always false regardless of their represented time, since they are different object references. This branch, apparently intended to detect a zero-duration date override (e.g. representing a fully blocked day), can never trigger. As written this is unreachable/dead logic, and any scenario relying on detecting start === end for an override silently falls through to the later branches instead of being handled as intended.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: comparing two newly created dayjs objects with `===` compares object references rather than values, causing the condition to always evaluate to false.

false_positives.candidate:
Date-override day matching depends on implicit server-local timezone

The date-override day match (`dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes").format("YYYY MM DD") === slotStartTime.format("YYYY MM DD")`) builds `dayjs(date.start)` without `.utc()`, so its displayed date/format depends on the Node process's local timezone. `slotStartTime`, however, is explicitly `.utc()`. If the server (or a developer's machine, or CI) is not running with TZ=UTC, this comparison can disagree with the rest of the file, which consistently uses explicit `.utc()`/`.tz()` conversions elsewhere, causing date overrides to be matched to the wrong day or missed entirely depending on deployment environment.

No test covers the primary fix: fixed-host date overrides blocking round-robin slots

The PR description states its main purpose is to make date overrides of fixed hosts taken into account for round-robin events so slots aren't offered when a fixed host is unavailable. The only test changes add a second timezone assertion to the existing single-user 'Check for Date overrides' test (no scheduling type / no hosts). There is no new test combining a ROUND_ROBIN event with a fixed host that has a date override and a non-fixed round-robin host that is available, to verify that the slot is excluded. Given the newly added/changed availability logic in `checkIfIsAvailable` (working hours and date-override checks per fixed host) contains at least one concrete bug (see other findings), this is exactly the scenario that should have automated coverage but does not.

Override timezone offset computed from a field that is typed optional without a fallback

`const organizerUtcOffset = dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone).utcOffset();` passes `override.timeZone` directly to `.tz()`. `TimeRange.timeZone` (packages/types/schedule.d.ts) is declared optional (`timeZone?: string`), so nothing in the type system guarantees it is set. If any caller of `getSlots`/`getTimeSlots` supplies `dateOverrides` without a `timeZone` (the field was only newly introduced and is only populated by the one call site touched in this PR), `.tz(undefined)` will silently fall back to some default/local timezone behavior rather than failing, producing incorrect offsets and therefore incorrect override slot times instead of a clear error.

Override offset adjustment can cross midnight but only the time-of-day is kept

The new override start/end computation shifts `override.start`/`override.end` by `offset` minutes (the difference between invitee and organizer UTC offsets) and then extracts only `.hour() * 60 + .minute()`. When the offset difference between organizer and invitee pushes the adjusted time across a day boundary (common for large timezone differences, e.g. near the International Date Line), the date portion is discarded and only the wrapped time-of-day is kept, which can make the override appear to apply on the wrong day or produce an incorrect time window instead of being excluded/moved to the adjacent day.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:

`prisma` is used without being imported, breaking compilation/runtime

The new refresh-token logic in getClient() calls `await prisma.credential.update(...)`, but this file never imports `prisma` (no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"` was added despite the new usage). This will fail TypeScript type-checking ("Cannot find name 'prisma'") and, if it somehow passes a build, will throw a ReferenceError at runtime the first time a Salesforce credential needs a token refresh, breaking the Salesforce integration entirely.

Salesforce token refresh bypasses refreshOAuthTokens, so credential sync never applies to Salesforce

Unlike every other updated provider (google, hubspot, office365, zoho-bigin, zohocrm, zoom, webex), the Salesforce CalendarService calls `fetch("https://login.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/token", ...)` directly instead of going through `refreshOAuthTokens`. As a result, even when APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are configured, Salesforce token refresh will always hit Salesforce directly and never use the self-hoster's sync endpoint, silently excluding Salesforce from the feature this PR advertises.

Webhook secret comparison is not constant-time

The shared-secret check `req.headers[...] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` uses a plain string inequality comparison. This is vulnerable to timing attacks that can let an attacker incrementally guess the secret by measuring response-time differences. A constant-time comparison (e.g. `crypto.timingSafeEqual` on buffers of equal length) should be used for secret/token verification on a publicly reachable endpoint.

Ambiguous credential lookup can overwrite the wrong credential

`prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { userId, appId } })` does not disambiguate between multiple credentials a user may have for the same app (e.g. multiple Google Calendar or Office365 accounts connected under the same appId). If more than one credential row matches, `findFirst` picks an arbitrary one and the subsequent `update` will overwrite that record's `key`, potentially corrupting an unrelated, working connection for a different account than the one the self-hoster intended to sync. The request schema has no way to target a specific credential (e.g. an external account id), making this unsafe for any app that supports multiple accounts per user.

No HTTP method restriction on the webhook handler

The handler does not check `req.method`, so GET/PUT/DELETE requests are processed identically to POST. For non-POST requests the body will typically be empty/invalid, causing the unguarded `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` call to throw, which is not caught anywhere in the handler and will surface as an unhandled exception/500 instead of a clean 405 Method Not Allowed response.

Redirect URI hardcoded instead of derived from appConfig.slug

This change replaces `WEBAPP_URL + \`/api/integrations/${appConfig.slug}/callback\`` with a hardcoded `WEBAPP_URL + \`/api/integrations/zoho-bigin/callback\``, while `zoho-bigin/api/callback.ts` still builds its redirect URI dynamically from `appConfig.slug`. This introduces an inconsistency: if `appConfig.slug` ever changes, the authorize URL and the token-exchange redirect URI will diverge, breaking the OAuth flow (redirect_uri mismatch errors from the provider). This change is unrelated to the credential-sync feature and appears to be an unintended regression.

No automated tests for the new credential-sync webhook or token-refresh helpers

This PR introduces a new externally reachable webhook endpoint that decrypts and writes arbitrary third-party OAuth credentials into the database, plus shared helpers (parseRefreshTokenResponse, refreshOAuthTokens) used across nine app integrations. None of this new, security- and data-integrity-sensitive logic has accompanying unit/integration tests (the PR description explicitly states no tests were added), despite the bugs identified in parseRefreshTokenResponse/refreshOAuthTokens that tests would likely have caught.

false_positives.candidate:
Reschedule flow cancels old EMAIL reminders immediately via SendGrid, reintroducing the exact limit bug this PR fixes

When rescheduling a booking, the old booking's EMAIL workflow reminders are cancelled with `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId, true)` — the `immediateDelete=true` flag causes an immediate SendGrid 'cancel' API call. According to the PR description, calling this SendGrid endpoint immediately is exactly what caused the original bug: SendGrid only allows up to 100 pending cancellations, and once that limit is hit, new cancellations fail silently and reminder emails keep being sent. The fix elsewhere (handleCancelBooking.ts, bookings.tsx `requestReschedule`) correctly avoids this by calling `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId)` without the immediate flag, deferring the actual SendGrid cancellation to the new CRON job that only cancels within the last hour before send. This reschedule code path is the one explicitly named in the PR title ('...and rescheduled bookings...') yet still uses the broken immediate-cancel strategy, so under moderate reschedule volume the same SendGrid pending-cancellation limit can be hit again and reminder emails for rescheduled bookings can still be sent.

A single failed SendGrid cancellation aborts cancellation of all other reminders in the same cron run

The new cancellation loop wraps the entire `for (const reminder of remindersToCancel)` loop (including the SendGrid `client.request` call for every reminder and the final `Promise.all`) in one try/catch. If the SendGrid cancel request throws for one reminder (e.g. transient network error, stale/invalid batch id), the loop stops immediately and none of the remaining reminders in that batch get their cancellation request sent during this cron invocation, nor are their WorkflowReminder rows deleted. Because the cron only runs every 15 minutes and only reminders due within the next hour are considered, a persistently-failing single entry can repeatedly block processing of the rest of the batch on every subsequent run (since the same failing item is encountered again before reaching later items), risking that otherwise-cancellable reminders are still sent by SendGrid because the cancel call never reaches them in time. Cancellation and deletion should be handled per-item with its own try/catch so one failure doesn't block the others.

Old booking's workflow reminders are cancelled before confirming the reschedule actually succeeded

The cancellation of `originalRescheduledBooking.workflowReminders` happens unconditionally right before calling `eventManager.reschedule(...)`, regardless of whether that reschedule call later succeeds. Further down, the code explicitly checks `if (results.length > 0 && results.some((res) => !res.success))` and merely logs an error without rolling back — the booking's calendar/video integrations may fail, but the original booking's reminders have already been cancelled irreversibly (for EMAIL, moved to immediate-SendGrid-cancel / for SMS, outright deleted from Twilio and the DB). This can leave a booking that effectively did not get successfully rescheduled with no reminders scheduled at all.

Defense-in-depth ownership check dropped from WorkflowReminder cancel/delete mutations

Previously (e.g. in workflows.tsx update mutation) the WorkflowReminder deletion query included an ownership guard directly in the Prisma `where` clause (`booking: { userId: ctx.user.id }`), so even if an upstream bug allowed another user's reminder id to reach this code, the mutation itself would affect 0 rows. The new shared helpers `deleteScheduledEmailReminder`/`deleteScheduledSMSReminder` (used from multiple callers including trpc routers) perform `update`/`delete` solely by `id`, with no ownership check baked into the query. This removes a layer of protection against reminder ids leaking across callers/users and now relies entirely on each caller's upstream query having correctly scoped the reminder list.

Generic past-due cleanup can delete a cancelled reminder before its SendGrid cancellation request is ever sent

The handler first runs an unconditional cleanup: `prisma.workflowReminder.deleteMany({ where: { method: EMAIL, scheduledDate: { lte: now } } })`, deleting any EMAIL reminder whose scheduledDate has passed, regardless of its `cancelled` flag. This runs before the new cancellation block that queries `cancelled: true` reminders due within the next hour. Because the cron runs every 15 minutes, if a reminder is marked `cancelled: true` less than one cron interval before its `scheduledDate`, the next cron execution may find `scheduledDate <= now` already true by the time it runs and delete the row in the first cleanup step — without ever having issued the SendGrid 'cancel' request for it. If SendGrid had not yet actually sent the email at that instant, it will still go out as originally scheduled, since it was never told to cancel. This narrow but real race window undermines the PR's goal for reminders cancelled close to their send time.

No automated tests for the new cancellation logic despite history of a broken prior fix

The PR description states that the previous fix (PR #6991) for this exact issue 'was wrong and didn't work as expected.' This PR introduces new, non-trivial logic (the `cancelled` flag lifecycle across emailReminderManager.ts, smsReminderManager.ts, and the new cron cancellation block in scheduleEmailReminders.ts) that is central to actually fixing the reported bug, yet no unit/integration tests are added to verify that cancelled/rescheduled bookings' scheduled reminders are correctly prevented from sending. Given the history of this exact feature being silently broken in production, the lack of test coverage is a significant risk for a repeat regression.

However: (1) individual per-group resources are created via AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource(), which never calls resource.setType(...) (unlike the legacy V1 GroupPermissions.initialize(), which explicitly sets `groupResource.setType("Group")`), so findByType(server, "Groups", ...) will not find per-group resources at all — it will only match the single 'all-groups' placeholder resource created during schema init (which does have its type set). (2) Even for that placeholder, `groupResource.getId()` is the authorization resource's own internal ID, not a GroupModel id; hasPermission(String groupId, ...) expects a real GroupModel id (it looks the resource up via `resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId)`, and resources are named by the group's id per resolveGroup()). In `isAccessTokenId(String expectedGrantShortcut)`, the matcher does:
```
if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;
return isUUID().matches(items[1]);
```
Two problems: (1) the grant-type shortcut occupies characters 4-5 (0-indexed) of the 6-char context prefix (2 chars session type + 2 chars token type + 2 chars grant type), so `substring(3, 5)` is off by one and will essentially never equal the intended shortcut; (2) even if the indices were correct, the condition is inverted — it returns `false` (no match) when the shortcut *does* match, instead of when it does *not* match. The net effect is that this matcher never actually validates that the token id encodes the expected grant-type shortcut; it effectively degenerates to just checking the UUID portion, silently passing regardless of the grant type encoded. All call sites added in this same file (`expectCodeToToken`, `expectDeviceCodeToToken`, `expectRefresh`, `expectAuthReqIdToToken`) rely on this broken matcher, so the new assertions provide no real verification of the grant-type encoding feature and could mask regressions.

false_positives.candidate:
close()/terminate() permanently destroy the shared queue pool, breaking processing after any rebalance

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() (and terminate()) calls self.queue_pool.shutdown(), which stops all OrderedQueueWorker threads and shuts down every internal queue.Queue permanently. The FixedQueuePool instance, however, is created once in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__ and reused across every subsequent call to create_with_partitions (e.g. after Kafka partition rebalances) — exactly like parallel_executor/multiprocessing_pool in result_consumer.py, which are intentionally only torn down in ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown() at final process exit, never per-strategy-close. Because arroyo calls close()/terminate() on the current strategy whenever it is being replaced (which happens on every rebalance, not just final shutdown), the first rebalance kills the workers and shuts down the queues. Any create_with_partitions call afterwards reuses the now-dead queue_pool: submit() pushes items into shut-down queues (raising queue.ShutDown, silently caught and the offset marked 'complete' without any real processing), so messages after the first rebalance are effectively dropped while the consumer appears healthy.

Uses Python 3.13-only queue.Queue.shutdown()/queue.ShutDown API

FixedQueuePool.shutdown() calls q.shutdown(immediate=False), and OrderedQueueWorker.run() catches queue.ShutDown. Both queue.Queue.shutdown() and the queue.ShutDown exception were introduced in Python 3.13. On earlier Python runtimes, q.shutdown() raises AttributeError; since that call is wrapped in a bare 'except Exception', the failure is silently logged rather than propagated, meaning the queue is never actually put into a shutdown state. Worker threads blocked in work_queue.get() are consequently never woken and will hang indefinitely instead of shutting down, defeating the entire purpose of FixedQueuePool.shutdown()/close().

Offsets are marked complete (and committed) even when processing raises an exception

In OrderedQueueWorker.run(), the finally block always calls self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(...) regardless of whether result_processor succeeded or raised an exception caught by the preceding 'except Exception' clause. This contradicts the guarantee stated in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy's docstring ('Only commits offsets after successful processing'): a message whose processing failed is treated identically to a successfully processed one, so its offset becomes eligible for commit and will never be retried or reprocessed — a processing failure silently advances the committed offset past the failed message.

test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts behavior inconsistent with the implementation

This test mocks the result processor to raise on the first call and succeed on the second, then asserts `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`, implying a processing failure should block the offset commit. But per OrderedQueueWorker.run()'s finally block, offsets are always marked complete regardless of exceptions, so the commit loop should still compute and commit an offset for test_partition once both items complete (which happens almost immediately since the mocked calls return synchronously). This makes the assertion likely to fail or flake against the real implementation, or indicates the test does not actually validate any failure-handling guarantee.

Per-queue queue.Queue() has no maxsize, so the claimed backpressure doesn't exist

Each internal queue created in FixedQueuePool.__init__ (queue.Queue()) is unbounded, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() never raises arroyo's MessageRejected to signal backpressure regardless of queue depth. Despite the docstrings on FixedQueuePool and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy explicitly claiming 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', no bound is enforced anywhere, so a slow or stuck group (or an overall slow downstream) can grow its queue without limit while the consumer keeps reading from Kafka, risking unbounded memory growth instead of the intended backpressure.

get_committable_offsets iterates the offsets dict without a lock protecting its structure

get_committable_offsets() takes list(self.all_offsets.keys()) and then separately locks per-partition to read self.all_offsets[partition]. The all_offsets defaultdict's key set can be mutated from another thread calling add_offset for a partition never seen before (defaultdict.__missing__ inserting a new key) without any lock protecting the dict's structure itself — only the per-partition lock (created lazily, after the key may already need to be inserted) guards the inner set contents. Enumerating dict.keys() into a list while another thread inserts a new key concurrently can race, and in CPython can even raise RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration, which would crash the background commit loop thread.

Offset commits are issued from a dedicated background thread instead of the main strategy thread

_commit_loop runs on its own daemon thread started in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.__init__ and calls self.commit_function(committable), which ultimately invokes the arroyo `commit` callback passed into create_with_partitions. Arroyo processing strategies are designed to be driven single-threadedly by the StreamProcessor's main loop (submit/poll/join); none of the other modes in this same file (serial, parallel, batched-parallel) invoke the commit callback from a separate thread. Calling `commit` concurrently with the main thread's own poll()/submit() activity deviates from that contract and risks races in whatever internal bookkeeping the Commit implementation performs, since it is not documented/guaranteed to be safe for concurrent use from worker threads.

close() shuts down the queue pool without draining it first

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() immediately calls self.queue_pool.shutdown() without first calling the already-implemented FixedQueuePool.wait_until_empty() helper. FixedQueuePool.shutdown() only gives each worker a 5 second join() timeout; if there is still a backlog when close() runs, items may not finish processing within that window (a timed-out join() does not stop the thread, it just stops waiting), so close() can return while unprocessed/uncommitted work is still in flight, risking those messages being left in an inconsistent processed/committed state depending on what happens after close() returns.

`userPermDenialCacheKey(checkReq.Namespace.Value, checkReq.UserUID, checkReq.Action, checkReq.Name, checkReq.ParentFolder)` (defined in pkg/services/authz/rbac/cache.go) builds the cache key purely from the parsed subject UID, action, name and parent folder, without including the identity type.
