Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`include_website_name` missing the `?` suffix breaks conditional inclusion

Every other manually-defined inclusion guard in this file follows the `include_#{attr}?` naming convention (e.g. `include_email?`, `include_card_image_badge_id?`, `include_card_image_badge?`, `include_suspend_reason?`), and the `untrusted_attributes`/`private_attributes` macros generate methods named with the trailing `?` as well. The newly added method is defined as `def include_website_name` (no `?`), so the serializer framework never calls it to decide whether to include the `website_name` attribute. As a result, `website_name` is unconditionally serialized for every user (even when `website` is blank, producing a `website_name: null` entry), instead of being gated by `website.present?` as intended.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same missing '?' suffix on include_website_name and its effect on conditional serialization. It does not mention the additional string-literal mutation concern, but matches the golden comment's primary issue.

false_positives.candidate:
`website_name` is not covered by the `website` untrusted-attribute restriction, leaking site info to low-trust/anonymous viewers

`:website` is listed in `untrusted_attributes`, which hides it from anonymous viewers of TL0 users via `scope.restrict_user_fields?`. The new derived field `website_name` (added at line 43/137) is computed from the same `website` data but is not included in that `untrusted_attributes` list, and its own gate (`include_website_name`, see separate finding) never checks `scope.restrict_user_fields?`. Consequently, even when the raw `website` value is correctly hidden for a restricted viewer, the derived `website_name` (hostname or hostname+path) is still exposed in the API response, leaking information the attribute list was designed to protect.

Untrusted-attribute test does not cover the new `website_name` field

The `untrusted_attributes` array used by the "with a TL0 user seen as anonymous" spec (`%i{bio_raw bio_cooked bio_excerpt location website profile_background card_background}`) was not updated to include `:website_name`. Since `website_name` is derived from the restricted `website` field but is not actually hidden for untrusted/anonymous viewers (see related bug in `user_serializer.rb`), this test gives false confidence that sensitive website data is properly hidden; it does not fail despite the leak.

true_positives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
postMessage origin check uses substring match instead of exact comparison

`discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1` rejects a message only if `e.origin` cannot be found anywhere inside `discourseUrl`. Because `indexOf` performs a substring search rather than an origin equality check, an attacker-controlled origin that is merely a prefix/substring of the real discourseUrl (e.g. `http://example.co` when discourseUrl is `http://example.com/`) will pass this check and be allowed to send `discourse-resize` messages that control the iframe's height, defeating the intended origin restriction.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same origin-validation vulnerability: using indexOf performs substring matching rather than exact origin comparison, allowing an attacker-controlled origin to bypass the restriction. The differing example domains do not change the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Access control relies solely on the client-supplied Referer header

`ensure_embeddable` authorizes embedding purely by comparing `request.referer`'s host to `SiteSetting.embeddable_host`. The Referer header is fully attacker-controlled on non-browser requests (curl, scripts, server-to-server calls), so this check can be trivially bypassed to call `/embed/best`, triggering TopicEmbed/TopicRetriever logic (including outbound HTTP fetches) for arbitrary allowed hosts without ever being embedded on the real site. It also doesn't verify scheme, so http and https referers are treated identically.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same reliance on spoofable Referer headers for embedding authorization. It omits the ALLOWALL clickjacking exposure and nil-referer fallback, and describes different consequences, but matches the golden comment's underlying referer-validation bypass.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
poll_feed assumes every feed item has a non-nil content field

`content = CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` calls `.scrub` directly on `i.content` without checking for nil. Many RSS 2.0 feeds only populate `description` and not a `content`/`content:encoded` element, so SimpleRSS would return nil for `i.content`, causing a NoMethodError that aborts processing of the entire feed for that run (sidekiq_options retry: false means the job silently fails with no retry).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: calling `.scrub` on `i.content` without a nil check crashes for RSS feeds that provide only `description`. The candidate matches the underlying issue even though it does not explicitly recommend the fallback.

false_positives.candidate:
Unsanitized raw HTML from imported content rendered directly in embed view

Posts imported via TopicEmbed.import use cook_method raw_html (see app/models/post.rb Post#cook), which causes Post#cook to simply `return raw` and skip PrettyText's sanitization pipeline entirely. That raw content (scraped via Readability from arbitrary remote URLs, or pulled from an RSS/Atom feed) is then rendered unescaped here with `raw post.cooked`. Any script tags or event handlers present in the source page/feed will execute inside the embed iframe (and via postMessage/window.parent access can potentially reach the embedding site). Since the content source is an external, non-Discourse-controlled URL/feed, this is a stored XSS vector that bypasses the normal content-safety pipeline used for all other posts.

X-Frame-Options value 'ALLOWALL' is not a standard directive

The X-Frame-Options header only defines DENY, SAMEORIGIN and ALLOW-FROM <uri> as valid values. 'ALLOWALL' is not part of the spec; some browsers may ignore the unrecognized value (making the header a no-op) while others could treat it conservatively and block framing, which would silently break the embed feature for some users/browsers. Omitting the header (the real intent here) would be the correct way to allow framing by any origin.

Outbound fetch of user-controlled embed_url has no scheme/SSRF restriction

`import_remote` calls `open(url).read` (Kernel#open from open-uri) on a URL that ultimately originates from the public, unauthenticated `embed_url` query parameter in EmbedController#best. The only restriction applied upstream (TopicRetriever#invalid_host?) checks that the URI's host matches SiteSetting.embeddable_host, but the scheme, port, and full path are attacker-controlled. This allows triggering server-side requests to arbitrary ports/paths on the configured host (SSRF), and relies on the Kernel#open/open-uri pattern which is also known to execute shell commands if the string begins with a pipe character — a defense-in-depth concern given this value flows from request params through two layers before reaching open().

Unhandled race condition on unique embed_url constraint

`TopicEmbed.import` checks `embed = TopicEmbed.where(embed_url: url).first` and only creates a new TopicEmbed via `create!` if none exists. There's a unique index on embed_url (see db/migrate/20131217174004_create_topic_embeds.rb), but the check-then-create is not atomic. Two concurrent imports for the same URL (e.g. the hourly PollFeed job and a user-triggered RetrieveTopic job, which can itself invoke PollFeed synchronously — see lib/topic_retriever.rb) can both see `embed.blank?` as true and both attempt `TopicEmbed.create!`, causing one to raise an unhandled ActiveRecord error (RecordNotUnique/RecordInvalid) and crash the job instead of gracefully falling back to the update path.

TopicEmbed.import mutates the caller-supplied contents argument

`contents << "\n<hr>..."` mutates the string object passed in by the caller via the `<<` operator rather than creating a new string. This is a surprising side effect for callers that reuse the string afterward, and will raise a FrozenStringError if the caller passes a frozen string literal (e.g. under `# frozen_string_literal: true`), which is increasingly common in Ruby codebases.

Full feed poll executed synchronously and redundantly on every embed cache miss

`perform_retrieve` calls `Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` directly and synchronously (bypassing Jobs.enqueue) whenever feed polling is enabled and the requested embed isn't found. This means every single unmatched embed request re-fetches and re-processes the *entire* configured RSS/Atom feed inline within the RetrieveTopic job, duplicating the work already done by the hourly scheduled PollFeed job. Under load (many simultaneous first-time embed requests), this can cause repeated, expensive network fetches of the whole feed and increases the window for the race condition described in TopicEmbed.import.

feed_key method is defined but never used

`feed_key` builds a Redis key intended to track feed modification state (e.g. for conditional GET / Last-Modified caching), but it is never referenced anywhere in poll_feed.rb or elsewhere in the diff. This looks like an incomplete feature: the feed is always fully fetched and fully re-processed on every hourly run with no change-detection short-circuit, which is wasteful for large feeds and puts unnecessary load on the external feed source.

Pre-existing migration modified to add force: true

This migration (dated 2013-12-23) already existed prior to this PR and is being edited to add `force: true` to `create_table`. Editing an already-committed migration changes its behavior depending on whether an environment has already run it: environments that ran the old version have a table without the force-drop semantics, while fresh environments running the edited version will drop-and-recreate on every migrate (or fail unexpectedly on table already existing in edge cases). The correct approach is a new migration if the table needs to be recreated, to keep migration history reproducible across all environments.

disqus.thor loses category assignment and original thread timestamp without replacement

The `--category`/`-c` method_option and the category-resolution logic were removed entirely, and the topic-creation call was switched from `PostCreator.new(user, title:, raw:, created_at: Date.parse(t[:created_at]), category: category_id)` to `TopicEmbed.import_remote(user, t[:link], title: t[:title])`, which does not accept a category or created_at. This silently drops two previously supported behaviors (assigning an imported thread to a category, and preserving the original Disqus thread's creation date for the topic's first post) with no replacement, which will surprise existing users of this import task.

No test coverage for referer-host mismatch rejection

The spec covers 'missing embeddable_host' and 'missing referer' failure cases, but never exercises the actual host-mismatch branch of `ensure_embeddable` (`URI(request.referer).host != SiteSetting.embeddable_host`), which is the core security check of the controller. A regression in that comparison (e.g. the substring/case-sensitivity issues noted elsewhere) would not be caught by this test suite.

poll_feed's core RSS-processing logic is untested

All tests in this file only verify the guard conditions in `execute` (feed_polling_enabled?, feed_polling_url, embed_by_username) and stub out `poll_feed` itself. The actual `poll_feed` method — RSS/Atom parsing via SimpleRSS, URL fallback logic, and the `CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` call that can raise on nil content — has no test coverage at all, so bugs such as the nil-content crash noted elsewhere would not be caught.

Transient 'loading' placeholder response is cached for 1 minute like the final content

`discourse_expires_in 1.minute` is applied unconditionally regardless of whether the controller rendered the real topic view or the transient 'loading' placeholder (which itself auto-reloads client-side after 30 seconds, per app/views/embed/loading.html.erb). If this response is cached by any intermediary (browser cache, CDN), the client-side reload after 30s can be served the same stale cached 'loading' page for up to 60 seconds, delaying display of the actual content well past when it became available.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Duplicate `self.downsize` definition silently discards the original method

Two `def self.downsize` methods are now defined (lines 145-147 and 149-151) with different arities: `downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` and `downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})`. In Ruby, the second definition overwrites the first at load time (Ruby emits a 'method redefined' warning), so the original 4-argument signature becomes permanently unreachable. Any existing caller elsewhere in the codebase that calls `OptimizedImage.downsize(from, to, width, height, opts)` with four positional arguments will now raise an ArgumentError (wrong number of arguments) or silently misinterpret `height` as part of the options hash. This is dead/conflicting code that should be removed/merged rather than left as two definitions.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify duplicate downsize definitions where the later dimensions-string signature overrides the original width-and-height signature, making it unreachable and breaking existing callers.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client-side upload size validation no longer respects per-type site settings

`maxSizeKB` in `validateUploadedFile` was changed from `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']` to a hardcoded `10 * 1024`. This removes the distinction between image and attachment size limits and ignores whatever the admin has actually configured (e.g. `max_image_size_kb`, `max_attachment_size_kb`). As a result, client-side validation can now accept files that the server would reject (if the configured limit is lower than 10MB) or reject files the server would accept (if the configured limit is higher), and the error message shown to users will state an incorrect maximum size relative to the server's actual configuration.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same hardcoded upload size limit replacing per-type site settings, causing client-side limits and error messages to diverge from server configuration. Not mentioning the 413 handler does not change the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Percentage dimension string is invalid for gifsicle-based animated downsizing

`OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", allow_animation: SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails)` passes a percentage string as the resize dimension. When `allow_animation` is true and the file is a GIF, this routes to `downsize_instructions_animated` → `resize_instructions_animated`, which runs `gifsicle --resize-fit 80%`. Gifsicle's `--resize-fit`/`--resize` options require an explicit `WxH` pair and do not accept percentage syntax, so the command will fail. Consequence: animated GIFs larger than `max_image_size_kb` will never actually be downsized (the shell command errors out every iteration), the while loop will exhaust all 5 attempts without reducing the file, and the oversized/animated original will still be uploaded, defeating the stated purpose of the feature for this file type.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: passing "80%" for animated GIF downsizing when animation is allowed invokes gifsicle --resize-fit, which expects WxH geometry rather than percentage syntax, causing downsizing to fail.

false_positives.candidate:
Downsizing an oversized animated GIF can permanently strip its animation

When `SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails` is false (the typical default), the downsizing call falls back to `downsize_instructions`, whose ImageMagick command reads `#{from}[0]` — i.e. only the first frame of the source. Because this logic is now applied directly to the user's original uploaded file (not just to a generated thumbnail), any animated GIF that exceeds `max_image_size_kb` will be silently converted into a static single-frame image before it is ever stored. This is a destructive, user-visible content change with no warning, caused purely by reusing thumbnail-oriented resize instructions on the original upload.

In-place resize uses the same path for input and output

`OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, ...)` uses the identical path for both the source and destination of the external `convert`/`gifsicle` command. Tools that open the output file for writing (truncating it) before fully reading/processing the input (gifsicle in particular, via `--output`) risk truncating or corrupting the source file before processing completes, resulting in a zero-byte or corrupted temp file being uploaded. A safer pattern is to write to a distinct temporary path and then replace the original once the conversion succeeds.

No handling for failed downsize attempts or files still over the limit after 5 tries

The loop `while attempt > 0 && tempfile.size > SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` calls `OptimizedImage.downsize` and decrements `attempt`, but never checks the boolean return value of `downsize` (which is false on shell-command failure) nor reports anything if, after 5 attempts, the file is still larger than `max_image_size_kb`. In both cases (repeated failures, or diminishing returns from 80% scaling not reaching the target), the code proceeds to call `Upload.create_for` with a file that may still exceed the configured size limit or may be corrupted, with no user-facing error or log entry indicating the size restriction was not honored.

Hardcoded 10MB cap replaces configurable max_image_size_kb for URL-based uploads

The API URL download limit changed from `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` to a hardcoded `10.megabytes`. This removes admin configurability: sites that configure `max_image_size_kb` smaller than 10MB will now allow larger downloads than intended before any downsizing occurs, and sites that configure it larger than 10MB can no longer fetch URLs beyond 10MB even though their own size policy would otherwise permit it. This also applies uniformly regardless of upload `type` (image vs. attachment), losing any type-specific limit that existed before.

413 error message now shows a hardcoded size instead of the configured max_image_size_kb

In `displayErrorForUpload`, the 413 (entity too large) handler replaced `Discourse.SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb` with a hardcoded `10 * 1024`. If the site's actual configured `max_image_size_kb` (or webserver/proxy upload limit) differs from 10MB, the error message presented to the user will state the wrong maximum allowed size, which is misleading and inconsistent with the rest of the validation logic.

No tests added for new image auto-downsizing behavior

This PR introduces non-trivial new logic (a bounded retry loop invoking external image-processing commands on the original uploaded file, with different code paths for animated vs. static images) but includes no new or updated specs covering it. Given the identified risks (gifsicle percentage argument failure, animation stripped from GIFs, in-place file corruption potential, and the changed `OptimizedImage.downsize` method signature), the lack of test coverage leaves these regressions and edge cases unverified before merge.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash

`tu = TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])` can return nil, e.g. if the logged-in user navigates directly to `/t/:slug/:id/unsubscribe` for a topic they have never visited/been notified about (no TopicUser record has been created for that pair yet). The very next line, `tu.notification_level`, then raises `NoMethodError: undefined method 'notification_level' for nil:NilClass`, producing an unhandled 500 error instead of creating/updating the preference (e.g. via the existing `TopicUser.change` helper, which already handles record creation).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same nil dereference: when no TopicUser record exists, tu is nil and accessing tu.notification_level crashes.

true_positives.golden_comment: Typo in property name: 'stopNotificiationsText' should be 'stopNotificationsText' (missing 'n' in 'Notifications')
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Typo in computed property name stopNotificiationsText

The computed property is misspelled `stopNotificiationsText` (should be `stopNotificationsText`). It still works because the template at app/assets/javascripts/discourse/templates/topic/unsubscribe.hbs references the same misspelled name, but the typo makes the binding hard to discover via search and is a latent trap: fixing the spelling in only one of the two files later will silently break the unsubscribe page's message.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same misspelled property, `stopNotificiationsText`, and specify the same correction to `stopNotificationsText`.

false_positives.candidate: Unsubscribe mutates notification state via a GET request with no CSRF protection The `unsubscribe` action calls `tu.save!` to change the user's topic notification level, but it is only reachable via GET (`skip_before_filter :check_xhr, only: [:show, :unsubscribe, :feed]` and `get "t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe"` in config/routes.rb). Rails' CSRF protection does not cover GET requests, so any authenticated user whose browser loads this URL as a side effect (e.g. an `` embedded on another page, a link preview/prefetch by an email client, or a security scanner following links) will have their topic subscription silently changed without consent. State-mutating actions should not be exposed as unprotected GET endpoints.

Unsubscribe copy overstates the effect for watching/tracking users

When the user's current notification_level is above `regular` (e.g. `watching` or `tracking`), the action only downgrades them to `regular` rather than muting (lines 107-111), but the user-facing text shown immediately after (`topic.unsubscribe.stop_notifications` in config/locales/client.en.yml: "You will stop receiving notifications for <title>") and the equivalent copy in the email (`unsubscribe_link` in config/locales/server.en.yml) both unconditionally claim all notifications for the topic will stop. A user who was `watching`/`tracking` and is merely downgraded to `regular` can still receive notifications for direct replies/mentions, contradicting what they were told.

unsubscribe_link translation now requires unsubscribe_url, risking MissingInterpolationArgument for other callers

The shared `unsubscribe_link` i18n string was changed to require a new `%{unsubscribe_url}` interpolation value. `Email::MessageBuilder#body` and `#html_part` (lib/email/message_builder.rb) call `I18n.t('unsubscribe_link', template_args)` whenever `opts[:add_unsubscribe_link]` is truthy, regardless of whether `unsubscribe_url` was supplied. Only `UserNotifications#send_notification_email` was updated in this PR to pass `unsubscribe_url`; any other existing or future caller of `build_email`/`MessageBuilder` with `add_unsubscribe_link: true` but without `unsubscribe_url` will now raise `I18n::MissingInterpolationArgument` and fail to send, where previously the same call worked fine.

No automated test coverage for the new unsubscribe feature

The PR introduces a security-sensitive controller action (`TopicsController#unsubscribe`), a new model method (`Topic#unsubscribe_url`), and a breaking change to the `unsubscribe_link` translation contract, but adds no controller or model specs covering: a successful unsubscribe for a `regular`-level user, the downgrade behaviour for `watching`/`tracking` users, the slug-mismatch redirect, or the case where no TopicUser row yet exists. The only spec touched here just adds `unsubscribe_url` to an existing MessageBuilder test's options without asserting that the value is actually rendered into the body/html output, or exercising the case where `add_unsubscribe_link` is true but `unsubscribe_url` is missing.

PR description gives no information about the feature

The PR description is just "Test 2", with no explanation of the new unsubscribe feature's behavior (including the watching/tracking-to-regular downgrade semantics), rationale, or what was tested, despite the change spanning 18 files including routes, mailer templates, and a new user-facing flow. This makes it hard for reviewers and future maintainers to understand intent or verify completeness.

true_positives.golden_comment: Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.

Plain Error thrown instead of TRPCError with proper code

true_positives.golden_comment: Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.

Cache timestamp is formatted with a hardcoded en-US locale

The cache-updated timestamp is formatted using `new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", {...})`, ignoring the user's actual locale/timezone preference used elsewhere in the app via `useLocale`/dayjs. For non-English locales this produces an inconsistent date format compared to the rest of the UI.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same issue: the date formatter hardcodes 'en-US' rather than using the user's locale from useLocale, causing inconsistent or incorrect date representations for other locales.

false_positives.candidate:
Cache deletion does not invalidate connectedCalendars query, leaving stale cache status in UI

The `deleteCacheMutation` only calls `onSuccess?.()` on success, unlike `disconnectMutation` which explicitly invalidates `utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` and `utils.viewer.apps.integrations` in its `onSettled`. If the parent component's `onChanged`/`onSuccess` prop doesn't itself trigger a refetch of the connectedCalendars query (it is optional and may be undefined), the dropdown will continue to show the old `cacheUpdatedAt` timestamp and cache-status UI after the cache has actually been deleted, giving the user incorrect information about cache state.

Directly instantiates CalendarCacheRepository, bypassing the CalendarCache factory/mock abstraction

Elsewhere in the codebase (e.g. GoogleCalendarService) calendar cache access goes through `CalendarCache.init(...)`, which is the abstraction responsible for choosing between the real `CalendarCacheRepository` and the `CalendarCacheRepositoryMock` (presumably gated by license/feature flag, given the mock exists specifically to disable calendar-cache behavior). Here, `new CalendarCacheRepository()` is instantiated directly, bypassing that selection logic. This means cache-status lookups run unconditionally regardless of whether the calendar-cache feature is actually enabled/licensed for the deployment, which is inconsistent with how the rest of the codebase gates this functionality.

getCacheStatusByCredentialIds ignores cache expiry, showing stale timestamps as if cache is active

`getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` groups by `credentialId` and returns `_max(updatedAt)` without filtering on `expiresAt >= now()`. As a result, a credential whose cache rows have long expired will still report a 'last updated' timestamp, and the UI (CredentialActionsDropdown) will present it as current cache status. This misleads users into believing cached data is still being served when in fact the next read will be a cache miss and hit the live API.

dev:cron now relies on npx tsx without adding tsx as a dependency

The `dev:cron` script was changed from `ts-node cron-tester.ts` (using the already-declared `ts-node` devDependency) to `npx tsx cron-tester.ts`, but `tsx` is not added to `devDependencies`. Using `npx` will attempt to fetch the package from the npm registry at invocation time (or use a globally cached version), which can produce version drift across environments and fails in network-restricted/offline CI or dev setups, unlike the project's convention of relying on locked workspace dependencies via yarn.

As a result, every consumer (getCalendar, videoClient, handleCancelBooking, etc.) still triggers loading of all app packages up front, but now each access additionally requires an `await`, adding complexity and promise-resolution overhead without achieving true on-demand/lazy loading. To actually defer loading, each entry would need to be a function returning the import (e.g. `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")`), invoked only when that specific app is required.

Example comment references a non-existent module path

The comment `// example: import("./example"),` doesn't match the actual folder name. The previous code's commented-out import referenced `"./_example"` (with a leading underscore), which is the real folder used to keep the example app excluded from the registry. If a developer later copies this comment to register a new app, it will point at a module that doesn't exist.

forEach with async callback no longer reliably initiates calendar deletion before later steps run

Same issue as in vital/lib/reschedule.ts: `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => {...})` now awaits the newly-async `getCalendar(...)` inside the callback, but forEach does not wait for the returned promises. The loop no longer guarantees the calendar/video deletion requests are even started before the function continues to send the reschedule email and returns. The surrounding try/catch also cannot catch rejections raised inside these detached async callbacks.

requestReschedule forEach no longer waits for (or even reliably starts) calendar/video deletion before sending the reschedule email and webhooks

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => {...})` was previously a synchronous callback that called `getCalendar` synchronously, so the deletion request was always issued inside the loop before the mutation continued. Now `getCalendar` is awaited inside the async callback, and since forEach ignores the promises returned by async callbacks, the deletion requests may not even be initiated before the code proceeds to `await sendRequestRescheduleEmail(...)` and subsequently dispatches BOOKING_CANCELLED webhooks. This changes the ordering guarantees of the reschedule flow and can leave stale calendar/video events behind while users are already notified of the reschedule.

Nested forEach(async) race widened by newly-async getCalendar, risking dropped deletions from final Promise.all

In the recurring-event branch, `bookingToDelete.user.credentials.filter(...).forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); ... apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent); })` is not awaited by the surrounding code. `apiDeletes` is only consolidated and awaited much later via `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` (line ~652), relying on other intervening awaits in the function to give these detached async callbacks enough time to push their results. Converting the previously-synchronous `getCalendar` call to `await getCalendar(credential)` adds an extra asynchronous hop before each callback even starts its inner loop, widening the race window during which `apiDeletes` may not yet contain the recurring-booking's calendar deletion promises when the final Promise.all executes, risking recurring-booking calendar events that are never actually deleted on cancellation.

getVideoAdapters resolves credentials sequentially instead of in parallel

The rewritten `getVideoAdapters` uses a `for...of` loop with `await appStore[appName as keyof typeof appStore]` inside, resolving each credential's app module one at a time rather than concurrently (e.g. via `Promise.all`). For bookings with multiple video credentials this unnecessarily serializes independent promise resolutions on every call to createMeeting/updateMeeting/deleteMeeting/getBusyVideoTimes, adding avoidable latency compared to a parallelized implementation.

No tests cover the new async appStore / getCalendar / getVideoAdapters behavior

This PR converts appStore's values to Promises and makes getCalendar, getVideoAdapters, and getCalendarCredentials asynchronous, touching booking cancellation, rescheduling, calendar/video event creation, and payment flows across many files. Several of these changes introduce race conditions around unresolved promises inside `Array.prototype.forEach` callbacks (see findings on vital/wipemycalother reschedule.ts, bookings.tsx, and handleCancelBooking.ts). No unit or integration tests were added or updated to verify that calendar/video events are still correctly created, updated, and deleted during these flows after the conversion, so these regressions would not be caught by CI.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
New isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) guard likely disables kill() for real flusher subprocesses

_ensure_processes_alive() now wraps the restart kill with `if isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process): process.kill()` (lines 253-257). Previously this call was unconditional (`self.process.kill()`). Processes are spawned via `self.mp_context.Process` where `self.mp_context = multiprocessing.get_context("spawn")` (line 53), producing instances of `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess`. `multiprocessing.Process` (the bare module attribute used here) resolves to the *default* context's process class, which on platforms whose default start method is not 'spawn' (e.g. Linux defaults to 'fork') is a sibling class of `SpawnProcess`, not its superclass. In that case `isinstance(spawn_process_instance, multiprocessing.Process)` is False, so the new guard silently prevents `process.kill()` from ever running on real flusher subprocesses in production. A hung/unresponsive flusher process detected by the health check would then never actually be killed, while a brand-new replacement process is started for the same shards right away — leaving two processes concurrently operating on the same Redis shard/segment data, which can cause duplicate flush/production or resource exhaustion.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

In join() the per-process wait/terminate loop (lines 337-347) uses `break` once `remaining_time <= 0` while iterating `self.processes.items()`. `break` exits the entire for-loop, not just the current iteration, so every flusher process that has not yet been visited in the dict is skipped completely: it is never waited on and `process.terminate()` is never called for it. Before this PR there was only one flusher process, so this had no visible effect. Now that there is one process per shard group (up to `max_processes`), if the deadline is exhausted while waiting on the first process(es) in the dict, the remaining per-shard flusher processes are left running un-terminated. Because they are daemon processes they will eventually die with the parent, but during controlled shutdown/rebalance they can keep producing to Kafka / polling Redis for shards that may already belong to another consumer instance, risking duplicate segment production and resource leaks.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that exhausting the deadline causes the loop to break and skip terminating remaining flusher processes.

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() calls `resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE, groupResource -> ...)` to enumerate group-scoped authorization resources, then calls `hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), ...)` and adds `groupResource.getId()` to the result set. However: (1) individual per-group resources are created via AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource(), which never calls resource.setType(...) (unlike the legacy V1 GroupPermissions.initialize(), which explicitly sets `groupResource.setType("Group")`), so findByType(server, "Groups", ...) will not find per-group resources at all — it will only match the single 'all-groups' placeholder resource created during schema init (which does have its type set). getResourceName() special-cases USERS_RESOURCE_TYPE to translate the resource's internal name (the user's UUID) into the user's username (or 'All users' for the catch-all resource), but no equivalent branch was added for the newly introduced GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE even though group resources are created the same way (named by the group's UUID via resolveGroup()). getSubGroups() previously computed `canViewGlobal = auth.groups().canView()` once and used `.filter(g -> canViewGlobal || auth.groups().canView(g))`, short-circuiting per-subgroup evaluation when the caller already has global view rights. The change replaces this with `.filter(auth.groups()::canView)`, which invokes canView(GroupModel) for every subgroup even when the admin already has global view permission. For FGAP V2, canView(GroupModel) performs a resource lookup and policy evaluation per call, so for groups with many subgroups this reintroduces an evaluation (and potential DB query) per subgroup instead of a single check, which is a performance regression compared to the previous behavior.

Removed short-circuit for global group-view permission when listing top-level groups

The change moves the feature check outside, so the listener is only registered if the feature is enabled at the moment registerListener() is invoked (typically once, at provider/session-factory initialization). If the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ feature is toggled on after this registration happens (e.g. in test harnesses or deployments that enable the feature dynamically after providers have already been initialized), RoleRemovedEvent/ClientRemovedEvent/GroupRemovedEvent cleanup of permissions will silently stop firing, whereas previously it would have resumed working as soon as the flag became true. testManageAllGroups() only verifies that granting MANAGE scope on the all-groups resource allows group creation/update; there is no test asserting that an admin granted only VIEW (or VIEW_MEMBERS) scope on Groups is still forbidden from creating/updating/deleting groups. The public static method `ModelToRepresentation.searchGroupModelsByAttributes(session, realm, attributes, first, max)` was removed outright (callers were updated to call `session.groups().searchGroupsByAttributes(...)` directly in GroupsResource). false_positives.candidate:
close()/terminate() permanently destroy the shared queue pool, breaking processing after any rebalance

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() (and terminate()) calls self.queue_pool.shutdown(), which stops all OrderedQueueWorker threads and shuts down every internal queue.Queue permanently. The FixedQueuePool instance, however, is created once in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__ and reused across every subsequent call to create_with_partitions (e.g. after Kafka partition rebalances) — exactly like parallel_executor/multiprocessing_pool in result_consumer.py, which are intentionally only torn down in ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown() at final process exit, never per-strategy-close. Because arroyo calls close()/terminate() on the current strategy whenever it is being replaced (which happens on every rebalance, not just final shutdown), the first rebalance kills the workers and shuts down the queues. Any create_with_partitions call afterwards reuses the now-dead queue_pool: submit() pushes items into shut-down queues (raising queue.ShutDown, silently caught and the offset marked 'complete' without any real processing), so messages after the first rebalance are effectively dropped while the consumer appears healthy.

Uses Python 3.13-only queue.Queue.shutdown()/queue.ShutDown API

FixedQueuePool.shutdown() calls q.shutdown(immediate=False), and OrderedQueueWorker.run() catches queue.ShutDown. Both queue.Queue.shutdown() and the queue.ShutDown exception were introduced in Python 3.13. On earlier Python runtimes, q.shutdown() raises AttributeError; since that call is wrapped in a bare 'except Exception', the failure is silently logged rather than propagated, meaning the queue is never actually put into a shutdown state. Worker threads blocked in work_queue.get() are consequently never woken and will hang indefinitely instead of shutting down, defeating the entire purpose of FixedQueuePool.shutdown()/close().

Offsets are marked complete (and committed) even when processing raises an exception

In OrderedQueueWorker.run(), the finally block always calls self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(...) regardless of whether result_processor succeeded or raised an exception caught by the preceding 'except Exception' clause. This contradicts the guarantee stated in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy's docstring ('Only commits offsets after successful processing'): a message whose processing failed is treated identically to a successfully processed one, so its offset becomes eligible for commit and will never be retried or reprocessed — a processing failure silently advances the committed offset past the failed message.

test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts behavior inconsistent with the implementation

This test mocks the result processor to raise on the first call and succeed on the second, then asserts `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`, implying a processing failure should block the offset commit. But per OrderedQueueWorker.run()'s finally block, offsets are always marked complete regardless of exceptions, so the commit loop should still compute and commit an offset for test_partition once both items complete (which happens almost immediately since the mocked calls return synchronously). This makes the assertion likely to fail or flake against the real implementation, or indicates the test does not actually validate any failure-handling guarantee.

Per-queue queue.Queue() has no maxsize, so the claimed backpressure doesn't exist

Each internal queue created in FixedQueuePool.__init__ (queue.Queue()) is unbounded, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() never raises arroyo's MessageRejected to signal backpressure regardless of queue depth. Despite the docstrings on FixedQueuePool and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy explicitly claiming 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', no bound is enforced anywhere, so a slow or stuck group (or an overall slow downstream) can grow its queue without limit while the consumer keeps reading from Kafka, risking unbounded memory growth instead of the intended backpressure.

get_committable_offsets iterates the offsets dict without a lock protecting its structure

get_committable_offsets() takes list(self.all_offsets.keys()) and then separately locks per-partition to read self.all_offsets[partition]. The all_offsets defaultdict's key set can be mutated from another thread calling add_offset for a partition never seen before (defaultdict.__missing__ inserting a new key) without any lock protecting the dict's structure itself — only the per-partition lock (created lazily, after the key may already need to be inserted) guards the inner set contents. Enumerating dict.keys() into a list while another thread inserts a new key concurrently can race, and in CPython can even raise RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration, which would crash the background commit loop thread.

Offset commits are issued from a dedicated background thread instead of the main strategy thread

_commit_loop runs on its own daemon thread started in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.__init__ and calls self.commit_function(committable), which ultimately invokes the arroyo `commit` callback passed into create_with_partitions. Arroyo processing strategies are designed to be driven single-threadedly by the StreamProcessor's main loop (submit/poll/join); none of the other modes in this same file (serial, parallel, batched-parallel) invoke the commit callback from a separate thread. Calling `commit` concurrently with the main thread's own poll()/submit() activity deviates from that contract and risks races in whatever internal bookkeeping the Commit implementation performs, since it is not documented/guaranteed to be safe for concurrent use from worker threads.

close() shuts down the queue pool without draining it first

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() immediately calls self.queue_pool.shutdown() without first calling the already-implemented FixedQueuePool.wait_until_empty() helper. FixedQueuePool.shutdown() only gives each worker a 5 second join() timeout; if there is still a backlog when close() runs, items may not finish processing within that window (a timed-out join() does not stop the thread, it just stops waiting), so close() can return while unprocessed/uncommitted work is still in flight, risking those messages being left in an inconsistent processed/committed state depending on what happens after close() returns.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset branch in get_result() passes cursor.offset directly as start_offset to queryset slicing when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset branch will raise an exception, not optimize anything

When `enable_advanced_features` is true and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative `start_offset` (and potentially negative `stop`). Django QuerySets explicitly disallow negative slice indices and raise an exception (`AssertionError`/`ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported`) in `QuerySet.__getitem__`. This means the newly-added "advanced" negative-offset pagination path is non-functional and will crash any request that reaches it (e.g. a superuser manually crafting a cursor string with a negative offset), rather than providing the described performance optimization.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug in OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset branch: when enable_advanced_features is true and cursor.offset < 0, the negative offset is passed directly as the queryset slice start. The candidate adds the resulting Django exception, but the underlying issue matches.

true_positives.golden_comment: In BasePaginator.get_result(), when cursor.is_prev is True, it sets start_offset = offset without clamping, allowing negative offset values to be passed to queryset slicing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Shared BasePaginator.get_result silently changed offset-clamping behavior for all paginated endpoints

`start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` modifies `BasePaginator.get_result`, which is the base class used by `Paginator`, `DateTimePaginator`, and other widely-used paginators across the whole codebase, not just the spans-buffer feature this PR is about. Previously, a negative cursor offset (e.g. from a tampered/corrupted cursor string) would fail loudly via Django's queryset slicing restriction; now it is silently clamped to 0 for forward cursors, changing pagination semantics without any accompanying tests or documentation of the new contract, and leaving the `is_prev` branch still able to pass a negative offset straight into queryset slicing (same crash risk as before, just for a different code path).
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly flags the same line and bug: when cursor.is_prev is true, start_offset is set to the raw offset without clamping, so a negative offset can still reach queryset slicing. The extra discussion of forward-cursor clamping is additional context, not a different issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key uses floor/ceil on a datetime key (order_by='-datetime'), causing TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unrelated, untested, privilege-gated pagination feature bundled into audit log endpoint

This endpoint now branches into a brand-new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` code path based on a client-supplied `optimized_pagination` query parameter, gated only by `is_superuser`/`has_global_access`. This change is unrelated to the PR's stated purpose (spans buffer eviction), has no new tests covering the branch, and (per the related finding in paginator.py) the underlying negative-offset logic it enables is broken and will raise an exception at runtime. true_positives.golden_comment: Accessing .has_global_access on organization_context.member can raise an AttributeError when organization_context is None, particularly for non-superuser non-member users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unconditional access to organization_context.member attribute can crash the endpoint

`enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` is evaluated on every GET request to this endpoint, regardless of the `optimized_pagination` query parameter. If the requesting user is not a superuser, `organization_context.member` is accessed; for callers where `member` is `None` (e.g. a non-member caller permitted through some other path) this raises an `AttributeError`. Additionally, `has_global_access` does not appear to be an existing attribute on the organization member RPC model used elsewhere in the codebase, which would make this crash on every non-superuser request to the audit log endpoint, not just when the new optimized-pagination feature is requested. This turns what should be an opt-in feature into a potential 500 error for normal customer use of the audit log API.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same core bug: the expression unconditionally accesses organization_context.member.has_global_access for non-superusers, which can raise AttributeError when member is None. The extra claim about the attribute not existing is additional but does not change the matching underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Misleading comment claims negative-offset support with no corresponding behavior change

The added comment states "Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios... This enables efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions" directly above `self.offset = int(offset)`, which is unchanged code. No validation or new behavior was actually added here; the comment implies a capability that doesn't exist in this file and is misleading to future readers trying to understand where negative-offset support is implemented or guarded.

Redirect-depth loop limit reduced 10x with explanatory comment removed

The loop bound for walking the redirect chain was reduced from `0, 10000` to `0, 1000`, and the comment explaining the known correctness limitation ("theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly") was deleted entirely rather than updated. This makes it 10x more likely in practice for deeply-nested span trees to hit the redirect-depth cutoff and be incorrectly merged/split, and removes the only documentation warning maintainers about this risk, with no explanation given for why the limit was lowered.

zpopmin eviction can remove the segment's root span, corrupting flushed output

When a segment's span count exceeds 1000, `redis.call("zpopmin", set_key, span_count - 1000)` evicts the lowest-scored (oldest `end_timestamp_precise`) entries with no protection for the span that is the segment's root (`is_segment_span`). If the root span's end timestamp happens to be lower than one or more of its children's (e.g. due to clock skew or async child spans finishing later), the root span's payload can be evicted from the sorted set while the separate `has_root_span` boolean flag remains true. Later, `flush_segments` in buffer.py determines `is_segment` by comparing `segment_span_id == val["span_id"]` only over the spans actually present in the set; if the root span was evicted, no span in the flushed output will have `is_segment: true`, even though the segment was flushed via the root-span timeout path. This silently produces segments lacking a root span marker, which downstream consumers expecting exactly one root span per segment may not handle correctly.

max_segment_spans parameter is now dead/disconnected from the actual eviction threshold

`SpansBuffer.__init__` still accepts and stores `max_segment_spans: int = 1001`, but nothing in the class uses this value anymore (the only prior usage, in `_load_segment_data`, was removed). The actual span-count cap enforced during insertion is now hardcoded as `1000` inside `add-buffer.lua` and is not derived from or passed through this configuration value. This leaves a misleading, non-functional configuration knob: changing `max_segment_spans` has no effect on behavior, and the real cap (1000) is off-by-one from the stated default (1001) and only discoverable by reading the Lua script.

Removed oversized-segment safety check and metric with no replacement observability

The previous check in `_load_segment_data` that dropped and logged (via `metrics.incr("spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded")` and `logger.error`) segments whose span count exceeded `max_segment_spans` was removed without any replacement. The new insertion-time eviction in `add-buffer.lua` silently trims excess spans via `zpopmin` and does not report whether/how many spans were evicted (the script's return tuple `{redirect_depth, span_key, set_key, has_root_span}` carries no eviction count), so there is no metric or log anywhere indicating that spans are being dropped from an oversized segment. This is a loss of operational visibility into data loss that previously existed.

No test exercises the new insert-time span eviction behavior

The PR's stated purpose is to add eviction during insert for the spans buffer (capping segments at 1000 spans via `zpopmin` in add-buffer.lua), but the only changes to this test file are adding the new required `end_timestamp_precise` field to existing `Span(...)` constructions. No test inserts more than 1000 spans into a single segment to verify that old spans are correctly evicted, that the segment is capped at the expected size, or that the root span survives eviction. The core new behavior introduced by this PR is therefore untested.

No tests added for new OptimizedCursorPaginator class

`OptimizedCursorPaginator` is a substantial new class (~90 lines) with a non-trivial negative-offset code path, but no test file changes accompany it in this PR. Given that the negative-offset branch appears to be broken (see related finding on queryset negative slicing), the absence of any unit test means this bug would not be caught before merging or in CI.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache key built from hash() of project id tuple risks collisions

The cache key `f"error_upsampling_eligible:{organization.id}:{hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))}"` relies on Python's built-in `hash()` of an integer tuple to disambiguate different project-id sets within the same organization. Hash collisions between distinct tuples are possible (hash() truncates to a fixed-width integer), which could cause one set of projects to incorrectly reuse another set's cached eligibility result for up to 60 seconds, silently enabling or disabling upsampling for the wrong query. A deterministic string key built from the sorted ids directly (e.g. joined by commas) would avoid this risk entirely and is no more expensive.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the cache key's use of Python's built-in hash() on project IDs and recommend deterministic serialization of the sorted IDs. The candidate emphasizes collisions, while the golden comment emphasizes cross-process randomization, but they identify the same bug and fix.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling eligibility check uses the wrong dataset variable

Inside `_get_event_stats`, the function parameter is named `scoped_dataset` (the dataset actually being queried for this specific call), but the eligibility check calls `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)` using the outer closed-over `dataset` variable from `get()` instead of the local `scoped_dataset` parameter. In the simple path these happen to be equal, but `get_event_stats_factory`'s `fn` calls `_get_event_stats` with different dataset values (e.g. `discover` for the errors-only/transactions-only split queries, or `split_dataset`) when handling dashboard-widget discover splitting. In those calls, the upsampling decision is computed against the wrong dataset, so the `count()`→`upsampled_count()` transform can be incorrectly applied or skipped for the dataset that is actually executed, producing inconsistent/incorrect counts for dashboard widgets using the discover-split code path.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: the eligibility check uses the outer dataset instead of scoped_dataset, causing incorrect upsampling decisions in dashboard discover-split paths.

false_positives.candidate:
invalidate_upsampling_cache is never called anywhere

`invalidate_upsampling_cache` is introduced with a docstring stating it 'should be called when the allowlist configuration changes to ensure cache consistency', but nothing in this PR (or apparently the rest of the codebase) calls it. As written, it is dead code, and the 60-second eligibility cache set in `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` has no actual invalidation path wired to allowlist option changes. This either means the function is unused dead code that should be removed, or an integration point (e.g. an options-changed signal handler) is missing, leaving stale upsampling decisions for up to 60 seconds with no way to force a refresh.

New upsampled_count() function is public, bypassing allowlist gating

The new `upsampled_count` SnQLFunction is registered without `private=True`, unlike other internal-only aggregate functions in the same converter. This means any user can directly type `upsampled_count()` in a Discover/Events query, bypassing the allowlist check in `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects`/`_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` entirely. Depending on how `sample_weight` is populated for non-allowlisted projects (NULL vs default value), this could either return misleading data or raise a SQL error (e.g. converting NULL to a non-nullable Int64), since the function assumes sample_weight is always present 'per our data model requirements' — an assumption the public API doesn't enforce.

Stray gitlink/submodule artifact added to the repository

A new top-level entry `sentry-repo` is added that is a gitlink pointing to commit `a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a` (the PR's own base commit), with no corresponding `.gitmodules` entry shown in the diff. This looks like an accidental artifact from a bad rebase/squash or local tooling leftover rather than an intentional change. Committing a dangling gitlink with no submodule registration can confuse `git status`/`git submodule` tooling and CI checkout steps, and should be removed before merge.

No tests for the public cached entry point or cache invalidation

The test file only exercises the private helpers `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, `_is_error_focused_query`, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`, and `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling`. The PR's headline feature — the 60-second caching behavior in `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` (cache hit/miss paths, correct bool-vs-None handling) — and `invalidate_upsampling_cache` are never directly unit tested. Given the PR title explicitly calls out 'performance optimizations' via caching, the caching logic itself (the riskiest new behavior) has no dedicated test coverage.

Misleading/contradictory docstring about cache freshness

The docstring of `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` states the function 'reads the allowlist configuration fresh each time... This is intentional to ensure we always have the latest configuration state.' In reality, its caller `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` wraps this function's result in a 60-second cache, so the configuration is not read fresh on every call — only on cache misses. This contradicts the stated intent and could mislead future maintainers into believing allowlist changes take effect immediately, when in fact they can be delayed up to 60 seconds.

Test helper overloads generic 'sample_rate' field and silently swallows all errors

`_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` writes into the generic top-level `normalized_data["sample_rate"]` key whenever `contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate` is present, for any event type processed by `store_event` (not just errors). This repurposes a field name that is also used elsewhere in Sentry for transaction/dynamic sampling semantics, risking ambiguity if both mechanisms ever intersect on the same event. Additionally, both exception-handling blocks use bare `except Exception: pass`, silently discarding malformed `client_sample_rate` values or unexpected `contexts` shapes, which can mask bugs in tests relying on this helper instead of surfacing a clear failure.

Transform only matches exact 'count()' string, silently ignoring aliased forms

`transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` only rewrites a column when its lowercased/stripped value equals exactly `"count()"`. Any other valid representation of the same aggregate — e.g. `"count() as total"`, or `count()` embedded in an equation — is left untouched with no warning or fallback, so the request silently uses the raw (non-upsampled) count. There is no test covering this partial-match limitation, and callers have no way to know the transform was skipped for their specific column form.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
"Should deny on explicit cache deny entry" test doesn't actually exercise the override behavior it claims to test

In TestService_CacheCheck's "Should deny on explicit cache deny entry" subtest, the comment says "Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked", but the code sets `s.permCache.Set(ctx, userPermCacheKey(...), map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false})` — i.e. it stores `false`, not `true`. Because the stored value is already `false`, `checkPermission` would return `allowed=false` from this cache entry on its own, and the subsequent default fakeStore (unset in this subtest) also returns no permissions, so the test would still pass (assert resp.Allowed == false) even if the new permDenialCache short-circuit logic were removed entirely. The test therefore does not actually validate that the denial cache takes precedence over a cached "allow" entry, which is the behavior it is meant to demonstrate. The permCache value should be set to `true` to make the test meaningful.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same test bug: the comment claims the cached permission allows access, but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so the test does not actually demonstrate denial-cache precedence over an allow entry.

false_positives.candidate:
Permission-denial cache key collides across identity types sharing the same UID

`userPermDenialCacheKey(checkReq.Namespace.Value, checkReq.UserUID, checkReq.Action, checkReq.Name, checkReq.ParentFolder)` (defined in pkg/services/authz/rbac/cache.go) builds the cache key purely from the parsed subject UID, action, name and parent folder, without including the identity type. Anonymous subjects ("anonymous:0") and the render-service subject ("render:0") both resolve to UserUID=="0" (see the test file's own usage of these literal subjects), so a denial recorded for one identity type (e.g. render service denied on some action) will be returned for the other identity type (e.g. an anonymous user) on the next Check call for the same namespace/action/name/folder, even though their actual permission semantics (getRendererPermissions vs getAnonymousPermissions) are completely different and unrelated. Unlike the existing permCache which deliberately uses separate key schemes per identity type (userPermCacheKey vs anonymousPermCacheKey, and no caching at all for render), this new denial cache does not preserve that separation. The result is an incorrect deny being served to a different identity than the one it was computed for, causing availability/correctness regressions (legitimate requests incorrectly denied) that only clear once the 30s denial TTL expires.

Per-resource cache miss now forces a full permissions DB requery on every mismatched Check call

Previously `getUserPermissions`/`getAnonymousPermissions` returned the cached permission map unconditionally whenever any entry existed for the user+action, regardless of whether it covered the requested resource, so a single cache entry served all Check calls for that action for the whole 30s TTL. Now, `Check` calls `getCachedIdentityPermissions` and, if the cached map doesn't contain the specific requested scope, always falls through to `getIdentityPermissions` which performs a full DB permissions query (deduplicated via singleflight only for truly concurrent calls). For workloads that call Check sequentially for many distinct resource names under the same action (e.g. authorizing each item of a list one at a time), every resource not already present in the cached scope map now triggers its own DB round trip, and is only protected from repeat DB hits via the new per-resource permDenialCache (keyed by name+parent) on subsequent identical calls. This can multiply DB load roughly proportional to the number of distinct resources checked, compared to the previous single-query-per-TTL-window behavior, and is not bounded/debounced beyond the exact (name, parent) tuple.

permissionCacheUsage metric mislabels a used-but-denying cache lookup as a cache miss

When `getCachedIdentityPermissions` returns a cached permission map (err == nil) but `checkPermission` evaluates it as not allowed, the code falls through to the line `s.metrics.permissionCacheUsage.WithLabelValues("false", checkReq.Action).Inc()`, recording this as a cache miss even though the cache was actually read and used to make a (negative) decision before falling back to the DB. This mislabels cache effectiveness, making dashboards built on this metric appear to show a lower cache hit rate than what is actually happening, which could mislead capacity planning/alerting based on this metric.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.

The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
KeyError risk when comparing authenticated user against missing 'sender' metadata

In `GitHubInstallation.dispatch()`, the new check `pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user") != integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` accesses `integration.metadata["sender"]` with direct dict indexing instead of `.get()`. Elsewhere in the same file (`build_integration`), `sender` is explicitly treated as an optional field (`if state.get("sender"): integration["metadata"]["sender"] = state["sender"]`), implying integrations can legitimately exist without a `sender` key in metadata (e.g. integrations created before this feature shipped, or if the installation webhook that populates `sender` was never received/processed). For any such integration, this line will raise an unhandled `KeyError`, crashing the reinstall flow with a 500 error instead of showing the graceful 'Invalid installation request' page that the rest of this pipeline is designed to show.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same KeyError caused by directly indexing integration.metadata['sender'] when the optional sender metadata may be absent. The additional context about the reinstall flow does not change the underlying bug.

false_positives.candidate:
New user-mismatch check can be bypassed when Integration row does not yet exist

When `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)` raises `DoesNotExist`, the code immediately returns `pipeline.next_step()` (line 482), completely skipping the newly added `github_authenticated_user` vs `sender` comparison further down. Since `sender` metadata appears to be populated by the asynchronous GitHub installation webhook rather than by this OAuth pipeline itself, if that webhook has not yet been processed when the user completes the OAuth dance (e.g. due to webhook delivery delay), the Integration row will not exist yet, this branch will be taken, and the newly-added authenticated-user validation will never run for that installation — defeating the security check this PR is meant to add for that race window.

Unhandled exceptions from OAuth token exchange and user-info calls

`safe_urlopen(url=ghip.get_oauth_access_token_url(), data=data)` (line 423) and `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` (line 434) are called without any exception handling. Only the subsequent `safe_urlread`/`parse_qsl` step is wrapped in a `try/except`. If GitHub's token endpoint is unreachable, times out, or `get_user_info` raises `ApiError` (e.g. GitHub API hiccup or rate limiting), the exception propagates unhandled and the user sees a generic 500 error instead of the intended 'could not verify installation' error page that this PR is supposed to guarantee for all failure cases.

test_installation_not_found no longer exercises the scenario it is named for

The test was changed to add a second request using a hardcoded, deliberately different `state` value (`"ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05"`) than the one the pipeline actually signs (`"9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3"`, used everywhere else in this file). Because of the newly added `OAuthLoginView`, this mismatched state now causes the request to fail at the `state != pipeline.signature` check inside `OAuthLoginView.dispatch()`, never reaching `GitHubInstallation`/`build_integration()`, which is what actually raises the 'GitHub installation could not be found' error this test is supposed to validate (the GH `/app/installations/{id}` 404 stub set up at the top of the test is now never hit). The test now only re-validates the generic state-mismatch path (duplicating coverage already implied elsewhere) while silently dropping coverage for the original 404-from-GitHub scenario.

No test coverage for failed OAuth token exchange

In `.topic-list.categories .category .badge-notification`, the color rule is still `color: scale-color($primary, $lightness: 50%);` and was not wrapped in `dark-light-choose(... , scale-color($secondary, ...))` like every other similar rule in this PR (e.g. the `th`, `td`, `.topic-excerpt`, `.top-date-string` and `div.education` rules a few lines above/below were all converted). As a result, in a dark theme this badge count text will keep using a lightened shade of the (dark) primary color, producing low-contrast/unreadable text against the dark background on the categories topic list, defeating the purpose of this PR for this specific element.

Light-mode lightness value changed unintentionally for .group-member-info .name (mobile)

Same issue as the desktop counterpart: originally `color: scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%);`, now `color: dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 50%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 50%));`. The light-mode lightness was changed from 30% to 50% rather than being preserved while only adding the dark-theme fallback, producing an unintended color change on mobile for the group member name text in the default theme.

The new rule is `color: dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 50%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 50%));`, changing the light-mode lightness from 20% to 50%.
