true_positives.golden_comment: The findMembers() call is now asynchronous and unhandled. The controller may not have member data immediately available, creating a race condition.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
removeMember/addMembers promises resolve before the member list refresh actually completes

In `removeMember` and `addMembers`, the `.then()` callback calls `self.findMembers();` but does not `return` it: `return Discourse.ajax(...).then(function() { self.findMembers(); });`. Because the inner async call isn't returned, the outer promise resolves as soon as the delete/add request finishes, not after the member list reload (`findMembers`) completes. Any caller that chains off `removeMember()`/`addMembers()` to know when the UI data is fresh (current callers don't, but this is a latent bug) will get a false 'done' signal before `members`/`user_count` have actually been updated.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: findMembers() is asynchronous but not returned/awaited from the removeMember/addMembers promise chain, so the outer promise resolves before the member list refresh finishes and callers can observe stale member data.

true_positives.golden_comment: In the next action, capping the next offset at user_count can produce an empty page (e.g., total equal to limit results in offset == total, showing 2/2 with no members). This can cause confusing UX on the last page.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Off-by-one error in totalPages computation produces a phantom empty last page

`totalPages` is computed as `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1`. When `user_count` is an exact multiple of `limit` (e.g. 50 members with the default limit of 50), this yields `floor(50/50)+1 = 2` instead of the correct value of 1. Combined with `currentPage` using the same `floor(...)+1` formula, clicking 'next' on the last real page will move to a non-existent page 2 of 2 that renders zero members, and `showingLast` will report false until the user is already past the real data. The formula should use `Math.ceil(user_count / limit)` instead.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same pagination off-by-one: when the member count is an exact multiple of the page limit, navigation can reach a phantom final page (e.g. 2/2) that renders no members. The candidate's totalPages/currentPage formula explanation is a semantic match for the golden comment's empty-page symptom, despite differing root-cause wording.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `totalPages` calculation using `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1` produces an extra page when `user_count` is an exact multiple of `limit`, leading to incorrect pagination. For example, with 100 users and a limit of 50, it reports 3 pages instead of 2, allowing navigation to an empty page.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Off-by-one error in totalPages computation produces a phantom empty last page

`totalPages` is computed as `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1`. When `user_count` is an exact multiple of `limit` (e.g. 50 members with the default limit of 50), this yields `floor(50/50)+1 = 2` instead of the correct value of 1. The formula should use `Math.ceil(user_count / limit)` instead.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same issue: the totalPages formula Math.floor(user_count/limit)+1 overcounts by one when user_count is an exact multiple of limit, producing a phantom empty page. The candidate's example and suggested Math.ceil fix align with the golden comment.

false_positives.candidate:
Public group members endpoint now hard-caps all groups at 50 members with no pagination UI

Previously, only automatic groups were paginated (capped at 200), while manually-created groups returned the full member list unpaginated. The new `members` action applies `limit = (params[:limit] || 50).to_i` to every group regardless of type, and the public-facing template `app/assets/javascripts/discourse/templates/group/members.hbs` (and its route `group-members.js.es6`) never passes a custom limit nor offers any 'load more'/pagination controls (unlike the admin group page, which does have next/previous). As a result, any group (automatic or manual) with more than 50 members will silently show only the first 50 members on the public group page with no way for a user to see the rest — a data-completeness regression compared to the previous behavior for manual groups.

Unconditional group.save() after membership mutation can report an error after the change already persisted

`add_members` and `remove_member` call `group.add(user)` / `group.users.delete(user_id)` (which persist the membership change immediately via the join table), and then separately call `group.save` to decide the HTTP response. If `group.save` fails for any reason unrelated to membership (e.g. a validation on `name`/`alias_level` that happens to be in a bad state), the controller will return a 422 error even though the membership change already took effect in the database. The old `update_patch` code for incremental membership changes never checked `save` at all for this reason. This inconsistency between the reported result and actual persisted state can confuse the admin UI (which only calls `findMembers()` to refresh on success).

Breaking response-format change to /groups/:name/members.json has no accompanying test update

The `members` action's response shape changed from a plain serialized array to `{ members: [...], meta: { total, limit, offset } }`. This is a breaking change for any consumer of this JSON endpoint. No spec file for `GroupsController` is included in this PR's diff, so there is no verification that the new shape is correct, and any pre-existing spec asserting the old array format would now fail. The PR should add/update tests covering the new pagination metadata and format for this public endpoint.

Username input is not cleared after successfully adding members

The `addMembers` action contains `// TODO: should clear the input` and indeed never resets `this.get('usernames')` after a successful add. After adding members, the user-selector field retains the previously entered usernames, which can mislead the admin into re-submitting the same usernames or being confused about the current state of the input.

Route no longer waits for member data before rendering, losing loading-state guarantee

The previous implementation used `afterModel` to await `model.findMembers()` before `setupController` ran, guaranteeing the member list and pagination metadata (`user_count`, `limit`, `offset`) were populated before the template rendered. The new code calls `model.findMembers()` from `setupController` without returning/awaiting the promise, so navigating directly to (or refreshing) an existing group's admin page will briefly render with stale/default values (`user_count: 0`, `0/0` pagination, no members) before the async fetch resolves, instead of Ember's route loading state being used to mask this.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The remove_member test uses xhr :put to call the remove_member action, but the route defines delete 'members' => 'groups#remove_member' requiring DELETE method.

The route provides the group's ID in params[:id], but the code attempts to read it from params[:group_id], causing the action to fail. This results in a broken feature when trying to access group memberships.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
should_block? mutates and persists match stats as a side effect of validation, causing double counting

`BlockedEmail.should_block?` increments `match_count`, sets `last_match_at`, and saves the record every time it is called. It is invoked from `EmailValidator#validate_each` (lib/validators/email_validator.rb:13), which runs as part of `User` validations. `UsersController#create` (app/controllers/users_controller.rb:168) explicitly calls `user.valid?` before calling `user.save` (line 172), and `save` internally re-runs validations. Because `email_changed?` is true for a brand-new unsaved user both times, validations (and therefore the BlockedEmail side effect) run twice for every single sign-up attempt against a blocked address, so `match_count` is incremented twice (and `last_match_at` recomputed twice) per attempt, corrupting the very statistics this feature is meant to track. The side effect is also persisted outside of the `User` save/transaction (validations run before the AR save transaction begins), so the counters are updated even if the `User` save subsequently fails, or if `valid?` is called anywhere else (forms, specs, console) without ever creating a user.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: BlockedEmail.should_block? mutates and persists match statistics as a side effect of a validation/read check. The candidate adds a concrete double-counting path, but the underlying concern is the same.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked email lookup and uniqueness are case-sensitive, allowing the block to be bypassed by case variation

`BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` and the `validates :email, presence: true, uniqueness: true` on line 5 do no case normalization. Elsewhere in the app, email comparisons are explicitly case-normalized (e.g. `UsersController#change_email` uses `Email.downcase`), but `BlockedEmail` does not. As a result, an admin who blocks "Spammer@EXAMPLE.com" will fail to block a sign-up using "spammer@example.com" (or any other casing variant), defeating the purpose of the feature. It also permits multiple rows for the same logical address differing only in case, since the uniqueness check is case-sensitive by default.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same root cause: BlockedEmail performs case-sensitive email matching/uniqueness, so casing variants of a blocked address can bypass the block. The candidate describes the same bug and security consequence, even with different wording and examples.

false_positives.candidate:
Non-atomic match_count increment risks lost updates under concurrent requests

`record.match_count += 1; record.last_match_at = Time.zone.now; record.save` reads the counter into memory and writes it back without any locking or atomic SQL update. If two sign-up attempts for the same blocked email happen concurrently (a realistic scenario for exactly the kind of repeated spam/bot signups this feature targets), both requests can read the same starting value and each save overwrites the other's increment, silently losing hits/undercounting match_count. This should use an atomic update such as `update_counters`, `increment!`, or a raw SQL `match_count = match_count + 1`.

rejectedEmails default array literal is shared across controller instances and never reset

`rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` assigns a single array object as the default value directly on the controller definition instead of creating a fresh array per instance (e.g. via `init`). In Ember, object/array literals used as defaults this way are shared by reference across every instance created from the same class/mixin definition rather than instantiated per object — a well known Ember pitfall. Because the array is also never cleared anywhere (no reset on modal open/close or `init`), once an email is pushed into `rejectedEmails` it stays rejected for the lifetime of that shared array object. If the "Create Account" controller is ever recreated (e.g. the modal reopened, or in a shared/kiosk browser session), a previously rejected email — even from an unrelated earlier attempt, or one that the server would no longer reject (e.g. an admin unblocked it) — will continue to be permanently flagged invalid client-side with no way to retry short of a full page reload.

Domain whitelist/blacklist validation behavior has no test coverage after being moved into EmailValidator

The domain-restriction logic (`email_in_restriction_setting?` plus the whitelist/blacklist branches) was moved out of `User` (previously `email_validator`/`email_in_restriction_setting?`, deleted from app/models/user.rb in this PR) into `lib/validators/email_validator.rb`. The new spec file only covers the new "blocked email" branch via `BlockedEmail.should_block?` and adds no example for `SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist`/`email_domains_blacklist` behavior, so this pre-existing, non-trivial logic is left untested after the refactor. Additionally, any prior spec that exercised the now-removed `User#email_validator`/`User#email_in_restriction_setting?` methods directly would fail since those methods no longer exist on `User`.

action_type column has no DB default or range validation, relying only on an app-level callback

The `action_type` column is declared `null: false` with no database default, and the only place a default is applied is the `before_validation :set_defaults` callback in app/models/blocked_email.rb (lines 21-23), which only runs through ActiveRecord's validation path. There is also no validation constraining `action_type` to the two defined enum values (`actions[:block]`/`actions[:do_nothing]`). The spec file's own comment ("If we manually load the table with some emails...") suggests bulk/manual loading is an expected use case; such inserts bypassing ActiveRecord callbacks would violate the NOT NULL constraint unless `action_type` is explicitly supplied, and any out-of-range value stored would silently be treated as "do nothing" by `should_block?`'s equality check rather than raising an error.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

true_positives.golden_comment: Mixing float: left with flexbox causes layout issues. Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Right-alignment of .panel now depends on unverified DOM nesting under the new flex container

`.panel` previously used `float: right;` to self-position within `.d-header`. It was changed to `margin-left: auto;` plus `@include order(3);`, which only right-aligns the element if `.panel` is a direct flex-item child of `.contents` (the element that now has `display: flex`). Likewise `.title { float: left; }` was removed entirely. If the actual template markup does not make `.title` and `.panel` direct children of `.contents` (e.g. if there is an intermediate wrapper), both the left title and the right-aligned panel will lose their positioning entirely, since no float fallback remains. The PR does not demonstrate (via markup reference, screenshot, or test) that this structural assumption holds.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag that the float-to-flex migration and removal of float alignment can misplace the header panel/title unless the expected flex-item nesting exists. The candidate captures the same layout regression, even though it describes the nesting condition more generally.

false_positives.candidate:
Avatar offset padding replaced with percentage value that is inconsistent across widths

.small-action-desc previously used padding: 0.5em 0 0.5em 4em (plus margin-top: 5px) to reserve a fixed left offset matching the floated 45px-wide .topic-avatar icon. It was changed to padding: 0 1.5% with the margin-top and the > p padding-top also removed. Since 1.5% is relative to the container width, the gap between the avatar icon and the description text will shrink or grow depending on viewport/container width instead of staying proportional to the fixed-size icon, and the removed vertical offsets likely alter text alignment versus the icon. No corresponding flex-basis/width was added to .topic-avatar to make this proportional spacing correct.

Removed bullet badge vertical-alignment fix without replacement

The previous rule `.badge-wrapper.bullet { margin-top: 5px; }` inside `.extra-info-wrapper` provided a specific vertical offset so bullet-style category badges aligned correctly with surrounding content. This sub-rule was deleted and replaced only with a generic `line-height: 1.5` on the parent, with no compensating offset for `.bullet` badges specifically. This risks a visual misalignment regression for topics that render bullet-style category badges inside `.extra-info-wrapper` (e.g. suggested topics list), and the PR provides no justification for dropping this targeted fix.

order() mixin added without establishing a flex parent

`@include order(2);` is added to `.extra-info-wrapper`, but the `order` property only has an effect when the element's parent has `display: flex`. Nothing in this file (or the diff) sets `#topic-title` or any ancestor of `.extra-info-wrapper` to `display: flex`. If the parent isn't a flex container (and none is introduced here), this declaration is dead code that gives a false impression the ordering is being controlled, while the actual rendering order is unaffected.

Non-existent vendor-prefixed property in align-items mixin

The `align-items` mixin emits `-ms-align-items: $alignment;` (line 121). This is not a property that Internet Explorer or any browser ever implemented (the correct and already-present IE10 flexbox alignment prefix is `-ms-flex-align`, on the preceding line). The `-ms-align-items` declaration is dead/invalid CSS that will be silently ignored by all browsers, adding no value and indicating the mixin wasn't verified against actual vendor-prefix requirements.

false_negatives.golden_comment: -ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.
-webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`include_website_name` missing the `?` suffix breaks conditional inclusion

Every other manually-defined inclusion guard in this file follows the `include_#{attr}?` naming convention (e.g. `include_email?`, `include_card_image_badge_id?`, `include_card_image_badge?`, `include_suspend_reason?`), and the `untrusted_attributes`/`private_attributes` macros generate methods named with the trailing `?` as well. The newly added method is defined as `def include_website_name` (no `?`), so the serializer framework never calls it to decide whether to include the `website_name` attribute. As a result, `website_name` is unconditionally serialized for every user (even when `website` is blank, producing a `website_name: null` entry), instead of being gated by `website.present?` as intended.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same core bug: include_website_name lacks the required trailing ? used by Rails serializer inclusion guards, so website_name is not conditionally included. It omits the secondary string-concatenation concern, but the primary issue matches.

false_positives.candidate:
`website_name` is not covered by the `website` untrusted-attribute restriction, leaking site info to low-trust/anonymous viewers

`:website` is listed in `untrusted_attributes`, which hides it from anonymous viewers of TL0 users via `scope.restrict_user_fields?`. The new derived field `website_name` (added at line 43/137) is computed from the same `website` data but is not included in that `untrusted_attributes` list, and its own gate (`include_website_name`, see separate finding) never checks `scope.restrict_user_fields?`. Consequently, even when the raw `website` value is correctly hidden for a restricted viewer, the derived `website_name` (hostname or hostname+path) is still exposed in the API response, leaking information the attribute list was designed to protect.

Untrusted-attribute test does not cover the new `website_name` field

The `untrusted_attributes` array used by the "with a TL0 user seen as anonymous" spec (`%i{bio_raw bio_cooked bio_excerpt location website profile_background card_background}`) was not updated to include `:website_name`. Since `website_name` is derived from the restricted `website` field but is not actually hidden for untrusted/anonymous viewers (see related bug in `user_serializer.rb`), this test gives false confidence that sensitive website data is properly hidden; it does not fail despite the leak.

true_positives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
postMessage origin check uses substring match instead of exact comparison

`discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1` rejects a message only if `e.origin` cannot be found anywhere inside `discourseUrl`. Because `indexOf` performs a substring search rather than an origin equality check, an attacker-controlled origin that is merely a prefix/substring of the real discourseUrl (e.g. `http://example.co` when discourseUrl is `http://example.com/`) will pass this check and be allowed to send `discourse-resize` messages that control the iframe's height, defeating the intended origin restriction.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same origin-validation bug: indexOf performs a substring check rather than exact origin comparison, allowing a crafted origin to bypass the restriction. The examples differ, but the underlying issue is identical.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
X-Frame-Options value 'ALLOWALL' is not a standard directive

The X-Frame-Options header only defines DENY, SAMEORIGIN and ALLOW-FROM <uri> as valid values. 'ALLOWALL' is not part of the spec; some browsers may ignore the unrecognized value (making the header a no-op) while others could treat it conservatively and block framing, which would silently break the embed feature for some users/browsers. Omitting the header (the real intent here) would be the correct way to allow framing by any origin.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same core problem: setting X-Frame-Options to ALLOWALL fails to provide valid clickjacking protection and effectively permits framing. The candidate omits the golden comment's additional referer-spoofing and nil-referer concerns, but it targets the same ALLOWALL header issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
poll_feed assumes every feed item has a non-nil content field

`content = CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` calls `.scrub` directly on `i.content` without checking for nil. Many RSS 2.0 feeds only populate `description` and not a `content`/`content:encoded` element, so SimpleRSS would return nil for `i.content`, causing a NoMethodError that aborts processing of the entire feed for that run (sidekiq_options retry: false means the job silently fails with no retry).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: i.content.scrub is called without a nil check, but many RSS feeds omit content and only provide description, causing a crash/NoMethodError. The candidate describes the same root cause and failure mode even without explicitly prescribing the description fallback.

false_positives.candidate:
Unsanitized raw HTML from imported content rendered directly in embed view

Posts imported via TopicEmbed.import use cook_method raw_html (see app/models/post.rb Post#cook), which causes Post#cook to simply `return raw` and skip PrettyText's sanitization pipeline entirely. That raw content (scraped via Readability from arbitrary remote URLs, or pulled from an RSS/Atom feed) is then rendered unescaped here with `raw post.cooked`. Any script tags or event handlers present in the source page/feed will execute inside the embed iframe (and via postMessage/window.parent access can potentially reach the embedding site). Since the content source is an external, non-Discourse-controlled URL/feed, this is a stored XSS vector that bypasses the normal content-safety pipeline used for all other posts.

Access control relies solely on the client-supplied Referer header

`ensure_embeddable` authorizes embedding purely by comparing `request.referer`'s host to `SiteSetting.embeddable_host`. The Referer header is fully attacker-controlled on non-browser requests (curl, scripts, server-to-server calls), so this check can be trivially bypassed to call `/embed/best`, triggering TopicEmbed/TopicRetriever logic (including outbound HTTP fetches) for arbitrary allowed hosts without ever being embedded on the real site. It also doesn't verify scheme, so http and https referers are treated identically.

Outbound fetch of user-controlled embed_url has no scheme/SSRF restriction

`import_remote` calls `open(url).read` (Kernel#open from open-uri) on a URL that ultimately originates from the public, unauthenticated `embed_url` query parameter in EmbedController#best. The only restriction applied upstream (TopicRetriever#invalid_host?) checks that the URI's host matches SiteSetting.embeddable_host, but the scheme, port, and full path are attacker-controlled. This allows triggering server-side requests to arbitrary ports/paths on the configured host (SSRF), and relies on the Kernel#open/open-uri pattern which is also known to execute shell commands if the string begins with a pipe character — a defense-in-depth concern given this value flows from request params through two layers before reaching open().

Unhandled race condition on unique embed_url constraint

`TopicEmbed.import` checks `embed = TopicEmbed.where(embed_url: url).first` and only creates a new TopicEmbed via `create!` if none exists. There's a unique index on embed_url (see db/migrate/20131217174004_create_topic_embeds.rb), but the check-then-create is not atomic. Two concurrent imports for the same URL (e.g. the hourly PollFeed job and a user-triggered RetrieveTopic job, which can itself invoke PollFeed synchronously — see lib/topic_retriever.rb) can both see `embed.blank?` as true and both attempt `TopicEmbed.create!`, causing one to raise an unhandled ActiveRecord error (RecordNotUnique/RecordInvalid) and crash the job instead of gracefully falling back to the update path.

TopicEmbed.import mutates the caller-supplied contents argument

`contents << "\n<hr>..."` mutates the string object passed in by the caller via the `<<` operator rather than creating a new string. This is a surprising side effect for callers that reuse the string afterward, and will raise a FrozenStringError if the caller passes a frozen string literal (e.g. under `# frozen_string_literal: true`), which is increasingly common in Ruby codebases.

Full feed poll executed synchronously and redundantly on every embed cache miss

`perform_retrieve` calls `Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` directly and synchronously (bypassing Jobs.enqueue) whenever feed polling is enabled and the requested embed isn't found. This means every single unmatched embed request re-fetches and re-processes the *entire* configured RSS/Atom feed inline within the RetrieveTopic job, duplicating the work already done by the hourly scheduled PollFeed job. Under load (many simultaneous first-time embed requests), this can cause repeated, expensive network fetches of the whole feed and increases the window for the race condition described in TopicEmbed.import.

feed_key method is defined but never used

`feed_key` builds a Redis key intended to track feed modification state (e.g. for conditional GET / Last-Modified caching), but it is never referenced anywhere in poll_feed.rb or elsewhere in the diff. This looks like an incomplete feature: the feed is always fully fetched and fully re-processed on every hourly run with no change-detection short-circuit, which is wasteful for large feeds and puts unnecessary load on the external feed source.

Pre-existing migration modified to add force: true

This migration (dated 2013-12-23) already existed prior to this PR and is being edited to add `force: true` to `create_table`. Editing an already-committed migration changes its behavior depending on whether an environment has already run it: environments that ran the old version have a table without the force-drop semantics, while fresh environments running the edited version will drop-and-recreate on every migrate (or fail unexpectedly on table already existing in edge cases). The correct approach is a new migration if the table needs to be recreated, to keep migration history reproducible across all environments.

The `--category`/`-c` method_option and the category-resolution logic were removed entirely, and the topic-creation call was switched from `PostCreator.new(user, title:, raw:, created_at: Date.parse(t[:created_at]), category: category_id)` to `TopicEmbed.import_remote(user, t[:link], title: t[:title])`, which does not accept a category or created_at. This silently drops two previously supported behaviors (assigning an imported thread to a category, and preserving the original Disqus thread's creation date for the topic's first post) with no replacement, which will surprise existing users of this import task.

The spec covers 'missing embeddable_host' and 'missing referer' failure cases, but never exercises the actual host-mismatch branch of `ensure_embeddable` (`URI(request.referer).host != SiteSetting.embeddable_host`), which is the core security check of the controller. A regression in that comparison (e.g. the substring/case-sensitivity issues noted elsewhere) would not be caught by this test suite.

The actual `poll_feed` method — RSS/Atom parsing via SimpleRSS, URL fallback logic, and the `CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` call that can raise on nil content — has no test coverage at all, so bugs such as the nil-content crash noted elsewhere would not be caught.

Transient 'loading' placeholder response is cached for 1 minute like the final content

`discourse_expires_in 1.minute` is applied unconditionally regardless of whether the controller rendered the real topic view or the transient 'loading' placeholder (which itself auto-reloads client-side after 30 seconds, per app/views/embed/loading.html.erb). If this response is cached by any intermediary (browser cache, CDN), the client-side reload after 30s can be served the same stale cached 'loading' page for up to 60 seconds, delaying display of the actual content well past when it became available.

postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

When `allow_animation` is true and the file is a GIF, this routes to `downsize_instructions_animated` → `resize_instructions_animated`, which runs `gifsicle --resize-fit 80%`. Because this logic is now applied directly to the user's original uploaded file (not just to a generated thumbnail), any animated GIF that exceeds `max_image_size_kb` will be silently converted into a static single-frame image before it is ever stored. In-place resize uses the same path for input and output

`OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, ...)` uses the identical path for both the source and destination of the external `convert`/`gifsicle` command. Tools that open the output file for writing (truncating it) before fully reading/processing the input (gifsicle in particular, via `--output`) risk truncating or corrupting the source file before processing completes, resulting in a zero-byte or corrupted temp file being uploaded. A safer pattern is to write to a distinct temporary path and then replace the original once the conversion succeeds.

The loop `while attempt > 0 && tempfile.size > SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` calls `OptimizedImage.downsize` and decrements `attempt`, but never checks the boolean return value of `downsize` (which is false on shell-command failure) nor reports anything if, after 5 attempts, the file is still larger than `max_image_size_kb`. Given the identified risks (gifsicle percentage argument failure, animation stripped from GIFs, in-place file corruption potential, and the changed `OptimizedImage.downsize` method signature), the lack of test coverage leaves these regressions and edge cases unverified before merge.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working-hours boundary check never evaluates the slot's end time

In the new working-hours check added to `checkIfIsAvailable`, both `start` and `end` are computed from `slotStartTime` (`const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();`). `end` should be derived from `slotEndTime` (i.e. slot start + event length) to verify the whole booking fits before the organizer's/fixed host's working hours end. Because `end` duplicates `start`, the check `end > workingHour.endTime` is equivalent to `start > workingHour.endTime`, so a slot whose start is inside the window but whose end (after adding eventLength) extends past the working-hours end time is not flagged as unavailable. This directly undermines the PR's stated goal of correctly respecting a fixed host's hours for round-robin events, allowing bookings that run past a fixed host's actual availability window.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point to the same bug: the working-hours check derives end from slotStartTime rather than slotEndTime, so slots extending past the end are not rejected.

false_positives.candidate:
Dead code: dayjs instances compared with strict equality always evaluate false

`if (dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes"))` compares two freshly created dayjs objects with `===`, which is always false regardless of their represented time, since they are different object references. This branch, apparently intended to detect a zero-duration date override (e.g. representing a fully blocked day), can never trigger. As written this is unreachable/dead logic, and any scenario relying on detecting start === end for an override silently falls through to the later branches instead of being handled as intended.

Date-override day matching depends on implicit server-local timezone

The date-override day match (`dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes").format("YYYY MM DD") === slotStartTime.format("YYYY MM DD")`) builds `dayjs(date.start)` without `.utc()`, so its displayed date/format depends on the Node process's local timezone. `slotStartTime`, however, is explicitly `.utc()`. If the server (or a developer's machine, or CI) is not running with TZ=UTC, this comparison can disagree with the rest of the file, which consistently uses explicit `.utc()`/`.tz()` conversions elsewhere, causing date overrides to be matched to the wrong day or missed entirely depending on deployment environment.

No test covers the primary fix: fixed-host date overrides blocking round-robin slots

The PR description states its main purpose is to make date overrides of fixed hosts taken into account for round-robin events so slots aren't offered when a fixed host is unavailable. The only test changes add a second timezone assertion to the existing single-user 'Check for Date overrides' test (no scheduling type / no hosts). There is no new test combining a ROUND_ROBIN event with a fixed host that has a date override and a non-fixed round-robin host that is available, to verify that the slot is excluded. Given the newly added/changed availability logic in `checkIfIsAvailable` (working hours and date-override checks per fixed host) contains at least one concrete bug (see other findings), this is exactly the scenario that should have automated coverage but does not.

Override timezone offset computed from a field that is typed optional without a fallback

`const organizerUtcOffset = dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone).utcOffset();` passes `override.timeZone` directly to `.tz()`. `TimeRange.timeZone` (packages/types/schedule.d.ts) is declared optional (`timeZone?: string`), so nothing in the type system guarantees it is set. If any caller of `getSlots`/`getTimeSlots` supplies `dateOverrides` without a `timeZone` (the field was only newly introduced and is only populated by the one call site touched in this PR), `.tz(undefined)` will silently fall back to some default/local timezone behavior rather than failing, producing incorrect offsets and therefore incorrect override slot times instead of a clear error.

Override offset adjustment can cross midnight but only the time-of-day is kept

The new override start/end computation shifts `override.start`/`override.end` by `offset` minutes (the difference between invitee and organizer UTC offsets) and then extracts only `.hour() * 60 + .minute()`. When the offset difference between organizer and invitee pushes the adjusted time across a day boundary (common for large timezone differences, e.g. near the International Date Line), the date portion is discarded and only the wrapped time-of-day is kept, which can make the override appear to apply on the wrong day or produce an incorrect time window instead of being excluded/moved to the adjacent day.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Non-atomic retryCount increment can race across concurrent cron invocations

Both the success-path failure branch (line ~184) and the catch block (line ~195) update retryCount by computing `reminder.retryCount + 1` in application code from a value fetched earlier in the same request, rather than using Prisma's atomic `{ increment: 1 }`. If the cron endpoint is invoked more than once concurrently (e.g. duplicate cron triggers, retried HTTP calls, multiple instances), two processes can read the same stale retryCount and write the same incremented value, losing an update. This means a reminder could fail many more than twice yet never reach retryCount > 1, defeating the intended cleanup logic and leaving broken reminders stuck in the scheduling loop indefinitely.

retryCount deletion branch is not scoped to SMS method

The new OR clause `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` in the deleteMany call has no `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` filter, unlike the sibling condition. The function is documented/intended to operate only on SMS reminders, but as written it will delete ANY WorkflowReminder row (EMAIL, WHATSAPP, SMS) whose retryCount happens to exceed 1, regardless of method. Since `retryCount` is a shared column on the WorkflowReminder model (not SMS-specific), any future code path that increments retryCount for non-SMS reminders (or any data migration/bug that sets retryCount>1) will cause this cron job to silently delete unrelated email/whatsapp reminders. false_positives.candidate:
Transient errors are treated the same as permanent failures, causing premature deletion of valid reminders

Any error thrown while scheduling the SMS (network blip, Twilio rate limiting/outage, temporary API failure, etc.) increments retryCount exactly the same way as a permanent failure like an invalid phone number. Because the cron runs repeatedly and only allows 2 failures before the reminder is deleted (deleteMany with retryCount > 1), a short period of transient Twilio/network issues across two consecutive cron runs will cause legitimate, otherwise-valid workflow reminders to be permanently deleted before the scheduled date, even though the underlying booking/reminder was fine. The comment above the deleteMany call still reads "delete all scheduled sms reminders where scheduled date is past current date", but the query now also deletes any reminder (regardless of method, see related finding) whose retryCount exceeds 1. The comment was not updated to describe this second deletion condition, which will mislead future maintainers reading only the comment about what rows are removed.

No tests added for new retry/deletion behavior

This PR introduces a behavioral change (failed SMS reminders are now deleted after two failures) that affects data integrity (permanent deletion of WorkflowReminder rows). No unit/integration tests were added to verify that retryCount increments correctly on failure, that reminders are deleted only after exceeding the retry threshold, or that successful sends are unaffected. A user who manually types a valid backup code on a mobile device can have it silently mismatched and rejected as 'incorrect', even though the code is correct.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: backup code comparison is case-sensitive (indexOf/exact match) while generated codes are lowercase hex, so uppercase input (e.g. mobile auto-capitalization) is incorrectly rejected. The candidate adds normalization/autoCapitalize details but points to the same issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup code validation/consumption has a check-then-update race (TOCTOU)

The backup-code login path reads `user.backupCodes`, decrypts it, checks `indexOf` for a match, then later re-encrypts and writes back the array with the used code nulled out (lines 139-156). There is no transaction, row lock, or optimistic version check between the read and the write. If two requests for the same user run concurrently (e.g. a double-submitted login or two tabs), both can read the same pre-update state, both pass the `index !== -1` check, and whichever update runs last overwrites the other's change — meaning the single-use guarantee promised by the UI text ('Each backup code can be used exactly once') can be violated: a single code can authenticate more than once, or one of two different codes used concurrently can end up still marked as unused.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same check-then-update race in backup-code consumption, where concurrent requests can validate and consume the same code before the update is persisted, violating one-time-use semantics.

true_positives.golden_comment: Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup-codes download Blob URL can leak if setup is cancelled before completion

`handleSetup` creates a Blob URL via `URL.createObjectURL` for the backup codes (lines 94-99) and only revokes the previous URL the next time `handleSetup` succeeds (`if (backupCodesUrl) URL.revokeObjectURL(backupCodesUrl)`). `resetState()` (line 71-75), which runs when the user clicks 'Cancel' at any step or 'Close' after viewing backup codes, does not revoke `backupCodesUrl`. If the user cancels after the password step succeeded (so a Blob URL was created) but before starting setup again, or simply finishes the flow, the object URL is never revoked and the Blob remains referenced for the lifetime of the page, which is a minor memory leak that is easy to avoid by revoking in `resetState`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same memory leak: the backup-codes Blob object URL created via URL.createObjectURL is never revoked on the cleanup path (unmount/reset/cancel), leaving the Blob referenced. The candidate's wording about resetState/cancel is a semantic match for the golden's unmount cleanup concern.

false_positives.candidate:
Backup codes are stored with reversible symmetric encryption instead of being hashed

Backup codes are encrypted with `symmetricEncrypt`/`symmetricDecrypt` using `CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY` (setup.ts line 68, next-auth-options.ts lines 140/154) rather than hashed. Unlike TOTP secrets, backup codes never need to be redisplayed after generation, so they should be hashed (similar to passwords) rather than stored reversibly. Anyone who obtains the DB plus the single symmetric encryption key (which protects many other secrets) can recover every user's plaintext backup codes, which is a stronger blast radius than necessary for a one-time-use credential.

"missing_backup_codes" message points to a non-existent settings feature

The new string `"missing_backup_codes": "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings."` is shown to users on login/disable when no backup codes exist, but this PR provides no settings UI or endpoint to regenerate backup codes after 2FA has been enabled — the only way to get new backup codes is to disable and re-enable 2FA entirely (which re-runs the setup flow). Telling users to 'generate them in your settings' is misleading and will create support confusion since no such control exists.

Previously, a successful TOTP verification called `onEnable()` immediately, letting the parent page refresh its 2FA-enabled state. Now, on success the code only does `setStep(SetupStep.DisplayBackupCodes)` (line 135); `onEnable()` is deferred until the user explicitly clicks the new 'Close' button on the backup-codes screen (around line 267). At this point 2FA is already enabled on the server (the enable API call already succeeded). If the user dismisses the dialog any other way (Escape key, clicking the overlay, closing the tab) before clicking 'Close', the parent component's `onEnable` callback never fires, leaving the UI out of sync with the backend (e.g. a toggle/switch that still shows 2FA as disabled even though it is enabled) until the page is reloaded.

No e2e coverage added for logging in or disabling 2FA with a backup code

This PR implements an entirely new authentication path (logging in via backup code) and a new disable path (disabling 2FA via backup code), but the only test addition related to these flows is a `// TODO: add more backup code tests, e.g. login + disabling 2fa with backup` comment. The existing tests only exercise download/copy/close of the backup-codes dialog during setup; the actual consumption of a backup code to log in or to disable 2FA (including the single-use/invalidation behavior) is left completely untested, despite being the core new feature of this PR.

FIXME comment added but the broken assertion is left unfixed

A new comment at line 50-51 explicitly documents that `await expect(page.locator('[data-testid=two-factor-switch]').isChecked()).toBeTruthy()` passes even when the switch is not checked (because `.isChecked()` returns an unawaited Promise, which is always truthy). The PR acknowledges this is broken but ships it unfixed, so the 'Enable 2FA' step in this test does not actually verify that the switch became checked, reducing confidence in the enable-2FA regression coverage that this PR also modifies.

`const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` followed by `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration !== "google_calendar"` accesses `.integration` without an optional chain. true_positives.golden_comment: Logic inversion in organization creation: The slug property is now conditionally set when IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED is true, instead of when it's false as originally intended. Inverted condition for assigning organization slug vs requiring billing

The condition for setting the `slug` field was changed from `...(!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug })` to `...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {})`, inverting the original intent. However, the nested recurring-event branch (lines 444-468) that deletes every remaining recurring booking instance from `bookingToDelete.user.credentials` and `updatedBookings` is executed on every iteration of the outer loop. After building `evt`, the code does `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars);` guarded only for COLLECTIVE events. `evt.destinationCalendar` is set to `null` when neither `eventType.destinationCalendar` nor `organizerUser.destinationCalendar` exists. In that case the optional chaining makes `push` a no-op, so the destination calendars collected for the other (non-organizer) hosts in `teamDestinationCalendars` are silently discarded and those hosts never receive calendar invites for a collective event. This is exactly the multi-host scenario the PR claims to fix, so the fix fails for organizers without a configured destination calendar.

organization.slug dropped from the dynamic-booking user select without apparent replacement

In the rewritten `loadUsers` function, the `prisma.user.findMany` select for the dynamic (no-eventTypeId) booking path used to include `organization: { select: { slug: true } }`, but this field was removed in the rewrite (only `...userSelect.select, credentials: true, metadata: true` remain). If any downstream logic in the dynamic booking flow (e.g. building org-aware links or multi-tenant routing) relies on `user.organization.slug`, it will now silently be `undefined`. This field removal is unrelated to the stated purpose of the PR (destinationCalendar array support) and looks like an unintentional regression.

No test coverage added for the actual multi-host destinationCalendar behavior

The PR converts `destinationCalendar` to an array across ~20 files and changes behavior for collective events with multiple hosts, but the only test changes are updates to expected JSON shape (`destinationCalendar: null` -> `destinationCalendar: []`) in existing single-host webhook e2e tests. The PR description itself states 'I haven't added tests that prove my fix is effective or that my feature works.' There is no test verifying that a collective event with two hosts using different calendar credentials actually results in calendar invites being created in each host's correct calendar — the exact scenario this PR is meant to fix, and the area where several of the above bugs (e.g. non-Google calendar providers always using host #1's calendar) would have been caught.

Inconsistent empty-value representation for destinationCalendar across handlers

Different handlers normalize a missing destination calendar differently now that the field is an array: `confirm.handler.ts` (line 179), `webhook.ts`, `paypal-webhook.ts`, and `deleteCredential.handler.ts` fall back to `[]`, while `handleNewBooking.ts` falls back to `null`. Consumers of the webhook payload (and any other code reading `evt.destinationCalendar`) now observe different representations (`null` vs `[]`) for the logically identical 'no destination calendar' state depending on which code path produced the event, which is an inconsistent contract that can break strict-equality checks or type assumptions downstream.

Hangout-link patch call can target an undefined calendarId

In `createEvent`, the initial `calendar.events.insert` call uses `calendarId: selectedCalendar || "primary"`, defaulting to `"primary"` when no destination calendar matches the current `credentialId`. However, the follow-up `calendar.events.patch(...)` call made when a hangout link is present (line 168) uses the raw `calendarId: selectedCalendar` without the same `|| "primary"` fallback. If no destination calendar entry matches the credential (so `selectedCalendar` is `undefined`), the event is inserted into `"primary"` but the subsequent patch to add the hangout link to the description targets an undefined calendar id, which will likely fail silently or error out, leaving the event without the hangout link update.

The Calendar interface now requires createEvent(event, credentialId), but some implementations (e.g., Lark/Office365) still declare createEvent(event) only—this breaks the interface contract (also applies to other locations in the PR).

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
forEach with async callback no longer reliably initiates calendar deletion before later steps run

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => {...})` now calls `await getCalendar(...)` inside the callback (previously `getCalendar` was synchronous). Array.prototype.forEach never waits for promises returned by its callback, so once getCalendar became async, the loop body suspends at the `await` and the surrounding `forEach` call returns before any of the calendar deletion requests are even issued. Execution then proceeds to `await sendRequestRescheduleEmail(...)` and the function returns `true`, with no guarantee that the calendar/video deletion calls have started, let alone completed. Previously, since getCalendar was synchronous, the deletion request was synchronously kicked off inside the loop before any later code executed. Additionally, the enclosing try/catch (lines 124-139) cannot catch errors thrown inside these detached async callbacks, so failures become unhandled promise rejections instead of being logged. Net effect: a reschedule can report success and send the reschedule email while the old calendar/video events are still pending deletion or were never actually requested to be deleted in time.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the candidate and reference concern the same bug: forEach with async callbacks does not await promises, so calendar/video cleanup work can race ahead of completion and errors escape the surrounding try/catch as unhandled rejections. The candidate's extra detail about getCalendar becoming async is consistent with that root cause.

false_positives.candidate:
Dynamic imports are evaluated eagerly, defeating the purpose of lazy loading

All entries of the appStore object are built with `import("./appname")` calls placed directly inside an object literal. Because this literal is evaluated once, synchronously, as soon as the module is first loaded, every one of the ~26 dynamic import() calls fires immediately and in parallel, exactly like the previous static imports. None of them is deferred until the specific app is actually needed. As a result, every consumer (getCalendar, videoClient, handleCancelBooking, etc.) still triggers loading of all app packages up front, but now each access additionally requires an `await`, adding complexity and promise-resolution overhead without achieving true on-demand/lazy loading. To actually defer loading, each entry would need to be a function returning the import (e.g. `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")`), invoked only when that specific app is required.

Example comment references a non-existent module path

The comment `// example: import("./example"),` doesn't match the actual folder name. The previous code's commented-out import referenced `"./_example"` (with a leading underscore), which is the real folder used to keep the example app excluded from the registry. If a developer later copies this comment to register a new app, it will point at a module that doesn't exist.

forEach with async callback no longer reliably initiates calendar deletion before later steps run

Same issue as in vital/lib/reschedule.ts: `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => {...})` now awaits the newly-async `getCalendar(...)` inside the callback, but forEach does not wait for the returned promises. The loop no longer guarantees the calendar/video deletion requests are even started before the function continues to send the reschedule email and returns. The surrounding try/catch also cannot catch rejections raised inside these detached async callbacks.

requestReschedule forEach no longer waits for (or even reliably starts) calendar/video deletion before sending the reschedule email and webhooks

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => {...})` was previously a synchronous callback that called `getCalendar` synchronously, so the deletion request was always issued inside the loop before the mutation continued. Now `getCalendar` is awaited inside the async callback, and since forEach ignores the promises returned by async callbacks, the deletion requests may not even be initiated before the code proceeds to `await sendRequestRescheduleEmail(...)` and subsequently dispatches BOOKING_CANCELLED webhooks. This changes the ordering guarantees of the reschedule flow and can leave stale calendar/video events behind while users are already notified of the reschedule.

Nested forEach(async) race widened by newly-async getCalendar, risking dropped deletions from final Promise.all

In the recurring-event branch, `bookingToDelete.user.credentials.filter(...).forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); ... apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent); })` is not awaited by the surrounding code. `apiDeletes` is only consolidated and awaited much later via `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` (line ~652), relying on other intervening awaits in the function to give these detached async callbacks enough time to push their results. Converting the previously-synchronous `getCalendar` call to `await getCalendar(credential)` adds an extra asynchronous hop before each callback even starts its inner loop, widening the race window during which `apiDeletes` may not yet contain the recurring-booking's calendar deletion promises when the final Promise.all executes, risking recurring-booking calendar events that are never actually deleted on cancellation.

getVideoAdapters resolves credentials sequentially instead of in parallel

The rewritten `getVideoAdapters` uses a `for...of` loop with `await appStore[appName as keyof typeof appStore]` inside, resolving each credential's app module one at a time rather than concurrently (e.g. via `Promise.all`). For bookings with multiple video credentials this unnecessarily serializes independent promise resolutions on every call to createMeeting/updateMeeting/deleteMeeting/getBusyVideoTimes, adding avoidable latency compared to a parallelized implementation.

No tests cover the new async appStore / getCalendar / getVideoAdapters behavior

This PR converts appStore's values to Promises and makes getCalendar, getVideoAdapters, and getCalendarCredentials asynchronous, touching booking cancellation, rescheduling, calendar/video event creation, and payment flows across many files. Several of these changes introduce race conditions around unresolved promises inside `Array.prototype.forEach` callbacks (see findings on vital/wipemycalother reschedule.ts, bookings.tsx, and handleCancelBooking.ts). No unit or integration tests were added or updated to verify that calendar/video events are still correctly created, updated, and deleted during these flows after the conversion, so these regressions would not be caught by CI.
